You cannot overwinter a Japanese maple indoors under living conditions comfortable to you. Bringing it inside pushed it out of its required dormancy and into its regular warm season growth mode. If it is too cold to remain outside over winter, then it needs to be moved into a protected location but one that stays above freezing but below 45F. Something like an unheated greenhouse, insulated shed or unheated but attached garage. Or depending on your location/hardiness zone, you could dig a hole and bury the container. You just cannot treat it like a houseplant...it is NOT!

Woodpeckers look for bugs, so those holes mean that you likely have some bugs inside your tree.  That said, I have a willow with an incredible number of holes and lots of woodpecker activity on most days, but it's been doing just fine for decades. On the other hand, it could be from sapsuckers.  They generally don't do much damage, but provide an entry for bugs and diseases.

I have done a lot of work with Photoshop but others may beg to differ and offer you something.  Your photo will be a challenge to Photoshop. It's difficult without spending LOTS of time, to replace or paint over those types of shadings.  Photoshopping is essentially replacing one color with another, so replacing a graded shade is tough.

Is there a basement under the Kitchen or are you on a slab?  If a basement, it's not that difficult or expensive to move water of gas lines and would give you more options. However, if you're on a slab, it will cost more b/c you will have to break into the slab.  You can probably move water or gas a foot or two to either side, but not much more.  If you're redoing the floors (it doesn't sound like you are), it may be worth it if you plan to change the layout. Cindy, from the internet: The main symbol of Opatija is the"Girl with a Seagull" statue. The statue was erected in 1956 by the sculptor Zvonko Tsara and is an example of modern culture. It is located on the seashore. There is a legend that seagulls are the souls of sailors who did not return from the sea. And in the city of Opatija there is a seagull who is"in love" with the sculpture. They say that a couple in love lived on the coast for a long time. The young sailor went to sea and never returned. Beloved throughout her life was waiting for him, and every day she went to the seashore. Seeing such love, it was decided to erect a monument - a sculpture of a young woman with a seagull in her hands. After some time, a seagull began to circle over the monument. She sat on the sculpture for a long time, not allowing other birds to approach her. Locals believe that this soul of a young sailor has returned.

Your house is very pretty! I've always been quite partial to this type of traditional ranch, with the decorative metal railings and the shutters. Such a sweet and timeless look.  I hope you embrace and maintain the style integrity, inside and out. You've gotten some great suggestions for paint colors and landscaping.  Painting the metal decorations and railings in a darker color would show them off nicely, too.  Semi-gloss or gloss looks better on the metal than a flat finish. Yes, the walkway needs a power wash, and edging.  A beautiful traditional look is to paint the walkway, and the porch steps/floor/foundation, too, if it is concrete.  Traditional colors for this are red, green, or gray, but probably others would look good also. I'd remove the front hedges completely.  They just hide your beautiful house.  Long term it is easier to maintain your structure if there are no shrubs, trees, or flower beds right up against the foundation.  Elsewhere in the yard is fine for plantings.  Colorful plants near the entryway in one or two containers are very welcoming and easier to maintain than hedges. There is a house in my own neighborhood that is not in the least trendy, but looks like something or other on it gets polished every. single. day.  It has the best curb appeal of them all!

”You have eleven feet. You do not have room for island OR the 12 inch depth cabinetry.“ Hmmm...  the OP has 137.5”. Which is 24” cabinet wall + 42” isle + 24” island + 36” isle + 12” cabinet wall = -.5”.  So steal 1/4” from each isle and you will be fine. Isles were at least 36” and then someone noticed 42” was a bit better and so they became at least 42”… now we are at least 48” apparently.  I don’t know what  the right answer is, but I do know that the lion’s share of kitchens don’t have 48” isles.  I also know that I agree with the OP’s idea of an island and cabinets on both walls because anything else is a giant waste of space. However, if you are concerned grab a couple of scratch and dent cabinets and create an island at 42” and see how you like it, I did that with IKEA cabinets when we were planning.  If that is too much money get a bunch of 24x18x18 moving boxes from Lowes.  Stack them two high and as wide as you need and then see how it feels working around them.  I am fine with 42” walkways, others may not be.

" what can I do to affect the end of season color? " Not much, really. While the chemical composition of the soil will determine in-season flower color, the coloration they develop at the end of the season is more a factor of siting and climate. Not too much sun, not too much heat, adequate irrigation, etc. What you can do is attempt to alter the in-season flower color to a uniformly lightish blue - no purple or pink. You can control the initial bloom color of a mophead hydrangea by soil pH control as long as the variety does not produce white blooms but after 1-2 months, they will begin a series of color changes that are less related to soil pH and more to the variety being grown, nutrients, weather factors, etc. Those are difficult to control factors. Be aware that if you do not happen to like a certain color during this progression of colors, you can deadhead them bloom by cutting it above the first pair of leaves without affecting future blooms in spring. And no, you will typically not get a second bloom in the same growing season from the stem if you deadhead; but you will normally get a bloom next spring. I would ask for a few cuttings when you see any hydrangea that produces those shades of color and then see if/how ell they replicate in your different soil nutrients, sun exposure, weather, etc.

If you are going to walk around your wrap around porch, you need room for furniture plus 3’.  Adirondack chairs need a lot of space because the legs sprawl, couches/love seats may look crammed in if the porch is too narrow.  If your porch furniture is more petite, you can get away with a more narrow space.  If you want conversation areas, it needs to be wider so the seating can angle otherwise you are sitting shoulder to shoulder like at the movies.

Several thoughts: - The person above who says the porch must be proportional to the house is 100% right.  Without knowing whether you're building a cute little cottage or a Southern mansion, we're all stabbing in the dark. - Are we talking about a true wrap-around porch that'll literally circle the whole house?  If so, do consider that you're making your first-floor rooms dark, as the porches will block natural light.  Back before air conditioning, this was a desirable thing in the South. - Consider that the porches on the four sides don't need to be equal.  Consider how you'll use each side ... perhaps you'll want just a couple rocking chairs and a table near the front door "to look inviting", but you'll want a wider back porch to provide cover for a dining table.  And you might want the sides "just for show".  Think through how you'll use the spaces, and you'll come to the right conclusions. - Go down to Lowes and walk through their patio furniture ... since it's March now, they'll certainly have nice stuff sitting out.  Take your tape measure and see how much space you'd need for this or that set ... over the years you'll certainly own multiple sets, but this'll give you an idea of how much space you need for a two-person seating area vs. a dining table.  Allow for walking space around your furniture groupings. - The best thing about a wrap-around porch is that a toddler can ride her tricycle allll the way around the house.

What bothers me about the stone dormer over the garage is that it really makes no sense from an architectural standpoint.  In real life you would never put a very heavy material (stone) over a lighter material (wood).  You would also never see a wood house with a stone dormer.  Traditionally, houses that are a mix of stone and wood either have stone on the lower half of the house and wood above it, or separate sections for each material.  While this is veneer and therefore weight is not an issue, it just looks silly to me and emphasizes the fact that it's either a veneer or fake stone. Many (most?) people probably would never have that thought and would think it's fine, though.  And I don't really see the point in spending money to remove it or adding stone to the garage.  The house's overall architectural style is not trying to look classic or authentic so this inauthentic detail doesn't really affect it one way or the other.

The more climate friendly refrigerants are flammable and cannot be installed in residential homes under the current fire building codes.  The American Innovation and Manufacturing (AIM) Act approved by Congress in 2020 authorizes the EPA to begin the phase out of R410a. However the neither Congress or the EPA have come up with a solution how to make the installation of a flammable refrigerant safe in a residential home. I would think after four years the fire prevention solutions have been discussed by the people who write the building codes. I suspect what the code officials believe what will be required will be expensive and not practical for many homes.

"The more climate friendly refrigerants are flammable and cannot be installed in residential homes under the current fire building codes."   .  A number of states have already approved the use of A2L refrigerants in their residential building code including Oregon, Florida, Washington, and North Carolina.  The ICC, which produces the International Residential Code, has language in the 2024 IRC allowing the use of A2L refrigerants.  The expectation is that most, if not all, states will have their building codes modified prior to January 1, 2025. The bottom line is that the phase down of R410a and the transition to other refrigerants isn't the end of life on earth as we know it despite the fear mongering.

My own parents have been gone for 18 years. Prior to deaths a mere seven weeks apart, they were together in assisted living. Their unit was quite compact . We had two twin beds, mom had her favorite chair, dad had his recliner. A table between, a small buffet with the tv, and a small drop leaf table with two chairs for dining in. I was there every single morning as nobody but me or one supremely helpful sister could get mom into the shower. In all, they were residents for 18 months and provided me a literal tutorial on how to get the best care, anywhere. It is to the best of your ability, a focus on that which truly matters. It is your presence. I was asked so very often, this question: " I thought you put them somewhere?!" "Yes, I did. They were not safe at home. It got beyond all our capabilities to manage both conditions. It got well beyond exhausting. But............this is respite, easing of continual anxiety,  not the absolute ABSOLVE". Our continual presence made allies and friends of the skilled help, and their care when we were not present was indeed wonderful. The bumps in the first few weeks were smoothed in short order - bonds were formed. It's just the way it is. You will find you need your family, your friends - you just need a damn village : ) All of that takes precedence over decor , which you soon come to realize is nearly irrelevant by comparison.

I did about the same as Seaborman.  I used a combination of foam from 1" through 2" thick. Sometimes it's easier to cut 1" thick pieces to get into some spaces so I'll do it in layers caulking the edges between layers to insure air tightness.  With foam you must make sure all the edges are sealed so warm moist air doesn't get in between the foam and rim joist and using Spray foam or caulking will do the job and I use both. You shouldn't use fiberglass insulation around the rim joists unless it can completely be sealed inside the cavity to keep inside moist air out to avoid condensation, and nearly impossible to do.  Rim joists are the boards around the exterior of the house the walls sit on, and if they rot out it's extremely  expensive to repair.  Your 100 years old  rim joists haven't rotted out because it's not insulated, but if it's insulated wrong it will rot out, so beware.

"I guess I need to install the cabinets first to determine how to position the lighting." No, there is no guesswork here.  Correct placement of undercabinet lighting is toward the front of the upper cabinets, just behind the light rail.  That way, the light is shed onto the center of the counter beneath it, where it is most useful.  If you install the undercabinet lighting toward the back, you are lighting mostly the backsplash where the light is not needed.  That's a lot of money to spend on undercabinet lighting to light the backsplash.  Furthermore, when you place the undercabinet lighting just behind the light rail (which you are calling a "valance", but it should be a light rail), you will not see it from a seated position. I do not know why you are installing new LED undercabinet lighting in that big bulky housing.  One of the major advantages of LED undercabinet lighting is how low-profile and slim it is.  I do like a diffuser on LED undercabinet lighting, but you need to shop for better quality than what you are showing.  Better quality meaning a modern slim-profile LED undercabinet light. "The entire kitchen will have close to 4000K light." What does "close to 4000K” mean?  Is it 4000K or not?  In any case, an entire kitchen lit by 4000K light is a surgery operating room, not a kitchen.  4000K is fine for your undercabinet lighting, but your overhead lighting should be a more comfortable 2700K or 3000K. "Any suggestions as to how that valance should be designed and sized are welcome." Typically a cabinet manufacturer or woodworker provides a light rail (it's not a valance) that goes with the design of the cabinets.  I.e. they can be designed with different profiles, such as just plain flat, or in Shaker style, or more ornate with beading and other embellishments that match the cabinetry.  Light rails range in thickness, depending on the design of the cabinets, typically 3/4" to 1-1/2" but there are other thicknesses too. "I know this is not ideal, but I ALWAYS hit my head on upper cabinet doors and they won’t be used much anyway." I do not believe this, sorry.  When you open a closet door, does it hit your body?  No, you step back.  When you open a base cabinet door, does that door hit your legs?  No, you step back.   When you open an upper cabinet door near to your head, do you just stand there and whack yourself in the head?  How is that possible?   Look, if you don't want upper cabinets, don't get them, lots of people don't get upper kitchen cabinets.  It's nothing rare or innovative.

all plants/roots need air.. as much as moisture... air circulation is  imperative with every plant... lack of air on roots is a bog.. where  little grows .. other than bog plants.. its also why so many plants fail  or fail to thrive in non draining clay soils.... you would use a plastic bag.. to increase humidity... but the is  no reason to seal the bag... i usually set the pot in the bottom.. and  stand the bag up.. open... sooo.. i suggest.. with further attempts..  dont seal the bag shut.. and you will probably have less issues with rot  and bad things happening... that said.. as noted above.. go for it.. whats to lose??? .. keep us posted... i would probably also harden it off.. dont just rip it from the  bag... and move it out to a low humidity furnace dry house... do it over  a few days or week ... sooo.. damp media.. pot it.. put it back in an open  back for a  few weeks while the water roots turn into soil/media roots... this will  stress them.. so make it easy for them ... again.. keep us posted.. ken

I have known mail carriers and here is the deal, City routes and rural routes are managed differently so YMMV. The black wall tile in the picture is laid using a 1/3 offset.  It's not unusual for 12 X 24" tiles to require this.  I think it looks fine on the gray wall.  I had to look at it a minute to see what they had done.  In your bathroom I don't know that I would do it that way (vertically).  If you want a vertical pattern, use a smaller tile on the shower walls and the larger size on the floor.  The shower floor should be an even smaller size so it will slope to the drain correctly.  When you use 12 X 24" tiles you (or your tilesetter) will have to use the offset specified by the manufacturer. Here are some pictures showing smaller vertical tiles in the shower and larger tile on the floor.  Also two pictures showing shower floors with small tiles.  If you're interested in a sleek, modern look, use the same tile in different sizes.  You can also lay the larger size horizontally on shower walls if you don't like the smaller size.  Smaller tiles laid vertically with no offset is a modern look.

A reduction in the flow of auxin across the abscission zone where the leaf is attached to the branch is the primary driver of the shedding process. A certain level of auxin flow is essential to keep an abscission layer from forming at the leaf attachment point. Anything that reduces the flow of auxin through the abscission zone brings with it the potential for shedding of foliage. Chill (especially sudden), a decrease in light intensity/duration, soil solution issues (too much or too little), nutritional deficiencies, root congestion, poor root health or disease, insect herbivory and diseases, are all cultural influences that can work individually or collectively to slow the flow rate of auxin and cause an abscission layer to form. The abscission layer is a corky layer that eventually forms a wall between a leaf and the living plant. Once it has formed, no water or nutrients can make way into the plant, and no photosynthate (food/sugar) can be moved from an affected leaf to other plant organs; so, the commonly held idea that dead leaves of branches can somehow rob living parts of the tree of resources like water, nutrients, or photosynthate is not valid. The only benefits that can be ascribed to early removal of dead/dying branches/leaves would come in the form of greater light penetration and air movement to the within the confines of the plant's outline (closer to the trunk). There is no problem in shaking the tree or gently tugging on a leaf to see if it is ready to be shed. Leaves that don't fall as a result of a jostle or gentle tug, but are obviously dead, should be removed by cutting through the leaf petiole with a pair of scissors so there is no risk of damage to the area in leaf axils where dormant/latent buds are waiting to be activated. This would be immediately distal to (above) where the leaf is attached. Ficus benjamina does not like to be moved, even from one spot in your home to another and will lose a lot of leaves. This paints with a brush too broad. Generally speaking, leaf loss resulting from repositioning a tree only occurs when the tree is moved to a spot with appreciably lower light, which reduces the flow of auxin across the abscission zone. Moving a tree to brighter light doesn't often cause shedding of foliage UNLESS to leaf itself is incapable of adapting to the increase in light. Something I wrote about the topic: Light Acclimatization The degree to which a leaf can 'acclimate' to changes in photo load is limited. IOW, you can't expect a leaf that emerged under a full sun light load to acclimate to light levels in a dim corner, any more than you can expect a leaf that emerged in a dim corner to acclimate to a full sun site; this, no matter how long you allow for gradual acclimation. Too, the plant's ability to adapt to higher light loads is greater than its ability to adapt to lesser light loads. Using a 1-10 numerical example to illustrate (numerical value of 1 is low light, 10 is high light): If a leaf emerges where the light level is measured at 5 units, it's range of adjustment might only be to 3.5 on the low side, but 8 to 8.5 on the high side. When the level of adjustment required is greater than what the plant is genetically programmed to deal with, the leaf is shed, and this can occur with conspicuous or relatively inconspicuous damage to the leaf. While shed leaves can never be replaced, per se, new branches can form (with new leaves along the new branches) in the axils of dying leaves or from latent buds immediately above scars left by shed leaves. Too, whenever a new leaf appears it will be perfectly acclimated to whatever the photo load is where the plant is positioned (within the limits of what it is genetically programmed to tolerate). Al

You're referring to: "The first phase of leaf abscission (shedding) is resorption, during which the plant extracts and repurposes nutrients which are mobile in the plant (nitrogen, phosphorous, potassium, magnesium) and other biocompounds." You'll notice that when magnesium is reclaimed from leaves it causes breakdown of the green pigment chlorophyll; this, because magnesium is central to the chlorophyll molecule. When chlorophyll molecules are broken down, chlorophyll can no longer mask colors provided by the other pigments, so the yellows, reds, and oranges, of the carotenoids become expressive. Once the abscission layer has formed, exchange of nutrients and other biocompounds across the abscission zone is no longer possible. IOW, all resorption occurs before the abscission layer is complete. Once complete, the leaves provide no advantage to the plant and can be removed. Trees vary significantly in how tenaciously the leaves remain connected to the plant. My neighbor has a very tall Fagus sylvatica 'Fastigiata' (pyramidal/ columnar beech) which still holds onto all of it's 2023 foliage. If the leaves were to be plucked from this particular tree, there would be significant probability that some latent buds would be damaged. Species in the genus Carpinus (hornbeam) are another plant that, though entirely deciduous, often hold their leaves until the spring push is underway. So, for these species, I do all leaf removal with a pair of defoliating shears.  Al

Wolf is beautifully made, but just cooks with hot air blowing around. Its as good as any hot air ie fan based cooker, its made to last, and easy to operate, slide out food, look at it while its cooking, and its temperatue accuracy is superb. Same with the cook top accuracy and controls. The AGA is totally different. Firstly the size issue: its oven do not have fans, instead its sides are cast iron. So the oven appear small, but they very deep, and the slide holder are part of the cast iron sides. So there is no wasted space. You slide in a tray of food on top of the cast iron ridges - which is not like a fance telescoping tray support in a Wolf. You have to pull an AGA tray out from the stove. However, any person can do that. The cast iron holds and radiates heat, which cooks differently to hot air (which is an insulator). An AGA cooks more like a BBQ kettle - they also use radiated heat. But an AGA has more even heat, and its temperature is consisentant, unlike a BBQ. Because of the few AGA controls, one cooks differently. If more than one oven is on, you might find the food is cooking quicker than you planned - so you can shift to another oven. And changing the oven or temperature will not hurt the cooking because radiant heat retains the moisture. There are no windows in an AGA oven either, so you open a door and have a look. Or push a temperature gauge into the food. Leaving the door open doesn't stop the cooking, as its radiant heat and the food keeps cooking - except from the door you've opened. With the Wolf, the fan stops when you open the door, and the cooking is greatly effected - its best to look through the glass door. AGAs also don't need normal cleaning - you brush them out. They are versatile too. If you like cooking, and are imaginative, and AGA is great. If not, the Wolf is a better choice. IMO the Wolf should have steam, but it seems they don't.

It's been only four years that I've been growing roses -- mostly old garden roses -- in Iowa, but I am beginning to be able to make some generalizations about hardiness.  I can attest that the following cultivars, once established, will survive a Zone 5 winter unscathed, or with very limited tip damage: 'Ardoisée de Lyon' Rosa blanda 'Charles de Mills' 'Erinnerung an Brod' Rosa glauca 'Isabella Skinner' 'Königin von Dänemark' 'Madame Hardy' 'Nuits de Young' 'Reine des Violettes' "Rose de Rescht" 'Shailer's Provence' 'Stanwell Perpetual' 'Tuscany Superb' 'Urdh' 'William III' 'Yolande d'Aragon' 'Zigeunerknabe' Though they are often rated to Zone 5b, I have found that most bourbons struggle here.  ('Madame Isaac Pereire' is singularly lovely, but needs an awful lot of coddling to produce one flush a year.  'Zéphirine Drouhin' dies back so much that it could not be called a climber, here.)  Most Austins will suffer a lot of dieback, and perform no better than most repeating old roses. Since it's still early days for so many of the cultivars I grow, I expect that certain roses, once established, will prove to be more successful. I assume you will be removing all of the exterior siding, stone, shutters and window trim.  I would simplify the exterior -- I like the second door you show (with the sidelights). As for the siding, I would try something like reverse board-and batten where the "battens" are applied first and then the boards are put on top of those, spaced so that the batten is visible through a on-inch or so gap between the adjacent boards.  It's a modern look that is not often used and is more appealing to me than is the common board-and-batten arrangement.  It works best with wide boards -- at least 10" wide, and up to 12" wide and ones that are relatively thick -- 3/4" or 1" thick.

If fertilizer was actually plant food, it could be said that a plant's diet consists of salts, a 'salt' being the product of the interaction between an aid and a base (vinegar and baking soda, e.g.). If the soil cannot be flushed regularly, the issue is two-fold. 1) The salinity of the soil solution increases over time, which makes it increasingly difficult for the plant to absorb water and nutrients. 2) The ratio of nutrients in the soil solution (each nutrient to the others) will become increasingly skewed. This is a critical factor because an excess (toxicity) of one nutrient can cause the plant difficulty in sourcing one or more other nutrients. Examples: A) Using a high-P(hosphorous) fertilizer in containers can cause a deficiency of  copper, potassium, copper, zinc, and especially iron. B) Dosing with magnesium just because someone on the internet suggested it's a good remedy for chlorosis, can cause an acute deficiency of calcium. So, for any self watering container, it's important to use a fertilizer that closely mimics the ratio at which the plant actually uses the nutrients. This helps to keep o/a salinity low because you'll be able to use less fertilizer; and, because the nutrient array is provided at the same rate at which the plant actually uses the nutrients, skewing of the % of nutrients in the soil solution is minimized. This is true whether you  use a synthetic soluble fertilizer or rely on organic soil amendments (often referred to as fertilizers) as your nutrient source. It is MUCH easier, more reliable, and it affords a greater measure of control, if you rely on soluble synthetic fertilizers for container culture. IMO the best choice for a 'go to' fertilizer for containerized plants is Foliage-pro 9-3-6. It has all nutrients essential for normal growth in a ratio that minimizes excessive salinity and skewing of nutrient ratios.   IF, you can separate the two pots so you can flush the soil regularly (at least once a month), it will solve the build-up/skewing problems. Questions? Al

It's very easy to drill a hole in the bottom of a terra cotta pot, which would allow you to flush the pot regularly. There simply is no effective way of managing salinity and fertilizer ratios w/o a regular flush. You could also buy a pot with a hole already in it (which fits your cache pot) and go from there. I'm retired now, but I owned a contract glazing corporation before I retired. Drilling holes in glass, ceramic, granite, stainless steel, cast iron, ....., and other very hard substrates is an every day occurrence for this type of operation. Something I wrote for container gardeners based on >42 years of experience drilling hard materials: Drilling holes in pots The 2 types of drill bits most appropriate for drilling holes in pots are diamond core bits for the highly vitrified (hard material - baked at very high temps - glass, ceramic, ......) pots, and a drill with several names for drilling clay pots fired at low temps, such as terra cotta. That (carbide) drill is called a 3-point drill, spear point drill, or a spade drill, seen here:   For the hard stuff, diamond core drills are best, though the 3 point drill will drill the hard stuff, too. Both are available in many sizes, with bits sized 3/8 or 1/2” best for pots. You can buy either type at big box stores, and they're not that expensive, but you won't find a 'set' of diamond core bits worth buying for $9. The bits last a long time, depending on quality and how you use/care for them. They are best used with a steady stream of coolant from a squeeze bottle (contact lens solution bottles work great for this) or with the work surface barely submerged. IE, put the pot upside down in a tub and fill the tub with water until it just covers the work surface. If you use a spritzer or squirt bottle, a 50/50 mix of antifreeze and water is an excellent coolant, and soapy water is better than plain water but not as good as the antifreeze mix. The coolant keeps the tool from over-heating, and in doing so, increases the life of the tool substantially - like triple or quadruple the number of holes you can drill. While drilling, apply very little pressure, just the weight of the drill motor with you providing only guidance is sufficient.  Drill at medium speed – somewhere around 1,600 rpm. NEVER use either type of drill mentioned above without a lubricated coolant. The heat will cause thermal shock and fracture in glass and ceramics and heat build-up  will destroy the tool.   Regular masonry bits are "ok" for drilling terra cotta or cement (you can make them work), but inappropriate for anything harder. The right tool makes everything easier.   Al

The caulking goobering up is why cabinets should NEVER be caulked. And your house is too dry, humidity wise. You need to keep it between 30-60%, summer and winter. . That’s why the wood has shrunk so much. The cabinets have normal telegraphing separation at the cross grain joins. Wood moves with varying humidity, shrinking and swelling. It moves more than the coating does. You will always get telegraphing lines of the coating breaking at wood joins. And that is why you don’t caulk the floating panels, ever. When the wood moves, you get what you got. Caulk goobers. Also, paint never improves the base quality of the cabinets underneath the coating. You cannot make a used Chevy into a new Mercedes by giving it a paint job. Some of your issues are that you started with a used Chevy and expected a new Mercedes. Or at least a new Toyota. Not going to happen. That loose join gapping you show was always there, because the quality was always what it was. Paint just made it noticable. A lot of ”painters” do not have a clue about how to properly finish cabinets. Command is NOT a professional cabinet finish. It is a ”paint guy’s” idea of a cabinet finish, when he knows nothing about cabinet finishing. All that caulk and paint will need to be stripped. You cannot put a better quality coating over a worse one. Any paint job is only as good as the worst layer. The cost to do that will probably be significantly more than buying new doors and drawers. Therefore, new doors and drawers should be purchased, and just the boxes be stripped. Heat guns are your friend. Then find a actual cabinet finishing pro who uses Renner, Envirolak, Centurion, Ilva, Milesi, etc. Those are all modern waterborne 2K finishes that are way more durable and chemical resistant than Command.

The caulking goobering up is why cabinets should NEVER be caulked. Never say NEVER.  The best practice when cabinets are constructed with fiberboard panels is to impede water absorption by either (1) finishing the edges of the panel, or (2) caulking between the panel and wood rails or stiles. When KCMA was certifying finishes they actually specified caulk or sealed edges on MDF panels.  Many good cabinetmakers will caulk MDF panels, many people who don't understand wood and when to caulk, will default to never using caulk and their cabinets are worse for it. ---- To some extent wood is wood.  You can get a good paint job on practically any wood or fiberboard surface if you put in the prep work.  Command is a decent product for cabinets and certainly when done well will give you a coating comparable to Advance without many of the drawbacks that Advance has.  The only problem being that Command doesn't self-level nearly as well and so it can't be brushed on and has to be sprayed on.  However, it also cures much faster and is more likely to be applied correctly in my opinion. What the OP has is just a bad paint job, the paint is put on way too thick... I can see the bridging and the orange peel on my phone screen.  There is no way to fix it really and that is the problem.  The painter is going to swear it can be repaired and the only way to repair it is to take it down to bare wood.  So you are likely going to continue to have bridging issues with any other type of repair.  Having said that, I do agree that the wood seems to be moving quite a bit but it is hard to tell what is a bridging failure and what is wood movement. Your best bet is to get several estimates from reputable cabinet refinishers and decide whether you are going to let your painter take another swing or get in a fight for the money you paid and then some. Your home needs a humidity control system, for the good of everything wood, and every person in the home.  Humans find too dry and too moist conditions uncomfortable, as well as the wood shrinking and swelling in those conditions. The humidity issues are at the core of many of the issues that you are having, and the company would like to wait until the humidity starts to rise, in order for many of the issues to self correct, as they will, when the wood starts to swell.  They will be back the  next winter though, if you do not address the home humidification stabilization. And you will have different but related issues in the summer, with high humidity, if that isn't addressed. Not a fan of Command.  There are much better coatings out there. But, the laborious prep process is the MOST important part of the process.  The cleaning and sanding shouldn't be cursory, and the doors should be removed for that. You can get a great looking paint job, initially, if the right prep is done. Any coating can look good over great prep.  It takes time, and time is money.  A great refinishing company costs more for that time, and the better quality coatings. They aren't that outrageously expensive, but they are more difficult to source.  So, that factors in the higher price as well. The bleed through from underneath suggest an appropriate stain blocking primer wasn't used. The existing dents that were not filled suggest that the company was a painting company, used to doing walls, and not doing cabinets.  The liberal overuse of caulking suggests the same thing. The large crack shown in the cabinet frame was likely always there, and is structural to the original cabinet build.  People don't notice the defects in the grainier wood cabinets they way they do in a single color painted ones, and that is truly the biggest issue here. You are placing the cabinets under a microscope, after an opaque coating was applied, that essentially reveals the existing issues that were there.  That's not a fair way of assessing anything.  Painting cabinets does not "fix" the issues that the cabinets have before painting them.  A good quality refinisher can address some of the issues, but used cabinets will always look used, and not new.  If your expectations were for them to look new, then you have incorrect expectations. The "cure" for  this is strip the boxes, and source new doors and drawers, and new end panels, with a different finisher. That finisher could even be you.  There's nothing very difficult about any of this.  It's just repetitive boring detailed labor, and a huge amount of time dedicated to it.

Yes, you absolutely can save it, particularly since the plaster crown is only on one side. We have done this numerous times in older homes. Much the same process as doing any dropped beam: Build two temporary support walls on both sides of the subject wall. Strip drywall (or lath/plaster, gyproc, whatever) from the designated opening area on both sides, right up to the the top plate on the kitchen side (but leaving the crown and a section of wall below the crown on the dining room side deep enough to reach the bottom of the beam spec'd by the engineer). Carefully remove each stud so as not to damage the plaster crown. Grind off the toenails sticking down from the top plate where the studs used to be. Install beam under plate and install support posts (making sure the latter will land on the steel beam in the basement ceiling). Remove temporary support walls, complete finishing, you're done. Not sure why the first few responders said saving the crown was impossible; like I said, we've done this a bunch of times as described here. Just for further clarification.  I am going to assume that the panels are wood rather than MDF.  You don't typically caulk wood panels because the movement is too much.  A solid wood panel that is 18" wide can move up to 1/4" with a five percent change in humidity.  MDF panels don't really move and the movement of the rails and stiles is inconsequential for paint and caulk (typically about .02"). Humidity may be the culprit, but it is not the biggest problem.  There are several mistakes in that paint job that are the real problem.  Paint on furniture shouldn't crack like that.  That is happening because the paint was sprayed too thick and the crosslinking in the coating overcame the adhesion to the substrate and is pulling the paint off the cabinet. If the coating were applied properly then I would expect the cracks to be fairly clean, even if they are wide.  E.g.   The area in green looks exactly like a wood movement crack should look on fresh wood.  The area in yellow is a bit jagged but I would consider that acceptable on a repaint or refinish of existing cabinets.  The lines can be wider, but they are crisp and clearly defined.   This is just a bad application of paint that is being exposed by a humidity problem.  Even fixing the humidity problem isn't going to fix that.  The paint was sprayed too thick and the crosslinking was much stronger than the adhesion to the substrate and so your paint is literally attached to other paint rather than the cabinets in some areas.  That is a problem with the coating application and it needs to be addressed by going back to bare wood and building up multiple thin coats to promote adhesion to the substrate. This was not an easy job.  I would have walked away from it, for a lot more money than the OP paid the painter because it is just too much work to do it right.  However, if I accepted the job then it would be on me to do it right. I don't really know what to advise in this situation other than getting estimates to repair from other companies and deciding which, if any, of them seem knowledgeable.  Then you actually have something to discuss with your painter.  However, without that, no matter what this board says, your painter is not going to take responsibility for their work because this is going to be a gigantic pill to swallow.

Mushrooms growing in potting soil are very common. They are almost always  saprophytic fungi or those that survive on the decomposition of any organic matter  in the potting mix - peat, bark, actual soil, etc. They are not harmful to the potted plants directly but can be an indication of excessive watering or high humidity. Rosemary is not fond of these conditions so any decline in the plant itself can be attributed to excessively moisture retentive potting soil, not the mushrooms it may generate. Remove the mushrooms as you wish but I'd strongly suggest repotting in a faster draining, less moisture retentive soil mix....something like one would use for cacti and succulents. Rosemary likes it lean and dry.

also keep in mind.. that many things slow down in winter.. as the sun declines ... even in FL though not as much as up north .... and as they slow down.. they dont need as much water as it may have needed in the high heat of summer ... either reduce water.. or change the media a gal notes... but even new media may not help.. if you continue to over water the plant... media is a water management system.. and as it wears out it loses its ability to retain the water the plant needs while shedding excess ... medium is manipulated based on the needs of the plant... i think of rosemary more as a shrub.. which would need a sip of water.. and then near drying before the next watering... it is not what we would call a water loving plant that wants to sit in a sponge of water ... taken to the extreme.. the woody roots will rot ... its apparent your media is rotting.. as that is what fungi does in nature ... they are natural biodegraders .... and again .... that is normal as the media ages and breaks down ... ken

Hi, Patrick, If you're not finding definitive best practices for insulating your home, it's probably because most of the research is done on performance of new construction homes rather than retrofits. Much of the retrofit studies in cold climates involve installation of continuous exterior insulation which you indicated isn't an option. A couple of points:  First, you know about the potential for condensation to occur and the need to prevent it.   Preventing condensation means effective air sealing which favors installation of high-density spray-foam insulation.  You'll also get a higher R--value in the wall cavities than you will with other types of insulation.  You can get good results with rigid foam, but you'll need to meticulously seal the perimeter and any penetrations with spray foam and those will need to function over time.  Spray foam is more forgiving of the vagaries of installation.  If the budget doesn't allow for filling the stud cavity depth with spray foam, I'd suggest a "flash and batt" system which is the system shown in the wall section you provided. I'd use mineral wool batts.  I would spend particular attention sealing windows and doors and I would invest in spray foam of your home's rim joist if it is accessible.    I'd also carefully consider whether you need humidification in the winter.  Increasing indoor relative humidity in the winter increases the driving force for moisture to move into the stud cavities when it may find a way to get you in trouble.

Pavlo Starykov (II think that’s his name - Starr Tile something is his company) - and his findings were that marble should be installed on a traditional built mud shower pan (as long as it was built correctly = a pre slope underneath the pvc liner’).   Shower pans with surface waterproof membranes trapped water underneath the tile (instead of water going down through the packed mud to the pvc liner - and then follwing the sloped liner to the weep holes of a clamping drain. Regarding the tile on the wall - water must be getting behind those tiles underneath the niche. To control the size, begin a 3-year long rejuvenation program while fullydormant and leafless (in winter) so you can see the stems' skeleton without foliage. On each year, you reduce the total number of stems by 1/3 as you wish. For example, in year 1, prune all the way down the 1/3 longest number of stems and leave the remaining 2/3 of the stems unpruned. In year two, prune all the way down and the next 1/3 longest stems and leave the rest of the stems unpruned. In year 3, pruneall the way down the last 1/3 number of stems and leave the rest of the stems unpruned. Pruning is an activity that can trigger leaf out and new stem growth so it is best done when the shrub is fully dormant. Rejuvenating a hydrangea that only blooms on new wood in winter will not affect future blooms. If you rejuvenate a hydrangea that blooms on old wood or on both old and new wood, this type of pruning will reduce blooms in spring but since you only cut 1/3 of the stems, it should not entirely eliminate flower buds. Alternatively, consider contacting gardening clubs to see if they can sell them.

Stick masking tape along the front edge with a nice fold at the bottom to catch drips of super glue. Apply the thin type super glue, making sure you've got plenty of squeeze-out and that the missing section is filled completely. If you're in a hurry, spritz it with accelerator. Don't wipe the excess away; it acts as a lubricant when you're scraping the overfill. Scrape the overfill off with a Ceramic razor blade, which won't leave metal marks.  Angle the blade at first, you don't want to pull your adhesive out of the nick. If you do, put a little more glue in and start over. The super glue will appear as a medium gray, but fortunately you have that in your top. You'll never be able to "unsee" this, so don't be too hard on yourself please. You'll probably be able to feel it, but polishing to flush isn't a DIY project. The best fix is to do the repair, then have a more rounded edge re-profiled and polished. Not only will most or all of the chip be eliminated, it will be less likely to chip in the future. Unfortunately, with this popular edge profile, this probably won't be the first time you'll do this.

You're way over-thinking this. You bring the stone to the sink, not the sink to the stone, with caulk color choice. Some clear big box GE Silicone 2 will provide years of perfect service. and will probably be your best bet. Your fabricator doesn't strap his sinks in place, they leak, and that's why he wants a negative reveal to cover his inevitable black/brown unsanitary mess. That and a slight positive reveal means he absolutely has to nail the sink center at templating. You can fudge a negative a bit. A slight positive reveal not only looks better, but it provides the best meeting between the sink flange and the bottom of the stone. It also protects the bottom of the stone from potential chipping; a negative reveal does not and it happens. Stick to your guns and have your sink strapped in place please. Hercules Universal Sink Harness or a couple Sink Straps. I've installed hundreds of sinks this way over many years with no callbacks or crud. Ever.

Soaking beans leaches out some of the sugars that cause gas, but also some of the vitamins.  Shortens cooking time, but with fresher beans, long cooking times not as much of an issue.  I use bay leaves, they also help with the gas.  I also have epazote and hing or asafoetida  for the same reason.  Bay leaves usually end up being my first "go to."  Not sure why they reduce gas, but they are generally good for digestion in the same way something like ginger is also. Well cooked beans eaten earlier in the day cause less gas.  If you have a slow gut in general, that's where you will run into the most trouble.  If your gut flora is accustomed to beans and other high fiber foods you won't have as much trouble.  Depends on how much of all that you eat in one setting.  The gas is caused by bean sugars fermenting in your gut, so you want them to move along, not stay too long.  Hence you want to cook them well so they are easier to break  down.  Some add baking soda to the cooking water but that causes more leaching so unless you have a specific issue, I don't find the need to gild the lily.  Some aromatics never hurt, garlic is good for you too, as is parsley.  Garlic doesn't bother me too much if I don't  overdo it with those types of vegetables. I usually cook beans with minimal seasonings at first, then take some out to freeze and season the rest for whatever dish I want to make with them.

Random thoughts: - First, this plan is full of jigs-and-jogs, which will cost more and give nothing.  You say you're going to alter the front to be more plain ... but that's expensive.  Why not choose a plan that already has a more simple shape?  This general layout is not uncommon. - I agree with people who say this is a dark plan ... I'd solidly reject it for this reason alone.  Even without the side porches, your main living space is enclosed and will never have direct sunlight.  Main living spaces are best on a corner so they can have direct light from two directions. - The living room will not be particularly large ... not after you allow for walking spaces all around the edges.  Where will you place the TV? - I think a family house with one large living space (enough for the family to comfortably gather) and a smaller "away space" (which can be closed off visually and acoustically) is ideal without being overkill.  You'll have that if you use the front study /bed as a den /TV room /rec room. - You mentioned a playroom.  Kids rarely actually use playroom for play ... they end up being a storage spot for toys.  If you're going to have one, the front study /bed would be the ideal spot. - You say you're thinking of using the downstairs study /bed for a nursery for future children.  Look at the pathway between the master bedroom and this nursery ... it'd be closer to go up the stairs, which are right by the master, to the upstairs bedrooms. - If you think this'll ever be used as a bedroom, especially as an adult bedroom, I'd add a pocket door to close off the bedroom /bathroom as a suite.  This would close off the coat closet and the downstairs bathroom ... but it'd only be closed at night. - You say you plan to homeschool, but I haven't heard any discussion about a homeschooling space.  This study /bed would be the ideal location. - Big problem with the breakfast nook:  it houses the only door to the backyard.  This looks okay on the plan, but once you add a table for 6, you'll be blocking the exit.  It'd be better to close off this door and add a slider (which requires no swing space) to the back side of the living room. - The kitchen could be better laid out ... for one thing, the sink is the most used item in any kitchen ... and this one's located on the far end.  I know someone placed it here so it would be under a window, but it'd be more functional in the middle of the kitchen. - I'll side with an above poster and ask why you need a breakfast nook, island seating AND a dining room ... and probably outside dining too.  Don't try to have every. single. thing.  Instead,  pick two and do them well. - I hate the laundry room's location.  It's far from the master, very far from the upstairs bedrooms.  With four children, you'll be taking so, so many extra steps for a never-ending chore. - Consider swinging the washer/dryer to the back wall.  Dryers are best on an outside wall ... cheaper to build, more fire safe as it's easier to keep the vent clean. - I love big pantries, but this one's inswing door is a problem.  It'll cover half the food.  Look at the plan, and you'll see ... to get something from the left side, you'd have to enter, close the door.  Inconvenient.  A pocket door or a barn door would fix this problem. - I'd do away with that clutter of doors by the laundry room and just have open storage.  With a family of 6, you'll need it.  Instead, add a pocket door to divide the whole mudroom /pantry area from the main house; that'll allow you to close off a mess or the noise of the washer/dryer. - I see two water heaters.  This house doesn't seem big enough to warrant that. - Do you see one of these small closets becoming a broom closet?  Realistically, a 3' broom closet is a must ... vaccum cleaner, cleaning supplies, paper products and more. - The master bedroom is quite far from any entrance.  I'd like to see an exterior door, perhaps to the porch, especially if you might one day be elderly in this house. - The master bath is about the size of a bedroom two children will share.  This could be cut down without any loss of function.  You really want to clean this huge bathroom + 3 small bathrooms each week?  It'll be years until the kids can help. - The closet is large, but it is not large enough to hold a center dresser.  Assuming a 24" deep dresser, you'd have 24" walkways around it.  Remember to allow 24" for hanging clothing and 14" for shelves.  Note, too, that the closet has the same problem as the pantry:  its swing door blocks access to clothing on one side. - Agree that this garage won't really hold three cars.  Realistically you'll be able to keep a car in each door + have storage space on the side with the larger door. - Upstairs two 12x14 bedrooms, and they'll have lovely natural light ... two kids can certainly share a bedroom this size.  It's not going to be luxurious, but it's certainly acceptable.  If you end up with 2 boys and 2 girls, this'll work out well ... if not, you will have unequal spaces.  Will that be okay with you? - I like that the closets will give a decent amount of storage -- and you have a linen closet upstairs for the kids' sleeping bags, suitcases and other things. - I'd cut off the hall access to an upstairs bath and expand that linen closet even larger.  You're not just dripping in storage in this house. - Upstairs bathrooms are simple but functional. Sap usually flows heaviest when the sun shines on the cane directly. Standards have that thick, bare trunk absorbing all that heat from the sun, pushing sap upward in a steady stream, a much greater amount than most rose canes arising from the base of the bush can push. It's something I first noticed when heading back newly budded plants, removing the tops of the stocks above the healed-in scion (bud). I found the only thing which stopped the "bleeding" from those stock piece cuts was melted candle wax. Elmer's Glue is water soluble. Sap is primarily water. It dissolves and washes away Elmer's Glue. Pruning Sealer is asphalt. Sap flowing up the stem can easily inflate that rubbery petroleum product like a balloon and burst it, so it continues bleeding. But, melt candle wax over the cut end and it seals it. You have to coat it all over so every possible spot for sap to escape is thoroughly covered. For those real heavy "bleeders", you'll find if you make those cuts either early enough in the day or late enough so the sun isn't shining directly on the plant, the sap won't bleed as heavily and you can seal the cuts with candle drippings more easily. Once the sap is bleeding steadily, it can be nearly impossible to get anything to stick well enough to stop the flow.

A third option:  check out blower kits for the gas fireplace and possibly a new gas insert.  The blower fan can be fairly discreet inside the box.  FWIW, I prefer gas as an alternative heat source because of rolling electric blackouts. What is a Fireplace Blower? A fireplace blower is a fan mounted on the exterior of the fireplace or inside the unit but outside the firebox itself. It is used to circulate air around the unit's hot exterior before pushing it back into the room. Fireplace fans help to circulate warm air and increase heat penetration into the room. However, they do not increase the fireplace's total BTU output; instead, fireplace blowers simply move air more effectively to increase the amount of airflow around the fireplace and the entire room’s ambient temperature.

In terms of net heat output, a gas fireplace typically produces more heat compared to an electric insert, even considering some heat loss through the chimney. Gas fireplaces can generate upwards of 20,000 to 40,000 BTUs, substantially more than a 10,000 BTU electric unit. However, the efficiency of your specific older gas fireplace may vary. A key factor to consider is the efficiency rating of the gas fireplace. While some heat is lost through the chimney, a well-maintained and properly functioning older model can still be effective in heating a large room. In contrast, electric inserts are 100% efficient at converting electricity to heat, but they usually produce less overall heat. For your large, cold room with vaulted ceilings, the gas fireplace might be a more effective option for creating a significant amount of heat. However, for consistent, efficient heating, ensuring that the fireplace is clean, serviced, and inspected is crucial.

I grow everything in containers, including a big collection of clematis, and you are right to be concerned about their health and vigor after a hard freeze. The roots of a plant are the parts most vulnerable to cold damage. And when growing them in a container, the roots are exposed to far colder temperatures than they would experience if planted in the ground. But clems are pretty tough vines. They often miraculously reappear after vanishing in the garden for a season or two. That yours is showing signs of new growth is a very good sign and repotting the clem ASAP in an adequately sized pot with fresh planting media is the best way to go. Just keep an eye on it and water and fertilize as necessary. It may not bloom heavily this season but it should still grow well. My potted clems also experienced a hard freeze - 15F - last month. But it has been warm and sunny the last few days and when checking all  my pots, nearly all the clems are showing buds and the beginning of new growth.

Hi, HU, The purpose of insulation baffles in an attic is to maintain an open path for air flow from the soffit vents to either the hip and/or ridge vent.  If there's no soffit vent, there is no potential for air flow and no need for a baffle. The efficacy of gable end vents is debatable.  The fact that they admit wind-driven rain and snow makes them something to avoid, in my opinion.  We install them in gables when needed for aesthetics, but we don't cut a hole in the wall sheathing so they don't allow air flow into the attic.  I also recommend against powered attic vents--they depressurize an attic and draw conditioned air from the living area which is replaced in summer by warm, potentially moist, air.

I know that your question is for a slate looking porcelain tile.  I just wanted to ket you know that as long as you purchase the correct type of genuine slate tile, it is easy to care for/maintain.  I have black (charcoal) gauged and honed slate tile from Brazil.  It does not have clefting/splitting issues - and can even be used outdoors.  My installer used a impregnating matte sealer on it.  However,  prior to being sealed, my older dog threw up on it - wasn’t noticed for a few days - and it cleaned up easily with no resulting marks/damage. Also, slate is not slippery - even though people will tell you otherwise.  I’ve lived with it in a bathroom + mudroom/laundry room.  It is not slippery. I am using MSI Montauk Black slate in my lake house because it is easy to maintain (and not slippery when wet).  It is also gauged but has a little more surface texture on some of the tiles.  You can sort through boxes in order to get the look you want.  I think that natural slate looks much nicer than faux slate,  As long as you don’t purchase slate mined from China - and stick with slate that originates from Brazil, your floors won’t require a lot of maintenance. FYI - while renting a condo in Aspen, CO, an entire bottle of olive oil was dropped and the entire contents spilled onto a slate floor.  Some of the oil soaked into the tile - however, it wasn’t difficult to remove it from the tile and we received a full refund of our deposit. The type of slate matters - some slate is porous and will cleft easily - others won’t.  Charcoal slate from Brazil is not expensive.  The MSI slate was under $4 sf for 12x24 size + around $4.60 sf for the 4x12  to be used in two of the bathrooms at the lake.  I’ve tested it - (including spilling many things on it + leaving pieces outside in freezing rain + temps below 10 degrees).  Zero issues re staining or splitting.

Would BM Swiss Coffee look very yellow next to extra white? Would Greek Villa be a better choice? Also considering Shoji and Aesthetic white. Chroma tells you how colorful a color looks. More Chroma = more color. Low Chroma = more neutral. The rule of thumb for white-on-white or off-white color schemes is there needs to be a difference of at least 0.20 in Munsell Chroma. That contrast means neither color will make the other look dirty or dingy. For Extra White, it's best to choose a color of white/off-white with a Chroma more than 52 ish. Pure White doesn't work with Extra White for that reason. All the other colors after Extra White are in order by Chroma; which in this case quantifies the amount of hue parent yellowness discernible. BM Swiss Coffee and Greek Villa are similar. Greek Villa is lighter, has more color by a smidge.

text: Never be in a hurry to do spring pruning if you are in a cold zone, 6 or lower, and have frequent late spring frosts, many of which are mild and of no consequences, but some are severe and will kill any new leafed out growth. Apical dominance causes the surviving buds at the highest point on a cane to sprout forth while the lowest down buds are essentially dormant.  Cut away the upper parts of the canes as is normally done at spring pruning, and lower, dormant buds are woken up and begin to leaf out.  Time your pruning so that the remaining buds on the bush are woken into growing when ALL danger of late frost is pretty much past.  Early to mid- April in zone 6 is a good time to prune. Moses

You need to satisfy the 1 1/8" subfloor thickness to reduce deflection.  So, add a second layer of subfloor as suggested in method two. You may want to stick to a high performance subfloor panel similar to Advantech. These will not swell when it gets wet. Make sure the joints are staggered between the two layers.  Useing foaming glue is ideal, along with screws that will not break through the bottom layer.

We had a somewhat similar situation in a house built late '70's.  3/4" particle board over 1/2" plywood.  Removed the particle board, screwed the 1/2 plywood to the joists (2 1/4" #8 screws) (originally only nailed).  Then spread Liquid Nails subfloor adhesive with a notched trowel and put down 3/4" plywood.  The 3/4" ply was screwed down with 1 1/2" #8 screws...into the plywood but not the joists.  Joints staggered and top plywood placed at 90 degree angle to the first layer. Our situation was a bit unusual given the 1/2" plywood.  Cheap ass builder.  Anyway, it was difficult to find information on how to deal with this and this approach made the most sense out of what info I could find.  I do know that, 10 years down the road, the floor still feels rock solid and has zero squeaks.

So the main furnace box cannot get rid of enough heat fast enough and the seals have begun to leak and it's overheating and shutting down. Chris, How old is the existing furnace? How old is the house? It's possible the ductwork is poor but are you just rehashing what the home warranty tech told you? Common reasons why furnace does this over heating bit isn't always tied to improper sized duct work (it can be), but it could be dirty evap coil -- heat builds in that box just after the furnace until the heat breaches the high limit / shuts furnace off. Could be due to failing blower motor that isn't fully ramping... could also just be a high limit that is failing too. Also a gas valve that is improperly set can over fire the furnace causing over heating issues. The reason I say this is: The home warranty company would most likely deny the claim if duct work wasn't right. Sounds to me this tech may be trying to game the system at your expense. If change the furnace to 3 ton then have another problem with AC they may then come back claim your HVAC system is now "mismatched" and deny the claim for a problem they created. This is why if the duct work was improper they would deny the claim now. I would say get another HVAC company involved. One that you pay for service as if you go the freebie route they may be no better than what the home warranty provided company is telling you. Have them diagnose the system and see what they say. (in other words don't call around for a free estimate, it's rare for those kinds of services to offer more than a price to just rip everything out -- if the system is greater than 20 years though? you have to be realistic. They don't last forever.)  I've repaired furnaces older than 20 years, but I live in a climate that really doesn't have much of a winter. So this equation can vary a bit. If the furnace is older than 20 years and you live in a colder type climate, it's probably ready for a replacement. But these over heating type issues can occur much sooner than that 20 year time period alot of it depending on who serviced it in the past. Like if you got the home warranty with a recent purchase of the house? That's how most people get twisted up in these things. First American is a bigger home warranty company as I've heard of them before. So what you're telling us here doesn't sound right. It sounds like the tech is trying to game the system to get at that spiff money if I had to guess. That is a house of cards that is going to crumble around him if that's the case. (you don't want your house to be a victim.) If the paid for service comes and tells you the same thing without being influenced then it's probably in your best interest to pay for a heat load calculation and look toward a new HVAC system both heating and cooling & new duct system to bring it all together. First things first.   Are you SURE what you see in lines is tree roots?   Bio-mass gardually grows inside septic lines to the point it renders field lines usless so that line replacement in a new location is required.  The stuff resembles tiny roots on a scope but easily distingused when pulled from line on snake.   how long has it been since tanks were pumped?   Are you sure pumper is finding ALL tanks.  Many systems have up to 3 tanks.  for now I'll assume this isn't bio-mass but if you decide that's what it is just say so and we can work on solutions. If roots are between house and cleanout you can get more bang from root killer.   At a time when little or no water will be dumped into lines,  block line at cleanout with something similar to this.   After line is blocked put your root killer in drain and use enough water to flush it down to and fill pipe above block.  You might pour 5 gallons or until water backs up in tub drain.   You can see that if killer just making contact with roots as it flows past roots as directed on product kills roots having killer stand in contact with roots for 2 or 3 hours should result in far more roots being killed.   I wouldn't think it neccessary for killer to stand more than overnight.   An alternate or additional remedy is putting killer in a root feeder similar to this and inject into soil near line in attempt to kill roots BEFORE they enter line.  Killer lingers in soil whereas when used as directed on container killer briefly contacts roots then flushed out into field which isn't bad if you happen to have roots out there as  well. houzz wouldn't allow link to root feeder so just look for Ross Root Feeder at big box or garden center.

Sorry this is so long... I am trying to be thorough. Plenty of people, both men and women, find themselves in a similar situation.  Unfortunately, it seems all too common for contractors to underbid jobs or oversell their quality in an effort to get your signature on the contract. So first, I am concerned about the job growing from $20,000 to $42,000.  There may be legitimate reasons for that, but often it is more than a little sketch.  Moreover, while most clients just pay to get out of the ordeal there are often legal protections in place if the consumer is willing to take advantage of them.  So what state are you in? There are basically three types of contracts (1) fixed-price, (2) cost-plus, and (3) time and materials. In a fixed-price contract the $20,000 would have been the price to complete all work they were contracted to complete.  Fixed-price contracts can grow as the scope of the work changes but typically these changes have to be handled via change orders, which are basically smaller fixed-price contracts that should be presented prior to the work beginning but when necessary may be presented shortly after that work is commences.  So in a fixed price contract you should be able to calculate the entire price of the job as the original contract plus all change orders provided in a timely manner.  In a fixed price contract you generally have the right to see all the change orders but no other detailed billing. In a cost plus contract the contractor's duty to the client is a bit higher because the client is absorbing more price risk.  In these contracts the work is done at cost and the contractor adds a fee (often a %) for the management of that work. In contract law "cost" has a very specific meaning... it is the amount actually paid less any discounts or rebates.  So in a cost-plus contract if the contractor pays a subcontractor $1,200 but gets $100 rebate then he must bill you $1,100 plus his fee calculated on that $1,100.  Because there is a higher level of trust in a cost-plus contract, the customer has the right to see all invoices that were paid to suppliers and subcontractors, and even the right to verify those amounts. A time and materials contract is most suited when one firm will do all the work without subcontractors.  Typically, these contracts are materials at cost and labor at a specified unit rate.  These types of contracts are often abused for several reasons.  Contractors often just add mark-up to their materials rather than passing along the actual legal contract.  Contrary to popular belief time and materials contracts are not actually for the time spent on the job, they are actually for the time reasonable and necessary to complete the job.  So a contractor can't take 14 hours to complete a 4 hour job and just bill you the extra amount.  Because they are the most abused they are also the most regulated by states and some states (California for example) have banned time and materials contracts for home improvements.  In a time and materials contract you have the right to a complete breakdown of that job, the time that job took, and the materials used. ---- Now for the next part... Getting help with assessing the work.  I have never found it particularly difficult to get one contractor to talk bad about another contractor's work.  I have found it difficult to get something in writing.  So I advise looking for someone to repair the work rather than someone to help you prepare for a meeting.  Simply note that you want to know what is wrong and what it is going to cost to make it right.  Leave your new contractor out of the dispute with the other contractor.  I have had really good luck with recommendations from lumber yards (not big box stores... actual lumber yards).  They interact with most contractors and will often tell you who they hold in high regard and may be able to tell you who they think may be willing to do it. Take notes on what this contractor tells you is wrong and use those notes in your discussion with your existing contractor.  If your existing contractor disagrees with the assessment simply ask them to put it in writing.  Making a contractor memorialize things is often pretty effective at cutting through the B.S.  It is easy to tell you a lie when there is no proof of it, however, that lie in an email can be used against them and they know it.  You can do this in a confrontational way and simply say I don't trust anything you are unwilling to write in an email or text, or the non-confrontational way and pretend you just want it in writing so you can understand it better because you are a bit confused. If you can't find a contractor willing to come on short notice, a home inspector with a contracting background is a great option.  If you are near a populated area you may be able to find a construction manager or construction inspection service to help you, but they can get pretty expensive.

Hopefully, you will be very disciplined and will always empty the DW as soon as it's done and immediately put any dirty dishes, etc., in the DW rather than stacking them on the counter in the sink.  Why not the sink?  Your sink is part of both the Prep Zone & Cleanup Zone.  That means any dishes you stack in the sink will be in the way of someone trying to prep and that person will need to take the dishes out of the sink to clean/wash veggies/fruit/etc. prior to using. If I were you, I would make some major changes.  However, if that's not possible, then I would at least: Regarding what appear to be cabinets on the back of the island -- you will likely only be able to access items in the first 12" or so of the cabinets b/c of the overhang (unless you have a small child who can crawl under the overhang and reach inside the cabinets). Regarding the island size -- most people are unable to comfortably reach much past 30" when leaning over the island.  This means that to be able to clean the entire island, it should be no more than 60" in one direction.  I say "comfortably" b/c you need to be able to use a cloth or sponge to wipe the island down and you will need to be able to have a firm hold on the cloth or sponge (i.e., not just throw/fling it out there and hope it gets all the crumbs, etc.). Your island appears to be: 1.5" Counter overhang in the front + 24"D cabinets + 24"D cabinets + 1" doors on the back cabinets + 18" or so overhang in the middle (so there is at least 15" for the end seats) = 68.5" Unless you and your entire family are very tall or have very long arms, you likely won't be able to reach the center to clean it without climbing onto the counter (which I do not recommend). Personally, I think you can do better function-wise. Regarding food storage...food should be stored in a cool, dry, dark space.  Putting the ovens in the pantry and even a window will not accomplish that.  (Windows can have blackout curtains, but they still let in heat if it's hot outside.)  In fact, ovens put out so much heat that you will have a very hot pantry when the ovens are in use!  Not only that, but you cannot easily keep an eye on the food in the oven(s).  Keep them in the Kitchen, don't put them in the pantry! Ditto DWs -- they put out both heat and moisture. With the ovens & DW in the pantry, you now have a hot, moist environment for storing your food.  (Add in light from the window and you now have exactly the opposite of what food storage should be!) BTW...that DW probably won't work the way you have it.  You need filler space b/w it and the cabinets around the corner to be able to open both it and those cabinets.  Given it's an appliance, you may need up to 6" of filler to account for the DW door depth & handle (if there is one).  Don't forget that if you have cabinet pulls/knobs, you need to account for them as well. Example of what I'm talking about (it shows a range, but the concept is the same with a DW).
