@Atheen - 7a - in Maryland, USA Two things I've learned when it comes to nursery and greenhouse ops: 1) their focus is on the bottom line ($) and not on the long term effects their care practices have on the plant subsequent to the point in time when the plant is sold. The (previously) conventional process of potting plants up to a larger pot (nursery can) before the plant became rootbound to the point where the root/soil mass can be lifted from the pot intact have been mostly discarded because of the cost of added soil, cost of pot, and particularly because of the cost of labor to properly care for nursery crops. This results in the sealing of many plant's fates due to the effects of root congestion; and, the effects of the new 'labor saving' method results in the sale of a very high % of plants that shouldn't even be sold; this because once a plant has been allowed to become that rootbound, the negative effects are permanent, unless a pair of hands at some point gets into the root mass to correct congestion and problem roots. 2) Very few employees of nursery and greenhouse ops have anything resembling a even a reasonably good working knowledge of A) the impact of root congestion on plant health, growth rate, and the plant's ability to defend itself against insect herbivory and disease pathogens, and B) how to correct the root issues and perform a full repot. Currently, and due to labor costs, extremely few nursery ops pot up in a timely manner, and very precious few do anything about trying to correct a plant that has become extremely rootbound. It has become cheaper to destroy the plant than to correct its congested roots. This is why nursery/greenhouse employees look at you like you have a third eye when you start asking questions about high quality grow media and/or performing full repots. It has, unfortunately, become almost a foreign concept for anyone other than managerial staff, and even if the staff understands what the effects of root congestion are and how to eliminate the issue, no action is taken because of the added work's impact on the bottom line. I wish I knew of a way to modify the 511 to make it a little heavier (so  planters wouldn't fall with the slightest wind), but I wouldn't know  where to begin on how to do that. This problem's resolution is actually quite easy. By a pot considerably larger than you think you'll need, and fill the bottom of the pot with bricks or large rocks. This 'ballast' not only provides added weight to help guard against toppling, it also reduces the volume of grow medium CAPABLE of holding excess (perched) water. For any given soil that supports perched water, the max ht of the perched water column, for that soil, is a constant. IOW, no matter the size or shape of the pot, the max PWT ht will be the same. You can see (below) that 1) roots are reluctant to grow into areas of saturated soil, which leaves roots susceptible to fungi that cause root rot, and 2) when using gravel and other small objects as a "drainage layer", the layer simply raises the PWT to a position higher in the pot than it would be w/o the layer. Obviously, this is highly undesirable.  Using large objects like like bricks/rocks as ballast doesn't cause the same problem. The benefit of using ballast lies in the fact that it displaces grow medium that would normally be 100% saturated w/o raising the ht of the PWT. If you have a bucket of water filled to the top, then drop a brick into the bucket, a volume of water equal to the displacement of the brick/ballast will overflow the rim of the bucked. On the other hand, if you have a 10x10 bucket with a drain hole filled with a grow medium that is supporting 4" of perched water soil (400 cu in), and you introduce a 2x4x8 brick at the bottom of that container, it will displace 64 cu" of soil saturated with PW. Since you can line the inside of a 10x10 pot with 4 bricks, leaving a hole in the middle of the arrangement, you can displace 256" of saturated soil with only 4 bricks. If you broke 2 additional bricks in half and added them to the bottom, you will have displaced 384 cu in of the 400 cu in capable of holding PW. The key to the bricks working as a ballast instead of a false bottom lies in the fact that there must be a continuous column of soil from the top of the soil line to the bottom of the pot to act as the wick through which the water is FORCED to flow out of the drain hole. Wicks work well, but items judiciously considered and placed in the pot to serve as ballast work better; and, once the planting is established, the ballast works passively for as long as the planting exists. Use bricks/rocks if you need weight, or an overturned pot/bucket, or empty soda bottles (cap on) if you want to keep things light.  I hope your hand gets better. Having less joints makes  for a better  rigid floor assembly.  Joints are weak spots. This is usually where problems occur first.   Having single length boards, you have deferred these problem areas to the perimeters of the room. Which reduces your problem areas. You're not dealing with bad mill work, bad cuts or carfstmanship.  Example: your first two photos. Single length floor boards will help keep your surface flatter. Less joints, less over and under wood, a more flatter and even floor.  Example: your mitered transition. A lot of old homes use single length floor boards.  These floors have stood the test of time. The reason why it is not used too often these days is cost.  It takes too much time and raw material to come up with select or clear grade flooring. Which drives up the cost. Also, delivery is a pain trying to mauever 16 ft. length bundles around the house/job-site. Regarding your closet, it's a small walk-in. Most of your floors will get covered with built-ins and items along the walls. you will probably end up with a 2x3 area left of visible flooring. It will look worst with a bunch of joints. What you have is fine.  You can tell the contractor, that you want visible staggered joints for the remaining of the project. Otherwise, whenever and wherever you can use single length boards, do so. You will have a flatter and stronger floor.  Especially for glue-downs and floating installations.

So I am going to have to tell you what you don't want to hear, which is that you should really repaint your trim.  You're right, PW is a terrible trim color. You don't have to do it all at once, just work through it gradually (as you can tolerate it), or pay someone to do it.  I'm sorry your ceilings are also this color! If you really can't stomach repainting the trim and ceilings, get the tint of Palace White cut in half and see how you like that on the walls.  Natural Wicker is close to the same LRV as Palace White, but is a different shade, so they have the potential to clash once you see them next to each other on large expanses of wall.  My floors are also orangey (going to refinish them along with the kitchen remodel), so I can tell you Simply White looks good as a trim color with floors like that.  And it will look good when the floors are refinished, too.  It's good investment to have a more adaptable trim color.  If you're still in that house in ten years and want to repaint again you will have a much easier time if you bite the bullet and start working on the trim now.

I have a Fantech LD-10 inline silencer that has been operating since ca. 2012 without issue.  I also have an LD-8, I think, between some ceiling registers and a secondary exhaust fan.  The question arose on the Appliance forum whether the nature of the muffler (porous sheet metal over sound deadening insulation) would be safety hazard.  Fantech specifies these for kitchen exhausts.  My thought is that due to the relatively low grease levels in residential hood ducts, the grease would behave like it does in standard ducts -- turn into a varnish.  Also, any fires that could potentially start in the insulation zone would be choked. I haven't personally opened up the duct to check it, so I cannot provide direct evidence that there is not a problem.  If the hood baffles are performing their task of capturing the large end of the particle spectrum and the air flow is blowing the rest outdoors with minimal condensation or impingement, then I think I'm OK. So does the OP believe that his or her cooking will be at the high end of residential grease generation, or more at more modest levels.  If the former, a discussion with Fantech may be in order. Keep in mind that the commercial ducts have to be welded, with access ports, and cleaned yearly.  They have a much greater burden then residential systems have.

@Elestrial 7a you're welcome! Hume isn't difficult to root compared to many others but it isn't AS easy as the multiflora types. That thick cambium really does the job for rooting and budding. It's the tissue which calluses then differentiates and forms roots. It's what heals together with the cambium tissue on the back side of the scion to form new capillaries so nutrients can flow between that of the stock and the scion or graft. If you cleft graft fruit trees, you line up the cambium of the graft variety with the cambium of the stock. Cambium is not only the circulatory system of the rose but it's also stem cell material. If the plant is wounded, it forms scar tissue to seal and heal the wound. If a piece of one plant is inserted into a second plant, it knits together to form new circulatory tissue so the new part becomes part of the whole. If cambium tissue is exposed to cool, dark, damp conditions, it forms callus which then forms roots. When that tissue exists as a thicker layer under the bark in the entire plant, some wondrous things can be accomplished. De la Grifferaie is also multiflora type and it's the stock used to make 8' tall (and sometimes taller) weeping standards. Huey flows sap to about 3', 4' is pushing it. IXL has pushed it over 5'. Burling has created up to 6' tall weepers using Pink Clouds. I budded four buds of  Baby Faurax in a 4' Hume whip in 1994 I rooted and they all took and grew. I gave that plant to a gardening client in 2015 when we sold in Encino and moved to the Central Coast. It isn't a multiflora type, but it's good to at least 4' in length in my experience. How much heat? The San Fernando Valley north of LA gets HOT. It's considered a Zone 9b, as is where I am now, however they are worlds different. The Valley gets warm quickly and remains warm most of the day. Here, we're 9 miles from the Pacific and the ocean breeze keep it rather chilly. The "heat" shown on the chart below is in the full sun, for an hour, perhaps three on a really "hot" day. Then, the ocean breezes kick in and it's like standing in front of a walk-in freezer. In Encino, I planted my rose seeds in November as that's when the temperatures would traditionally be cool enough to allow for germination and maturation before the summer heat hit. Here, I can literally pollinate year round and plant most of the year because the temps remain low enough for germination as well as not so high it cooks the seedlings. Old climate where there was heat.   Here.   I wrap cuttings to get them to callus then plant outdoors to allow them to finish rooting and growing. Huey and Fortuniana would not keep going after being unwrapped. IXL, De la Grifferaie and Pink Clouds do here. I obtained 44 rooted Fortuniana stocks and grafted to them in August when we CAN get heat. Everything simply turned black. The multiflora types all pushed growth. Does that help give you an idea? As for budding, Hume is best for "T" buds like Huey, where you have to wait for the stock to really be vigorously growing so the sap is flowing fully and the bark lifts easily. Pink Clouds and the other multiflora types can be "T' budded, but that thick cambium allows you to chip bud very easily and that is significantly easier for you to learn to do. It requires much less skill and practice. Burling has long promoted Pink Clouds because it remains in condition for budding much of the year. The heat lovers are best when the heat is highest so the sap is flowing fully. There are many tutorials on line how to chip and "T" bud. I have a blog post about it here, with photographs. http://pushingtheroseenvelope.blogspot.com/2014/11/chip-budding.html There are a number of other posts on my blog about what I'd budded with photos of how they turned out. And, if you're interested in wrapping cuttings for rooting, you can start here and then scroll forward to glean the discoveries and suggestions as they revealed themselves. There are even posts about rooting longer whips for standards. http://pushingtheroseenvelope.blogspot.com/2011/05/wrapping-cuttings.html

It will take a bit of math, but you want the correct size for the wall. If you’re choosing wall art for a predominantly empty wall, your wall  art should take up about 60% to 75% of the available empty wall space  (the portion not covered by moldings or furniture). The first step is to measure the height and width of the wall. Next, multiply the measurements by both 0.6 and 0.75. The tub making the toilet bubble is a clear indication that the drain venting was improperly installed. The bubbling occurs when a slug of drain water is pushing air in front of it and the air can't escape, that's the purpose of the vent piping, to let air in and out as needed. So the trapped air being pushed exits via the toilet causing the bubbling. That's also the likely reason the toilet doesn't drain properly and repeatedly plugs, the trapped air also slows the toilet solids from moving down the piping causing the solids to slow down and settle out mid-pipe. Then the next flush of solids runs into the first, and from there things spiral into a blockage. The only way to fix the problem is to redo the underfloor piping correctly. If you're on a a slab, that's a huge issue to break up all the concrete and replace the drain piping; you will likely never get the plumber to admit their mistake. If on a crawlspace the fix is much easier. The builder may have sufficient clout to get things fixed but they may balk as well.

I agree that it could be a venting issue - but I'm not nearly as convinced as the person above. I'm more inclined to believe a buried broken drain or joint that came apart because it wasn't glued properly before it was backfilled. I'm also going to bet that this is on a slab. Have a company remove the toilet and scope the drain from there first. If that comes back negative, take a good look at the venting (scope it from the roof if you need to). If it's a broken pipe under the slab, it will be expensive. This is a warranty issue and only becomes the homeowner's problem if they aren't assertive with the builder.

What's the sun exposure like in that spot? Does water pool there, or is it just a damp area? We sometimes see this if the contractor laid pavers over a concrete slab and there's nowhere for the water to go, but given that you indicated a gravel base I don't think that's the issue. I would reach out to your installer and ask them to take a look. It may just be an issue where things need to dry out a bit as we head into spring (the fines in the gravel base hold way more water than you would expect), but better to let them put eyes on it.

You can hire a drain company or a septic company to use a scope with camera to follow the line from the toilet to the tank. They can tell you if there is a clog in the line, a bend in the line, improper slope, a crushed pipe, etc. They use a water jet to clear an obstruction.

This is just a bad idea.  There are likely better ways to solve whatever problem you are attempting to solve.  You are turning two shallow tall cabinets into a rotating double sided full depth cabinet.  The rotation itself is going to require more room than the cabinet. You could likely accomplish the same type of access with overextension drawer slides and pullouts.  You could do hinged drawers that pull out and hinge open giving you drawers that essentially become two drawer sets 30" wide and 12" deep from a stationary 15" wide cabinet. However, if you have to have a rotating cabinet for some reason... The only reasonable way to make it safe is to run a steel tube (conduit) from floor to ceiling and mount the cabinets to the tube using ball bearing pillow blocks.  So long as the tube runs through the center of the lazy-susan and is properly mounted to floor and ceiling you will be safe. I was planning on putting very light weight items in it and I suppose the lazy Susan base must be extra secured to the floor. They are 6' tall cabinets... they are going to be massively unstable with feathers.  Also there is no practical way to mount them to the lazy-susan to secure them.  It is a 6' long lever, even empty the cabinets would likely tear themselves apart in a few rotations.  It is just pieces of wood held together with screws and glue.  To mount a 15" wide cabinet to spin it you are going to have to make it do things that wood, screws, and glue don't like doing. First, your cabinets need to be wood or plywood, fiberboard isn't going to work and then you would likely need to epoxy in some all-thread and it is going to need to be deep (like 10").  Then you are going to have to secure it to a commercial grade lazy-susan or it is just going to rip that apart. In the end, there is no way that is the most economical, useful or practical solution.

Was going to suggest a layout bascally the same as Beverly's.  There's no particular reason to add doors -- most bathrooms in the US are all in one room, with the possible exception of the toilet, if you want that. You can have a pony wall to make the toilet feel more private, and the cabinetry on the other wall helps a bit too.   She has put a makeup table on the upper wall, but you could also put any combination of storage, or a bench for sitting on, or a shelf for tub things.  You'll need hooks for towels somewhere too.

Overall it's a nice, clean, straightforward layout.  A couple thoughts: Have a lot of space so would like to have double vanity, Not the dreaded, ubiquitous duplicate sinks ... double the cost, double the upkeep, nothing in return ... though at least with roughly 9' of space, you're not doing it at the expense of drawer space. I'd consider moving the make-up area over to this side and adding a linen closet on the exterior wall.  A person sitting at the make-up area would block access to the shower and the toilet. A linen closet in this area would be a budget-option (significantly cheaper than the cabinetry linen tower you've drawn in by the make-up table), and even a small one does so much ... I'd make it shallow, maybe 15-18" ... that'd allow you a hamper on the bottom half of the closet /towel and toiletry storage above. Freestanding tub and walk in shower. They look good.  Is the shower about 4x4?  While not luxurious, it will be comfortable.  I'd do just what ACM shows in the above picture ... pony walls halfway up.  That slashes your glass in half /slashes your glass cleaning in half, and it also allows you ample space for hidden storage niches.  You can plan a lovely space all day long, then have ugly shampoo bottles become the focal point.  Include more niche space than you think you need. Very important thought:  Where do you see your towels being hung?  For the shower + for the tub.  Don't forget hand towels at the vanity.  I don't see an obvious choice for the shower. Very important thought:  You want to place your shower controls on the pony wall ... not under the shower head.  This will allow you to reach in /turn on the water without committing your body to the initial cold spray. Not super important to have separate toilet room but if a design makes more sense than I am open to it. No door.  If you leave it as you've described now, natural light will extend throughout the space.  If you block it off, you'll lose the light and make the space more cumbersome to clean.  And it might hold in moisture from the shower. I would also remove the small wall to the left of the cabinetry straight ahead of the door; it doesn't appear to serve any purpose.  Though now that I type that, I wonder if it's necessary for support. Other thoughts: - I'd consider rotating that cabinetry nearest the toilet so it'd serve the toilet instead of the make-up area ... or at least turn the bottom half.  You need space now to store toilet paper, and, especially if you plan to be old in this house one day, you'll likely one day need some sort of medical supplies near the toilet.  My grandparents both did ... for different reasons.  It'd be so easy to create that now. - Where -- if anywhere -- do you see a hamper fitting in? - Where will your trash can(s) be placed? - What thoughts do you have on window coverings? - Do you plan to store cleaning products in the bathroom? - I'd consider one large mirror over the vanity.  It'd be better to reflect light from the over-tub window.  It'll also allow you to see more of yourself /your outfit in the mirror.

The very small footprint houses in many neighborhoods here, 12-15 feet wide a lot of them, all had vestibules inside the front door, that might be no wider than 3 feet and just long enough to get in and get the door closed. Opening it up created more space around the door but nobody puts furniture that close to the front door without some sort of barrier there, and if there is a chair there it is the last chair anybody sits in because it's a little unnerving to sit with your back to the front door immediately next to you. Some people have started putting something back again. I didn't have room to put a vestibule in because of my front door position, but I did put in a wall that is less than 2 feet deep, and that small bit of wall makes the room feel a little better because of that slight separation.

I'm not sure Pearly White is the right choice for your house.  You have a lot of warm wood (leaning orange).  Pearly White has a gray undertone. If you have already done this and Pearly White is the right color for you, then I would have the kichen, living, dining rooms painted the same color. I love color, too, so I get where you're coming from, but it looks like you have enough going on without three different paint colors in those rooms.  If you really want to mix it up, I think the dining room is the space to experiment in.  But do large samples before going all in.  Honestly, you can do whatever you like, I am just trying to help you to not waste your time and money.  I have painted three houses top to bottom at this point and there have been a couple times when I thought I had the perfect color and changed my mind at the point I did a larger sample.  No one likes to repaint a whole room (I have done that at least twice I can remember :-)). A room like the office/guest room is a good place to have a different color than the rest of the house.  Sea Salt is a popular color, but it can lean blue or green, depending on the lighting, so sampling is necessary.

Klem's idea about a jumper duct is an easy DIY fix for the issue. It's also referred to as a deKiefer bypass or transfer duct. https://buildingscience.com/documents/information-sheets/information-sheet-transfer-grilles-and-ducts If using such a transfer duct, one could add a thermostatically controlled blower fan such as below to keep air circulating through the powder room: https://www.amazon.com/gp/product/B0792QR5YT/ref=ppx_yo_dt_b_search_asin_title?ie=UTF8&psc=1 The vent blower normally works like this; in the summer, when it senses cold air in the duct, the fan comes on to boost cool air into the room. In the winter, when it senses warm air in the duct, it turns on to boost the warm air into the room. The summer and winter settings are switched appropriately in the spring and fall for the oncoming season. In Klem's application, the summer setting would be used in the winter; when the fan sensed coolness, it would boost warm house air into the room. Likewise, one would use the winter setting in the summer; when the fan senses warmth it would boost the cooler house air into the room. The fans are quiet as well as they are not on/off controlled, when a setpoint is reached the fans start slowly and increase in speed as the delta from the setpoint increases. I used the vent fan in another way. I reversed the location of the thermistor temp sensor (from the duct to the room side) and physically reversed the fans to blow into the duct (all easy to do). I placed the unit in an exhaust duct in my TV electronics closet, set it on the winter mode, and it exhausts the warm air from the electronics when the closet warms up (pulling cooler room air in from under the door).

Euro dishwashers and American dishwashers differ in width dimension.  If your cabinets are set for US dimensions, then a 3/8" (vague memory; probably difference between 30 inches and 75 cm) wood shim is needed on one side.  The Mieles of my experience screw into the walls on each side, so a snug fit is needed.  The shim need not be very deep, front to back. If the counter is stone and the floor is on concrete, then I wouldn't expect much vibration transmitted via those sides of the cavity.  This leaves gaps and sides and maybe back, depending on how it is configured.  Quality cabinets use 3/4 side plywood, but only 1/4 often at the (usually wall) back of the cabinet.  I'd slap some Evercoat Q-Pads or equivalent onto the back once I fixed the side gaps.  Then, if persistent, anti-noise coverings designed for dishwashers may be needed.  Be sure that thermal management is not degraded.

The wood shim blocks noise just like the cabinet sides do. In the directions below, the inherent assumption is that the cabinet sides are perpendicular to the cabinet faces. Measure the gap; measure the Miele width.  The difference, less a bit for clearance, is the shim thickness.  Any clearance values should be in the Miele installation instructions. Cut the shim from scrap material used for the cabinets, or have the cabinet manufacturer cut one for you (if a custom cabinet set) or find a finish carpenter.  You likely want the viewable edge to have a matching finish, although that is up to you. Length of the shim, top to bottom is from floor to stone countertop. Depth of shim, front to back, needs to be sufficient to be flush with the cabinet frame and extend far enough so that the Miele mounting screws have meat to go into. Screw the shim to a cabinet side, taking care to use a length of screw that doesn't penetrate into the cabinet volume, then attache the dishwasher.  Mine has three screws, as I recall, on each side.  There should be caps that cover the screws and keep water from leaking out. Important!  Do not screw in the dishwasher until it is snug against the stone countertop, leveled in all directions, and properly aligned with the cabinet faces.  Whenever my dishwasher has had to be removed, I have spent upwards of an hour doing recursive alignment until satisfied. Is your dishwasher on wheels?  Do you have the installation directions?  You may be able to download them or order them from Miele parts dept.

I fear that there is a misunderstanding about make-up air by the OP.  The hood flow and the MUA flow (including house leakage) are always equal.  What happens without deliberate MUA is that the hood blower, by its nature, adjusts flow to balance its performance against the pressure loss from cooktop to outside to cooktop.  In doing so, it lowers the house pressure relative to the external (outside) pressure.  This can cause back-drafting of combustion appliances depending on whether there are any and how they are operated.  Back-drafting brings carbon monoxide into the house. The 400 CFM rule is at best an attempt to balance competing economic issues against safety issues and depends on a certain level of house leakage, something modern construction tries to avoid.  Whether using a blower that is rated only for 400 CFM will actually be safe is a question that requires a lot more information to answer than we have, possibly more than the OP has. Back-draft susceptibility is summarized below.  Note that this back-draft susceptibility data was provided by another forum member a few years ago as an image.  (I haven't found the source of this, but it is believable.) ***** Mechanical-Draft Appliances Heating systems with fan-powered exhaust systems can withstand higher negative pressures than natural-draft appliances. Some types of fan-powered systems are much better than others, however. In order of effectiveness, the choices are: « Sealed-combustion. Also called “direct vent,” these appliances draw all combustion and dilution air from outside. These can typically tolerate negative pressures in the range from 25 to 50 Pa. * Power-vented. These draw their makeup air from indoors and are also called fan-assisted, forced-draft, or mechanical-draft. These can typically tolerate up to 15 to 20 Pa of negative pressure. * Induced-draft. These have a small fan added for energy performance, not to overcome house depressurization. These can typically tolerate 5 to 15 Pa of negative pressure. By comparison, an atmospherically vented furnace can back-draft with as little as 5 Pa of negative pressure, and a gas water heater will have spillage at 2 or 3 Pa. Fireplaces can start having problems at about 3 Pa. Canadian codes limit negative pressures in homes with atmospherically vented equipment to 5 Pa. U.S. codes do not currently address the issue (in a plainly spelled out "prescriptive" number). 1 pascal = 0.00402 inches, water column 1 atmosphere = 407 inches, w.c. ******** tl;dr: MUA renovation expense may or may not be needed for safety even with a 400 CFM rated blower.

I don't know how big of a tree you're talking about but it's important to get as big of a root ball as you can handle. A larger tree could be quite large and require a hydraulic loader or the like. Picea glauca is drought tolerant to a point, after it is well established. It prefers consistently moist soil but will endure a dryer area if you keep it moist for the first year or two after planting, if no rain. A dug tree can take 3 years to fully establish. The bigger the tree and how badly the roots were butchered when you did the digging, will determine how long it takes for the tree to replace the roots that you left in the ground when moving. Mine have survived some pretty dry summers the past few years but one of the smaller ones lost its top 16" due to it getting too dry several years in a row. It has recovered since.

A yuzu tree grown from seed has proven to be reliably hardy for me unprotected on a roof terrace in an urban setting. I have found that the decisive factors for me for winter hardiness are next to the genetic predisposition of the plant the size of the stem and the pot size. The pot has to deep enough to minimize the perched water table and prevent it from completely freezing through when the Arctic temperatures hit. Aside from its hardiness, yuzu is attractive to me for be very fast growing when given the right conditions, namely warm days and nights and plenty of moisture and fertilizer. My loft apartment provides plenty of heat in the summer and I was able to get a meter and a half of growth on a tree in one summer. That was impressive. These factors make me consider using it as a rootstock for getting plants up to size before I try to overwinter them on the balcony. I recall reading that the Japanese used yuzu for a time as a rootstock for satsumas and it pops up as a rootstock every now and then in scientific papers but perhaps someone on this forum has experience with it as a rootstock already and can report of their findings. I presume it would be a good match for plants which are considered to be related to yuzu, like sudachi or kabosu. I plant to graft my yuzu on it this season if the seedlings that I germinated last month grow fast enough.

While this is obviously not the highest level or work, it doesn't seem irredeemably bad.  At this point I think there are some things that need to be addressed and some expectations that need to be adjusted. First and foremost, to really give advice we need more pictures that show the entire job, not just the items that the OP feels are problematic.  Let's also note that many great contractors will have a punch list to finish projects. Going picture by picture here are my thoughts. Picture 1:  This is a picture of the tile behind the range and the only problems seem to be the cuts against the ventilation system which are not going to be that noticeable.  There certainly should be some grout touchup in a couple of places, but after a few touchups this doesn't seem bad. Picture 2: This doesn't look that bad.  Someone needs to come clean the tiles a bit but other than the tiles against the cabinets, that no one is going to see, this seems fine.  The corner isn't really that bad given how crooked the walls are.  No one is supposed to finish the unfinished bottom of cabinets, it just isn't done unless there are special circumstances.  There are plenty of fantastic cabinets that don't have finished bottoms. Picture 3: I have no idea what I am looking at so it is impossible to comment on it. Picture 4:  The contractor needs a better blade and a someone needs to slow down and do a better scribe, but I strongly suspect that at this price point that usually gets caulked.  Finishing the toe-kick area needs to get done but that is a fairly small job and can easily be fixed and is not really a big job. Picture 5: This is really a non-issue.  It needs to get fixed but a dab of construction adhesive and it is done.  These sometimes get tacked on if there is work left to be done, but again, this is really nothing more than a few seconds to fix. Picture 6: This is the biggest issue.  That first tile really needs to be replaced so the cut is a bit tighter and the corner line is a bit thick, but the walls are as crooked as the day is long and the grout line might have been left thick so it was harder to notice.  I am not sure if the contractor was hired to tear down old walls and true them up, if so then there is a real problem.  However, if this was not a down to the studs remodel then crooked walls are just something you have to deal with as best you can. The garbage:  In my area the standard operating procedure for small updates and remodels is that contractors will place the construction debris in the appropriate area/container and will not haul away debris unless paid for doing so.  This is because the disposal rates are much more favorable to homeowners than businesses, so few people want to pay four times more just because the business is doing it.  However, most will load the debris into the container when it is on the premises. This might actually be a terrible job, but at this point it is a bit much to say so for sure.

Constant Beauty dianthus are an entire line of perennial pinks and carnations (14 cultivars in total) that have been bred specifically to be extremely heat tolerant, thus extending their flowering period. Traditionally, dianthus are cool weather plants, blooming heavily in spring, snoozing quietly through the heat of summer and then possibly offering a modest rebloom when the cooler weather of fall arrives. These (CB's) were developed and bred by Green Fuse Botanicals in CA to ignore heat and drought and offer continual flowering and should be widely available through any retailers. Just search under the Constant Beauty trademarked label. I think the term "genetically modified" was throwing me off :-) While these plants are certainly the result of very careful and selective breeding, there is no genetic modification in the sense of gene splicing involved. That sort of horticultural technology is almost exclusively reserved for large agricultural crops were the return on the millions of dollars involved in arriving at a GMO'd product is assured by future sales of plants and/or seeds. To the best of my knowledge, I am not aware of any ornamental crop that as been genetically modified beyond the selective breeding already mentioned. It is just not economically feasible. I'd be interested in seeing whatever literature is available that documents Proven Winners claims.

Historically, an original late 18th c. early 19th c house on which this is based would have had 6 over 6 in the upper windows and 6 over 9 in the lower windows if  the lower sash is long enough that the divisions would be of nearly equal size in both sashes. They tried not to have obviously different sizes of panes in the same window, and also tried to have similar proportions of panes in all. The 1830s houses I lived in were primarily 6 over 6, but if the window had a small upper sash, they were 3/6, or a long lower sash 6/9, and the top floor which had a half sized window had 3/3 so it looked like a single 6 lite sash. It was all about proportion. When one house did a modern replacement, they just did 6 over 6 in every window no matter what the sashes looked like so the half window looked silly with 12 tiny panes in it, and the large lower sash on the first floor had 6 overly long pane in it out of proportion with the upper half of that window.

Breakers are intended to protect wiring from overheating due to overloading and thereby causing fires.  They also perform other tasks such as ground fault safety and providing a means to depower a circuit.  So long as the breaker was appropriate for the wiring when originally installed, then you can re-use it. However, your phrase "shared with another" makes me wonder just what configuration you have.  Do you have one two-pole breaker feeding two devices 240 Vac each, or two two-pole breakers, or one two-pole breaker that you think is feeding two devices 120 Vac each, one per pole, or what? If you intend to replace a receptacle rated for 35 or more amperes with one rated for 15 or 20 amperes, then the receptacle should be of the breaker type rated for 15 or 20A.  This not only protects the receptacle, but also limits current into an internally shorted device connected to the receptacle. If you actually have two 2-pole breakers being used, and you want to have one circuit operating at 20A with a 20A 240 Vac receptacle, then that circuit's breaker should be changed to a 20A two-pole breaker. What type of plug is part of the new convection oven?  See https://www.americord.com/nema-charts for help with this question.

Roasted Fennel and Farro Salad Recipe INGREDIENTS 2 to 3 fennel bulbs (about 1 1/4 pounds without fronds), halved lengthwise, cored and sliced ½-inch thick (about 3 cups) 4 thyme sprigs Salt and freshly ground black pepper 6 tablespoons extra-virgin olive oil, plus more as needed 1 cup pearled or semi-pearled farro 1 bay leaf 1 orange 3 tablespoons red-wine vinegar, plus more to taste 1/8 teaspoon red-pepper flakes, plus more as needed 1 cup mixed herbs, such as parsley, dill, cilantro and mint 1/2 cup coarsely chopped pitted green olives 1/4 cup thinly sliced pitted dates 3 scallions, thinly sliced 1/3 cup crumbled feta (optional) PREPARATION Step 1 Heat the oven to 425 degrees. On a rimmed sheet pan, combine fennel, thyme, a large pinch of salt and black pepper, and 2 tablespoons oil, and toss to coat. Spread in an even layer. Roast until golden brown and tender, 20 to 30 minutes, tossing after 10 minutes. Discard thyme. Step 2 While fennel is roasting, make the farro: In a medium pot of salted boiling water, add farro and bay leaf. Cover and cook until tender according to the package directions, usually 10 to 25 minutes. Drain, discarding bay leaf, and pour farro into a large bowl. Step 3 Grate about ¼ teaspoon zest from the orange into the bowl with the warm farro, then halve the fruit and squeeze in the juice. Stir in remaining 4 tablespoons olive oil, vinegar and ¾ teaspoon salt. Taste and add more salt, vinegar or grated orange zest if you like. Step 4 Add roasted fennel and red-pepper flakes, and toss to combine. Stir in herbs, olives, dates and scallions. Mix in feta, if using, and almonds right before serving. Taste and add more salt or vinegar, and a little more olive oil for added richness if you'd like.

Many people have never been lucky to have a shower with volume control.  Once you have used one, you will always want to install one. Think about the sinks in public bathroom with motion activated faucets ... those faucets are either on or off ... and the on volume is usually too much and splashes all over, but you can't adjust it.   At home, most of us have volume controls on our sink and kitchen faucets ... why wouldn't you want that in your shower too? I hate staying in hotels and having to use the showers with no volume control!

"Is the volume control really necessary?" Nope, because the flow of water from modern shower heads and hand showers is severely limited. In the "old days" showers were virtual fire hoses so the flow had to be controlled by a valve. Today's shower heads are limited to 2.5 gpm (1.8 gpm in California) so no volume control is needed. My Hansgrohe Croma Showerpipe (thermostatic; 2.5 gpm shower head) has no volume control and I don't miss it. If you want a valve with a volume control, be sure it's separate from the temperature control so you don't have to reset the temperature every time you shower. So avoid any old-style, single-handle controls.

I’ve had worm bins for more than a decade. Multiple bins. I had one bin that got nothing but coffee grounds, because I wanted matter that was already fine so I didn’t have to sift it. Not only did that worm bin do well, it had to be divided it had so many worms in it. I've had worm bins that did far worse (a failed banana peels only experiment comes to mind). I had to give away one or two bins because they got so over-populated and they had cofee grounds as part of their diet for sure. I’m a fan of science (I’m a computer engineer after all) but sometimes science is hard to quantify without more details than fit on a web page. The amount of caffeine in coffee grounds is not easy to measure because it varies on a lot of factors. How old are the grounds? How much water was used in relation to the amount of grounds (eg how strong was the coffee)? Were the grounds fresh or bagged from a grocery store? What kind of beans were used; different beans have different acidity levels, caffeine and oil contents. How did you store the grounds after use—water in the grounds will seep down so a large 20# container of grounds will have more acidity and caffeine in grounds at the bottom than at the top. And finally how was the coffee prepared? French press? A paper filter dip system? Metal filter drip? Those all change acidity and caffeine levels in subtle ways. Even more factors like how dark the roast. For garden and vermicomposting, acidity levels in grounds are just as important as caffeine. Many times caffeine is almost immeasurable in spent grounds while acidity can be through the roof, or vice versa, depending on all those factors above. I’m a coffee connoisseur and I’ve been giving grounds to my worms for a long time so I just go by my gut, but in 10+ years never had a wom bin die from cofee gorunds and so far my roses haven’t complained either.

Neem oil will certainly not hurt the plant but it is not the most effective treatment for scale. Many types of scale have a hard or solid exterior 'shell' that limits the effectiveness of most contact pesticides. Any treatments need to be applied to the nymph or larval stages before they develop that hard exterior. A systemic is the most effective treatment but not considered organic. Horticultural oil works also but again, like neem oil, you need to be very conscious of the timing.

I agree with GG; I have found the light horticultural oils to be more effective than neem oil. Also less smelly. By some standards horticultural oils are organic; I don’t really mind one way or the other in this case, as it will stay on the outside of the fruit and washes off easily in the kitchen. With oils one is trying to smother the scale. Even after killing an adult scale their eggs can hatch from under its dead body. These hatches can go on for some time. One must repeat at an interval of about 7 to 14 days for some time; perhaps months. Temperature will affect the time it takes for hatching, and the time it takes for new scale to reach breeding age. At some future time one can clean all the dead scale and sooty mold off the leaves and stems with insecticidal soap (and some elbow grease). Best of luck.

I can share our recent experience of remodeling in a high cost of living area. We gutted the kitchen, primary bathroom, upstairs bedrooms, bathroom and playroom. We went with a design build firm that's been around a long time and got personal recommendations from friends who have used them for multiple phases. We thought that going the design build route would eliminate the problem of having someone design a plan that ends up being out of budget. And it was our first major remodel, and the whole thing was overwhelming. However, if I had it to do over again, I would hire a separate architect, kitchen designer, builder and interior designer. When you go the design build route, you get whomever is assigned to your project, and not necessarily the people from the firm that you might choose on your own. I also thought that they would all talk to each other since they're at the same firm. We still had some things in our design that the build team said didn't make sense. I think that hiring a separate architect and builder who have regular meetings would accomplish the same communication or maybe even better results. For us, selecting a firm was stressful; I think the idea of having a rough plan and getting numbers for it is outdated. Building and remodeling is busy and competitive, and they are not going to spend time figuring out an estimate for you. Not one of the four firms we interviewed even tossed out ideas for what we could do. They listened to our list of wants/needs and said "we can do that." You have to look at other things in order to choose your team, and then cross your fingers that you made the right choice. Look at past projects, call past clients, see if their style is what you want. We hit it off with the sales person from our firm, but then we never saw her again. So I'd ask if you could meet the people who would be on your team. Other tips are to visit the project every single day. Have everything in writing, and then follow up if you don't get an answer. I think you need to up your budget, especially if you're talking about moving walls and adding on. And try to research every thing on your own--trust but verify. I would also try to have people on your team who have kids or experience living with people and can make practical recommendations about organization and flow. Do an inventory of your kitchen and plan where everything will go in your new space. Ask questions in a respectful way but also understand that things can get missed. No one is going to care about this project more than you are, and you need to make it your full-time job. Move out if you can. And take pictures because it's amazing how quickly you get used to a new beautiful space and forget how the old one looked. :)

When interviewing for GC's we had people give an hourly rate (no), someone who wrote the estimate on the back of his business card (no), someone who told me to have my husband call him for the discussion (no), and finally found our GC at our local Home Show. He gave references, arranged for us to see a couple of his jobs, and his estimate was a line-by-line estimate and came in on budget. Do not rush this stage of the process.  But I think we were lucky as the 6-month reno went very smoothly. Right now we are doing some major work and we have a contractor and an interior designer (hired separately) who is invaluable to both of us. We fired the first one who wouldn't listen. You need people who actually listen and and who are respective of the way you live and of your budget.

For our whole house reno, we hired an architect, GC, and an independent CKD.  All communicated with each other, when the need arose. I feel the homeowner has much more control, when hiring each professional separately.  This way, you get to choose the pro, not the design build firm.  You’ll want to be able to discuss concerns, design choices, and any changes that come up, directly with each pro…which often doesn’t happen with a design build firm.  See the many threads here, about disappointments with design build firms. For all that you’re planning, I also believe your budget is a bit low. Oh, just want to mention…it really helps the reader, when a long post is in paragraphs.

text: Creating the illusion of more space in a tiny bathroom, especially in a basement setting, can be challenging yet rewarding. With the right design choices and strategic use of elements, you can transform your 42x96 bathroom into a seemingly larger and more inviting space. Here, we'll explore practical and creative ways to maximize space and enhance the overall feel of your small bathroom:

I wouldn't seek out an individual or firm based on their pedigree.  Rather, I'd look to assemble an experienced team with a good track record on projects similar to yours and which seems like one you can work with.  Design/build firms offer a built-in team approach.   Some have architects and/or engineers on staff.  Some will contract those services as needed.  Alternatively, you can hire the individual expertise of an architect, kitchen designer, and remodeler and serve as liaison or you can serve any or all of those functions. If you'd like to act as your own general contractor for the life experience, go for it.  But don't expect the product of that endeavor will be less expensive, faster to execute or will give you more "control."   You pay for your "education" in remodeling.

After looking at your first floor plan, it seems that you have a lot of space to work with, but it's not laid out to best advantage. First impressions--the kitchen is small and yes, oddly laid out.  It might make sense to move it into the space where the dining room is now, turn the breakfast nook into a large mudroom/pantry, and use the existing kitchen as a dining area. All that requires a lot of work and planning, so I'd get an architect involved straightaway.  Any time we've done any large-scale improvements, we used an architect who put the plans out to bid.  However, as someone said, it's possible that builders/GCs have enough work that they don't need to do that anymore.  It's imperative that you get references--I've only hired registered architects, but some are definitely better than others. If you want to keep within the footprint and leave the kitchen in the space it occupies now, then a good design/build firm might work.  We renovated our kitchen a few years back (pre-Covid) and used a family-owned kitchen and bath firm.  No sales people--the owner was our main contact and he gave us a detailed estimate, which was spot on.  His kitchen/bath designer was great, but I did preliminary layouts.  We are in a very high COLA and without moving any walls, the project came in at about $150K.  Of course there were unforeseen problems that added to the cost, but we went with a good mid-range cabinet company and high end appliances.  All new plumbing, electrical, flooring. If you intend to stay in the home for a long while, which I totally understand (low mortgage rate, good schools/neighborhood), then do your homework and plan very well.  We had all planning, purchasing and delivery of materials done before one bit of demo began.  The entire process took about 3 months.  We did not move out, but because the work was done in the summer, and we trusted the workers, we went on vacation for a lot of the time. Good luck with the project and keep us updated on your progress!

My zone just became 6a, not sure when.  I was 5b. Last winter was hard on plants in Maine, lots of plants everywhere didn't bloom, even if they reliably bloomed for years.  I find my hydrangea does better when  pruned to be shorter, the buds on the ends of the stems frequently die anyway. I'd prune it in the spring.   If it hasn't bloomed often, give it lots of water in the summer, trim it in the fall and heap leaves over it in the winter, to mulch it.

It sounds like this shrub is a type of hydrangea that may already have developed dormant, spring 2024 flower buds at the ends of the stems. Big Leaf and Mountain Hydrangeas, which typically produce mophead form blooms or lacecap form blooms, do that and they should be planted where they can attain their estimated size at maturity (height/width) and then they should be rarely pruned to control size. These types of hydrangeas develop dormant, spring 2024 flower buds anywhere from July through September-ish 2023 inside the stem ends and the buds then open and resemble tiny broccoli heads in 2024. Under normal conditions, the bud at the end of the stem typically opens and blooms but, there are back up flower buds located lower down the stem that can also open if the one at the end gets killed by late frosts/pruning stems prematurely/etc. The leafless stems of these two types of hydrangeas should not be pruned now as they are currently loaded with dormant, flower buds. If they still remain leafless by the end of June (or maybe even wait until July if near Canada), you can then prune them all the way down. Pruning these types of hydrangeas to control their size is typically tricky and risky. Prune at the wrong time and you get no spring blooms. Once the shrub stops opening new flower buds in spring/early summer, you then have a short time before the plant begins the process of developing dormant, spring flower buds (for next year) inside the stem ends. On the other hand, if this hydrangea is a smooth or panicle type of hydrangeas, you are looking at leaf buds along the stems and there will be no flower buds until somewhere between mid spring or summer so these stems can be pruned as late as very early spring without affecting 2024 flower bud production. For pictures to help you identify the type of hydrangea that you have, go to this link: https://plantaddicts.com/types-of-hydrangeas/

Relative means "in relation or in proportion to something else".  When referring to relative humidity the relationship of "something else" is the moisture vapor as a percentage to the total amount of moisture the air can actually hold at a specific temperature.  Warm air can hold more moisture vapor than cold air can so RH is just the ratio. A 5 gallon jug can hold more water than a 1 gallon jug, if they both were filled 50% full they don't hold the same amount of water each and it's only a percentage of what they can hold.  The same principle applies when humidity is measured as a percentage, so think of 70 degrees as the 5 gallon jug and 40 degrees as a 1 gallon jug.  If you want to know the actual volume of moisture in the air it's expressed as "absolute humidity" and expressed as grams per cubic meter of air (g/m3. There are tables and charts to express humidity as relative or absolute.  Your outdoor absolute humidity for 40 degrees at 70% RH is about 32 g/m3  give or take a gram, and your indoor absolute humidity for 70 degrees at 18% RH is again about 32 g/m3 give or take a gram. To sum it up the actual humidity in the air outside and inside is actually the same amount.  To add more air vapor inside to feel comfortable you must increase Absolute humidity to 54 g/m3 (or about 40% Relative humidity.) Hi, Gabe, I think you've got issues with your relative humidity monitoring device.  Based on my psychrometric chart and antique eyes, If you take outdoor air at the conditions indicated (45F, d.p. = 35F, R.H. = 68%) and heat it to 68F, you get a relative humidity of 32%  That's within ASHRAE's prescribed comfort range of 30% to 60% R.H. albeit at the low end or the range. As for measuring the relative humidity of the air stream leaving your air handler, it's both incorrect and not particularly relevant.  If you vary the air temperature between 88F and 98F the relative humidity varies from 18% R.H. at 88F to 12% R.H. at 98F (again, according to my psychrometric chart and antique eyes.)  I suspect your electronic meter is limited at the low end of the measurement range by the particular type of sensor installed. Now for the non-quantitative part:  If you think it's too dry, then humidify the air to achieve the desired comfort level, irrespective of what the relative humidity reading is. For the sake of completeness, a couple of notes about prior posts: "If you want to know the actual volume of moisture in the air it's expressed as "absolute humidity" and expressed as grams per cubic meter of air (g/m3."   A gram is a unit of mass.  Absolute humidity has units of mass of water/unit volume of air. "To add more air vapor inside to feel comfortable you must increase Absolute humidity to 54 g/m3 (or about 40% Relative humidity.)"  You don't add "air vapor," to increase relative humidity you add water to the air. Normal convention is to stick to a single set of units--either metric or Imperial.  It would not be appropriate to indicate a temperature in degrees F and an absolute humidity in gm/m3.

" I’m still unsure why the air is not closer to 30% RH at 68F based on the humidity of the outside air."   You're trusting the indication of an inexpensive, uncalibrated electronic device. Take a simple dry bulb temperature and a simple wet bulb temperature utilizing a sling psychrometer and use a published psychrometric chart to determine relative humidity.

“I clicked newest and it showed one five minutes ago and then it progressively went one hour, three hours ago, and 20 hours ago.” I’m not saying there’s nothing wacky, this site is notorious for wacky stuff that only happens to some people, but what you describe above is exactly what’s supposed to happen. If you want it in chronological order you should click oldest.

You might recall using a sling psychrometer in 5th grade science class.  They don't need batteries or calibration. They consist of a dry bulb and wet bulb thermometer which can be slung around to get the wet bulb reading.  If you're questioning the accuracy of a digital thermohygrometer, it's a simple way to check if the reading is in the ballpark (I keep both in my briefcase of troubleshooting tools.) You can buy a serviceable one for less than $20 and you can find a psychrometric chart on the internet for free.

Who doesn't have a calibrated digital thermo hygrometer? I have 3 and costs were between $80 to $300.A calibrated traceable hygrometer I bought for around $80 years ago was calibrated and certified to be within it's accuracy range for humidity of +/- 2%, or a 4% swing and only for a year, and could be substituted for a  sling psychrometer which has the same accuracy range.  But it's old and calibration service is more than just buying another one for $100+.The one you used has a 8% accuracy swing and not for the full RH range that isn't certified to maintain advertised accuracy even out of the box, so it's far from being even close to accurate.  If you want a digital full range hygrometer calibrated and certified to be within a 2% swing with a fast sampling speed you're looking at $400 or more not to mention calibration service fees to maintain calibration.What you need is Humidifier if your house can't retain passive humidity sources such as showers, laundry, dish washing, cooking ect.   Your HRV does not transfer humidity but a ERV does with limitations.  I've searched for humidifier options for a HRV and found none.  The only other option is to install a humidifier in the HRV fresh air outlet, or a portable humidifier.  A steam humidifier would the best option if you decide to install one after the HRV and would require a water source, electric and controls to only allow operation when the HRV is running using a simple sail switch and a humidistat connected in series.I use a small Honeywell portable humidifier in my shop and they call it a vaporizer, whatever but it's just a heating element in water. Violets grow best in bright indirect light. Eastern exposures are preferred, but others will work with some modifications. Northern exposures will provide plenty of light in the summers, but you may need to supplement with some artificial light in the winters. Southern or western exposures are often too bright unless you have shade trees or a sheer curtain or blinds angled upward. Artificial light such as LED or fluorescent will give the most consistent results as it can be set with an automatic timer.

One of two things are generally responsible,high water pressure or loose washer.   Unless you have this at other toilets and/or faucets we will assume loose loose washer and that you know how to replace faucet washers.  Check washer screw in angle valve to see if it's snug.   Tighten if it isn't snug,reassemble and and hope hammer is gone.  If that doesn't cure it you can try replacing ballcock washer (not all have replacable washers) .  If washer isn't replacable or new washer doesn't fix it you will need to replace ballcock.    If you aren't piticularly handy with minor plumbing repair I suggest finding valve located near floor beneath toilet and turn it clockwise 1/4 turn.  If you hear the hammer next flush,turn another 1/4 turn clockwise.   Continue this routine until hammer stops or water ceases to fill tank.  If there's no joy you will need to replace ballcock.   Good luck

Aside from going perpendicular to the floor joist.  Flooring should run along the longest length of the house. Example: 40' x 25' , flooring should be laid along the 40' dimension. Most single residential homes are wide at the front with a short depth like the example above. Flooring will always run from left to right. Condos, townhouses and multi families are narrow at the front and deep towards the back. So, flooring runs from front to back. Having a continuos run is the best look and more budget friendly.  It provides a faster installation since, there is no change in direction. Which means you are not setting . up a new starting line or layout. You are also, using less waste because there are less cuts along the narrow dimension of the rooms or house.

But certainly if you have some large thermal mass next to a plant, like a brick or concrete wall, the temperature won't drop as fast. With regard to leaf moistness, I'm betting that if you set aside a squash leaf and a pepper leaf to dry, the squash leaf would dry out first. Why? Because the surfaces are slightly more moist. Squash leaves are covered with these urticating hollow bristles that may conduct moisture. Pepper leaves are smooth and waxy. The leaves that are moister are ones that will be cooler. It is well understood that plants can get frost nipped if the temperature is above freezing but if there is wind. That's because moisture on the plant evaporating cools it below the air temperature. I heartily support GG's statement above. One might state such if one were referring to seedling/mature native trees in their wild normal haunts, but it is simply way off the mark when considering non-native and exotic plants in soils and conditions way out of the ordinary/customary for those species. I will defy any gardener to be successful with planting and growing almost any tree on a disturbed soil property - like many urban conditions and most new home lots where most A horizon soil no longer exists - without significant effort to improve soil fertility, texture, compaction, etc.  Perform a COMPLETE soil test - not just NPK - and learn about general amendments to recreate quality soil conditions where they are lacking.  As noted everywhere, tree roots don't stop growing at driplines, so plan to improve soil qualities and fertility throughout your property. All plants - mature trees or otherwise - need available nutrients and moisture when going through their growth cycles, and especially if they are stressed by any number of environmental factors.  Due to maintenance practices, many even undisturbed garden soils lack nitrogen at the normal level.  Whether you like "... enriching the fert industry..." or prefer to go about this via more organic methods, your plants won't care if there is available N when they need it. A very simple example:  note when female plants of most of the genus Ilex are ripening their fruit.  If nitrogen is not able to be adequately taken up from the soil, the plants will reallocate nitrogen from green leaves, resulting in a noticeable yellowing/lighter greening of the foliage.  An  appropriately timed dose of nitrogen during this period of the Holly lifecycle can ameliorate this condition. I am a long way past my era of landscape management, but there are drips, wraiths, silhouettes, and fleeting memories of the proper terminology and practices in soil health and management.  Work is involved, and rapid results are rarely effected.  That's why trees should last a lifetime...

text: Hi, First of all, congratulations on your first house with a nice large garden. A few good points have been mentioned already with the screening and boundary fences. For me you need to make a wish list of what you need, would like to have, and dream of in your garden. You have already mentioned veg, and seating area. Think of a style that you like, there is also no reason to mix different styles as this is more common now like a contemporary layout and hard landscaping with a cottage flowing style of planting. I would also consider loosing that large shed, three reasons, one it looks rotten at the base, two, it's in the wrong place, and three, I think it may be far to large for what you need. Carful consideration of the sizes of the spaces for each area, like may your main patio/terrace big enough so it fits your garden furniture comfortably without you feeling like your falling into the borders and still leave room for people to walk around without tripping over things. Thinking of focal points and views through the garden. Do you need room for children to play? A garden is the largest room of your house and can be one of the most enjoyed to relax in and unwind or destress from a busy day. I would consider getting in a professional designer if not to do a full design, to at least have a consultation and walk around the garden with you to advise on solutions and possible ideas. Some designers will even do a rough sketch for you on site of how it could look, although not to an exact scale. Doing a garden is not a cheap thing, although there are thinks were you could save with the right advise. Getting it wrong by just doing a bit at a time will leave you with a garden that does not flow, better to follow a plan and do what you can when you can and afford it. That way you will end up with a beautiful space you can admire and enjoy. All the best Ian

Hi Emily, What a lovely blank canvas you have in there! It is a sizeable space and with the right layout you wont even notice the weird shape. I couldnt agree more with @AGI Landscapes! The planning of a garden is often overlooked but it is a very important step as mistakes can be expensive (and yes, also agree 100% that the cost of doing a garden is most times hugely underestimated - and I think that popular garden revamp TV shows have a lot to answer for that). A well designed garden will match up what you want out of it (and therefore a wishlist is a first step), your tastes (inspirational pictures that you like are very helpful), the nature of the garden space (this includes its shape, natural conditions, any problems to be overcome etc) with aesthetic awareness to create a space that not only looks good but that also works and flows well for you. Because your garden is big, getting a design done could be very helpful as you could do the build step by step as budget allows without loosing sight of the big picture. Some designer like me offer online based services which could be cheaper than in person. If you are interested at all, you can find more details on my website. www.therootedconceptgardendesign.co.uk Best of luck with your garden! Deborah

The HVAC contractor is proposing a dual fuel system with a Bosch heat pump. It is being promoted as a more cost effective system then an AC only equipment. I am skeptical this is true. Bosch Inverter. It sounds like it's the Bosch IDS 2.0 or greater. Bosch doesn't make AC only equipment. It's important to know the difference. Oregon has large regions of humid climate an inverter as like the Bosch will do a much better job of dehumidification on it's own due to 1% steps up and down. (longer run times). Cost efficient operation, less energy used. The con with that is less extremes for this climate. But the need for dehumidification is less due to the way this machine runs. The heat it provides when adequate may be or may not be gravy depending on Nat. Gas Prices compared to electricity prices. If gas is cheaper, then run the furnace. Probably as simple as switching the stats to emergency heat. Whole home dehumidification system can easily cost in the realm of $5k (probably more today due to inflation) depending on sizing among other factors, then you have yet another system to repair and maintain. To be clear the whole home dehumidification system is built for "control" of humidity levels with in the home. Meaning you have set points for the dehumidification system to achieve. Provided it's adequately sized and working it will dehumidify to those levels you set from the control. The Bosch Inverter is an air conditioner / heat pump that runs on temperature. Dehumidification is performed as a function of operation. If the temperature is satisfied and the Bosch is off there is no dehumidification. So understanding of this is illustrated here to help you grasp the understanding of what it is. I have a Bosch IDS 1.0 at my own home installed in Oct. 2019. It dehumidifies well for my often humid climate of Katy, Texas. Dehumidification aspects versus temperature often confound people. As you can have low temps and high humidity, just as much as you can have low humidity and high temps and vice versa. If humidity is a problem, adjust the thermostat a few degrees lower. In my opinion any thing below 50% RH in your home is good. 55% is borderline high. 60% RH or more is too high. 30% RH is too low. If you have high humidity and low temps, provided you can stand the "cold" the Bosch is built to run in virtually any weather where other systems fall drastically short. Example: Outdoor ambient temps lower than 55F often cause damage to lower end systems. The Bosch can run in AC mode down to approximate 15F outdoor ambient. In heat mode the Bosch can run down to -4F. There are protections with in the equipment that will prevent it from running in a nefarious condition. Other equipment outside the inverter realm, do not provide those protections. The Bosch is a stallion, to put it bluntly. (especially the IDS 2.0 or greater)

Aesthetic is not a color of white or off-white - it's too dark to fit in either category. It's a Light Near Neutral. Darker than Simply White and also more color. Simply White is def more neutral.   With Light Near Neutrals and whites, don't have to be concerned with a difference in Chroma. I mean, it doesn't hurt to apply that rule of thumb - quantifying the contrast between two colors is good info to know - but it's not critical like it is with white/off-white. The reason it works is Simply and Aesthetic belong to the same hue family. You do want to test carefully. Aesthetic is at the beginning of the Yellow hue family over near the end of the Yellow-Red hue family in color space. Which explains why some may sense a flash of plum-brown/violet. That's doesn't mean Aesthetic White has "purple undertones". Colors don't have undertones. Aesthetic is a low chroma color and low chroma colors in this part of color space *can* shift and look purple-ish. It's a matter of lighting and context *IF* it happens. Big IF. Again, that does mean it has purple undertones. Nothing sneaky or hidden or under anything. It's just a color light relationship thing that we can be aware of and look for.

I’m not a pro but I’ve designed and renovated several homes while lurking on Houzz. The biggest problems I see with your floor plan are that both entry traffic patterns go right through your kitchen and your secondary bedrooms are still very small. There’s also no separate kids space/play room for your future kids to spread out to as they grow so those small bedrooms will feel even smaller with toys or desks packed into them. I assume your mom’s bedroom would be in the storage/gym area but she’d have to share that bath with guests and access the bedroom either through the shared bath or through the mud room, which isn’t ideal. The kitchen is massive but anyone sitting at the island would be facing a wall rather than the entertaining space and yard. I’m currently in the midst of a full gut remodel on my own home, turning it from a 1200 square foot 2 bed/1 bath home into a 2600 square foot 4 bed/3.5 bath home so I know how difficult it is to rework an existing space. In my case the additional square footage came from building up and adding a dormer to capture previously unusable second floor space.  Is there any way you can build up, even if it’s only for your master suite or the two kids rooms and a bath? You may find it’s more cost effective to stay with the existing footprint and build on top rather than enclosing your patio and converting your garage to living space. By adding those spaces to your interior you’re creating a pretty square house, which means a large windowless space in the middle no matter how you lay it out.  Look for cpartist’s posts for a very detailed explanation on the importance of a house’s shape in its design and layout. If building up isn’t an option then I’d try to find a way to reorient the kitchen so it’s not a traffic path (turn the island 90 degrees?). I’d also close off the door into the bathroom in the entry so that is private to the storage/gym area and relocate the other secondary bathroom to between the bedrooms. That bathroom is then in a better spot for guest use and equal distance to the secondary bedrooms. Pushing the middle bedroom down also makes those two bedrooms more similar in size so your kids won’t fight about who gets stuck with the smaller interior room. It can be very discouraging to have your dream project criticized and torn apart, which is why I never put my floor plans up for review and rather lurked through all the floor plan posts to gather and experiment with ideas. I went through about 50 different iterations and several packets of tracing paper over 7 years before finally deciding on the plan that worked best for my family. While the final plan isn’t perfect it allowed us to keep much of the original structure while enlarging and modernizing it. Best of luck in finding the right layout and getting your project off the ground.

19.5" depth front-to-back is way too shallow.  Even moreso if you are not going wider than the 36" range.  You did not say what range you have, but check its depth measurement.  It is likely around 26-28" deep front-to-back.  You would be spending all that money on a hood that won't even cover the front burners.  That means the smoke and grease will float up over the front of the hood getting it dirty, rather than the smoke and grease going up the exhaust.  I would get a 24" depth hood. Make sure your hood insert is made with baffle filters not mesh filters and not a "hybrid baffle-and-mesh filter".  Just baffle filters.  Also check the exhaust duct diameter that goes from the hood to the outside.  Your hood should have a duct diameter or 8" or 10".  If the duct is smaller, you will have a noisier, less effective hood through no fault of the hood.

I agree with Kazzh.    Unable to afford to do the whole frontage in one go lots of people in your situation would add a pitched roof to the porch or get a new front door.   But what you end up with is a house with a confused identity.   You need a complete plan that either embraces the 1970s architecture or removes that style completely and replaces it with an alternative.   It your house is a one off then the latter gives you the most options.   If your house is on a street of similar houses you are forced to go down the 70s route.   I like this architecture and lots of people do but I bet you can look at other peoples “improvements” and see how it is easy to get it wrong. Your house is an example of piecemeal “Improvements” because I suspect the original window divisions were uniform and the stone between the garage and front door has been added later.   If it were my house I would remove the stone.   I would have the tile removed, insulation added and then retiled.    I would replace the flat roof with another flat roof but add insulation and edge detailing so it looks more substantial and more expensive.    I would replace the windows with aluminium thin framed alternatives and make the divisions faithful to the 70s.    And then landscaping and external lighting.  To be done well this all needs a complete plan. Money and a professional eye to avoid the typical duck ups that most people made in the 90s and 2000s when they thought they were improving these houses. So live with it for a while and save up because to do it well will be expensive.

This comes from design media, (Houzz, HGTV, Pinterest, Instagram) where wall features are added for a variety of reasons. On HGTV they are added to renovations because they are relatively inexpensive, eye catching, but completely impersonal unlike art, so they appeal broadly to potential buyers of flips, for example. On Pinterest or Instagram these things are done, because again, they are easy, eye catching, inexpensive, and again, really impersonal, unlike taste in artwork, so they can be presented as vignettes and get a lot of clicks and likes. The problem with PInterest and Instagram and such is that they are often without any context of any sort with regards to the rest of the room or house. I know an influencer who creates stuff over and over in one isolated corner of a room, that has nothing to do with anything else in the apartment. It's like a little stage set. So people see these, the pictures are kind of fun, and then they want to do them. A much earlier phenomenon was the "Puddled drapes" thing in the early 2000s on Trading Spaces and such. text: As noted in the references I linked to, damping off is a big problem for onions in both home and commercial plantings. See also this piece by Bayer. https://www.vegetables.bayer.com/za/en-za/resources/disease-guides/onions/damping.html They make the point that onions are most susceptible to damping off at low light levels and high soil moisture in the flag leaf stage. That's where you have ONE stem popping up, as what we're looking at here. I should add that overfertilization just induces more fungal growth, so it's best to NOT fertilize seedlings until they are more mature. Strong lighting and good ventilation will help dry the soil surface, which tends to prevent it as well.
