2" is what code requires, and to physically handle the rate of discharge most modern washers have. Not sure if it's understood, but that 2" includes the standpipe, P-trap, and branch line in the entirety back to the main waste line (given no other fixtures on that branch). Older houses typically only have 1 1/4" or 1 1/2", and often in galvanized pipe, which can corrode inside causing the effective size to be less. So hooking up any washer to less than 2" older piping is a risk, you just don't know. To combat this, discharging into an adjacent utility tub solves it. Also in Europe, becoming more available in the U.S., are combo washer/condensing dryers that do not discharge at the fast rate.

You will have to plan the mural layout and positioning to determine what part of it makes sense to lose behind the bed, but still centers the scenic on the bed. Typically murals of this sort are put in hallways or dining rooms because in a dining room the primary furniture is floating in the middle of the room and does not cover substantial parts of the mural. One of the reasons that these murals tend to come in a version meant to be mounted over a wainscot or chair rail is because it lifts the foreground of the scene up so that it can be seen even if there is some furniture against the walls. With a full length installation --which I tend to prefer over the shorter versions, in general--in this bedroom you are going to "lose" all of the people in the scenes because they are going to be in a band about a foot above the floor. That may be fine, but it will remove a lot of the extra color in the mural, because the people are the only part of the mural not in the green/brown range. In traditional murals, as opposed to digital, where you can rescale the entire image probably infinitely, the adjustments for length within certain parameters, were made by adding a lot of sky        at the top, not ground at the bottom. The much simpler 1960s mural in my house came with enough sky on it to make 10 foot drops if I recall correctly, but it was all at the top. There was very little room for adjustment at the bottom, and it had a free form bottom that faded into background at the bottom too. This mural probably starts with the main images all the way at the bottom of the drop. This is messy, but this is where the foreground ends up in a full length version.

Rush selecting an optimal hood that meets ventilation requirements is pretty much doomed.  At best, you will just have to buy from a quality manufacturer based on some parameters we can suggest.  It is much better to understand what requirements drive the parameters you end up with. Rather than providing you with a pile of links to review, for which you may not have time, let's start with what size your cooktop is, whether it is gas or induction or electric coil, and whether you cook stir-fry and sear meat or just simmer stuff with your most prolific greasy plume coming from simmering bacon.

Alright.  Let's assume that minimalist will do.  I'm going to choose 60 ft/min (CFM/sq. ft.) as the required air flow rate into the hood aperture.  How big is the aperture?  Do you want an aperture that overlaps the front-to-back cooking zone, or just the back 18-inches, say, and anything to be cooked that is greasy or odoriferous gets cooked at the back? Example: Wolf hood liner 34 x 22.  (19" front to back is also available; calculated in parends.) Effective entry area approximately 5.2 sq. ft. (4.5 sq. ft.)  Multiply by 60 yields 300 CFM (270 CFM).  These are actual CFM values, and blowers must be chosen to achieve these at various pressure losses due to baffles, ducting, and make-up air (MUA) restrictions.  Simple approach for centrifugal blowers (not VaH squirrel-cage blowers) is multiply by 1.5 to get rated CFM, which calculates to 450 CFM (400 CFM).  At these levels, local code enforcement might not require deliberate MUA, but some is a good idea for reasons you can search out on this forum. Note that for more vigorous cooking (smoke point of hot oil), I would recommend 90 CFM/sq. ft. Duct diameter should keep full power flow rate (300/270) air velocity in the duct between 1000 and 2000 ft/min.

A great number of this type Dendrobium like to be grown "hard and fast" during the summer--meaning, lots of sunlight, water and fertilizer.  In the fall they would like a cool dry spell to trigger blooms.  The fast growth in the spring and summer encourages them to sprout new canes with lots of roots. When you cool them down and reduce the water, the canes will shrivel, drop most of their leaves and stop growing.  The flowers will be produced from the cane joints, where little bumps will form on one side of the cane, and grow into a cluster of blooms.  If the plants do not get the cool dry time, most often they will just grow new canes from many of the joints, and pretty quickly turn into a mass of new  canes and roots.  That's what your plant looks like in the photo.   in the winter, you can just remove the newer lateral canes that have a nice set of roots, and put them in regular orchid bark mix, and have a new plant.   I worked for a greenhouse once that kept a large number of this type Dendrobium.  They grew them outside under shade cloth during spring and summer, with lots of water and fertilizer.  In the fall, on the morning after the first frost, It would be "all hands on deck" to move them all into the big greenhouses where they were hung from pipes suspended from the ceiling of the houses.  In the big greenhouses they would get no fertilizer, and almost no water, and would be a mass of blooms for a large part of the winter.   Keep up the good work. Bill

I lived in an early 19th C house that had very tall pocket doors that lined up with the windows, (this is another thing, window heights almost always used to be higher than door heights. This lining up of the tops of doors and windows is a late 20th or 21st century thing and I think it started when people started designing things directly on a computer), then lower than the pocket doors were the main room doors, and shorter still were any closets or other built in secondary doors. The idea being why would you give a Closet the same importance as the entry to the room. The upper floors of my current house has standard size doors, but the first floor, which has windows all the way to the ceiling, the room doors and openings all match this (92") but the closet doors and the basement door are all standard height. It's for handling stains and soils that respond accordingly to heat.  The onboard heating element heats the water to generate steam, which emanates through the drum perforations.  Temperature choices are unavailable being that the machine must control the temp to a specific target to produce the steam.  The fill level (in the outer tub) is minimal during the steam process so there's less volume of water to be heated. Steam is at the same *temperature* (212°F) as boiling water, but steam contains more heat *energy* to vaporize the water.  Delicates or items subject to heat damage reasonably shouldn't be exposed to the steam.  Reasonably, follow similar restraints as ironing (steam vs. lower temperature dry-press).

Sienna, Depending on the machine, most will start with a warm wash and heat the water to a higher temperature with a built in heating element. This does increase stain removal by a wide margin, but is not ideal for a majority of loads. The long wash time increases wear, the heat can cause fading for dark items, and energy use is increased. Though, it does increase removal of greasy or oily stains. I like to run the steam option on rags because of this, however when this option is selected you can not run a prewash. Some machines 'generate' steam and inject it into the tub, like DADoES said, which IMHO doesn't do very much. Consumer Reports tested the steam cycles on some unspecified washers about 10 years ago and found that the increase in cleaning performance was minimal compared to the increase in energy consumption and cycle time. However, if you increase the soil level or wash time on any machine, cleaning performance will improve. Any additional exposure to detergent solution will improve stain removal even without agitation.

It’s so easy to seal it yourself.  Requires no skill so you don't have to wait on your fabricator to do it.  Just buy sealant at Home Depot - the “511 Impregnator Penetrating Sealer”.  Get the 16 oz size which is the smallest.  That small bottle will still outlast you in the home.  Do NOT get the one that says ”enhancer”. You wipe it on thinly.  Wipe off any excess and any drips down the backsplash.  Keep the windows open, or if the weather is too cold, run the hood exhaust. Having said all that, marble is a porous stone.  You can prevent the water stains your OP mentioned.  The oil stains you later mentioned may be a little tougher to prevent. That is the nature of marble.  In Europe they have marble in kitchens and bathrooms that are decades old and are etched and stained and nobody cares.  You can’t alter the intrinsic makeup of marble, but the sealer will help prevent most stains.

Your "before" room is not only narrow, it's visually narrowed because it has so many things cluttering up the walls.  My thoughts: - Could you bring the machines "forward" and add a closet at the end of the room?  This'd allow you CLOSED storage for things like the ironing board.  You could still hang coats on the door to the closet. - Do you actually use the sink?  My mother had a sink in her laundry room while I was growing up, and we literally never used it.  I've never had one as an adult /never wanted one.  In my opinion, losing the sink would free up a good bit of space /allow you to do some of the other things you want. - No, I wouldn't go with a full-sized kitchen sink.  Nor would I use a farmhouse sink, which would project into the narrow space.  If you keep the sink, I'd downsize it. - Why do you want the butcher block countertop?  For folding?  if you keep the sink, could you get a sink-cover that'd allow you to make that area into a countertop? - Are you married to keeping those big machines?  I had those big things, and -- when they died -- I replaced them with smaller, traditional machines that were common two decades ago.  Not missing the monster-sized things at all. - You say you're not using the cabinets because you can't reach into them -- that's largely because these large machines make it harder to reach things above them.  I'm only 4'11", and -- now that I have smaller machines again -- I can reach the bottom shelf of my cabinets.  I keep emergency food storage in the upper shelves. - If you rearrange so you can reach into the cabinets, could you hang the dog leashes INSIDE the cabinets?  Maybe a pegboard on the inside of a cabinet door? - No to a storage bench -- you don't have the space.  Not unless you give up the sink /put the bench in its place.  If you keep the sink, could you go with a trough sink and have open shelves for shoes underneath? - Someone suggested stacking the machines.  Before you go that direction consider whether you're tall enough to adequately reach the dryer (I'm not -- again, 4'11"); go down to Lowes and reach into their machines.  Also ask yourself, how will you pull stacked machines out from the wall to clean the lint?  I'm all about fire safety. - You didn't mention the hang-to-dry space over the sink.  Is this something you're currently using?  I hang LOTS of stuff to dry, and I'd definitely use it, but -- if you're not -- this would be a great spot for a shelf.

If you’d consider it, look at smaller top loaders as Theresa has suggested. The laundry in my other house was as narrow as yours and we have big front loaders.  I downsized to smaller top loaders and I made sure I could reach the dryer bottom.  Mine are Samsung; great price from Costco but I would not recommend because the dryer has already been repaired once.  I don’t miss the huge machines and am still able to wash king sized bedding.

text: Most of what Chris said is correct, but reducing your mowing height is not. There are hundreds of types of grass seed and seed mixes for lawns, different types of grass have different mowing heights, i.e., look at golf courses, you have the rough, longer grasses, the fairway, medium cut and the greens cut very short. I would always recommend leaving your grass cut height for a garden lawn to a minimum of 20mm. Two reasons for this, one, grass is a plant and it needs to photosynthesise and for this it needs leaves, if you keep chopping of the blades of grass to short, you are reducing its leaves and it will become weak over time, and thus you will have to keep feeding and watering more. Second, leaving the grass that bit longer will stop light reaching the ground and will prevent a lot of weeds germinating as the longer grass will smother them out and it will need less watering. Besides, when ever you cut your lawn, when cut long or shortish it will always look smart. If you really want a short lawn get the right grass seed mix, but beware, the shorter the grass, the more maintenance is required to keep it looking good. Ian

I would arrange the furnishings this way. Use the entry wall for a narrow table and mirror or art above Use the sectional to define your foyer entry area. IMO this is a more balanced layout for the room so that all the heavy items are not placed on one wall. If you want a larger TV you require a longer wall.  Get window coverings so no one can see the TV.  BTW, why would you hang the TV as if it's a sports bar?  Your TV should be much lower.  See the diagram below for proper height.  You can mount a sound bar directly below the TV so you can have surround sound. In my arrangement, all seating faces the TV, not in yours.           For the entry table you could select a console panel end table and have the large wicker bench I should below slide under the table.  That way you have a place for shoes that is ventilated and a bench for people to sit when required.

How deep are the shelves?  They shouldn't be any more than 12"D, especially along the 5' wall.  That gives you 24" of aisle width.  While that's a bit tight, it's enough to load/unload food in the pantry. 12"D is the "sweet spot" for pantry storage.  Not so deep that things get lost in them but deep enough for the majority of items...cereal boxes, cans 2 or 3 deep, pantry containers, most small appliances, etc. You could put deeper shelves with baskets on them, maybe even pullout baskets/shelves for things like potatoes or very small items. For the shelves themselves, I would either use solid shelves or put plexiglass on the shelves so things are balancing on the wires and to prevent spills from going from the shelf where the spill originated all the way to the floor, including all over the items stored beneath the spill. We had wire "pantry shelves" in our old pantry and I hated them!

I'm still not completely clear as to exactly what surface you presently have. My understanding is the pool was sandblasted to remove the paint. Is the original concrete shell's surface exposed? Or was the paint over a plaster finish? The proper method to tile a pool's surface whether it's the entire pool or just the waterline border, is that original concrete surface (substrate) must be exposed. Any paint or plaster must be removed. When I say plaster, I mean a cementitious material that is troweled onto the surface. Popular plaster manufacturers these days are Diamond Brite, Pebble Tec, Hydrazzo, Wet Edge, etc.... Years ago it was called Marcite or a marble finish. If there is plaster under the paint, it must be removed. The best method is a water jet blaster. It will remove all the plaster and expose the substrate. Trying to chip the plaster off is pointless. This is a specialized piece of equipment, and this process can be expensive. But, it will remove all unwanted material. Generally speaking, proper methods include that the surface must be prepped with a water-proofing material and layers of special mortars to provide a sound base to apply the tile. The surface must be sound and free of loose material. Any cracks or fissures must be addressed. Laticrete is one company that has guidelines for installing tile specifically for pools. Mapei is another company. Some contractors though have found other ways to provide a lasting job. Tiling and entire pool will be an expensive process. The job is labor intensive, and it's not done in a day or so. Most tiled pools use glass tile which can be expensive in itself. The contractor saying the "glue" makes me guess an adhesive is the plan. That's not advisable. Adhesives/glues are typically used just for quick repairs of tile just to last the season before completely re-doing. I hope this information helps.

Discospondylitis  mimics the symptoms of degenerative myelopathy.     this condition is mostly prevalent in certain breeds, most especially GSDs, pembroke welsh corgis, boxers,  chesapeake bay retrievers, rhodesian ridgebacks.     before this was given a name, it was often diagnosed as  hip dysplasia.     in reality, it is a genetic disease of the spinal cord.     it's a cruel disease in that it is catastrophic but painless.    the onset is gradual but 100% fatal with no treatment and no cure. it cannot be definitely diagnosed until a post mortem is done on a sample of spinal cord tissue.    it is presumptively diagnosed after everything else has been ruled out (disc disease, injury, hip dysplasia, etc.). i lost my male corgi to DM, diagnosed via analysis of spinal cord tissue.      there has been a years-long study into dm at columbia university in missouri.    the really sad thing about it is that it's considered an "old dog disease" in that the onset of symptoms normally doesn't happen until the age of 8-9 years so very few breeders test their breeding dogs for the gene.    because of this, DM is running rampant in the corgi breed.     simon came from a show home, i got him when he was about 4 years old, retired from the show ring.     thankfully, he was never used as a stud dog.     his symptoms started at the age of 9 and i opted to euthanize him 18 months later as the paralysis was spreading.    i have always wanted another corgi but i have yet to find a breeder within a reasonable distance of me who does test for the gene.    it was agonizing to watch  him slowly decline and i simply won't put myself (or another dog) through that again, ever. https://vhc.missouri.edu/small-animal-hospital/neurology-neurosurgery/facts-on-neurologic-diseases/degenerative-myelopathy/

This happened in my garden with banksia lutea (Yellow Lady Bank's rose), and also 'Cl American Beauty' (1909 - not to be confused with a HT and a HP with very similar names which are repeat bloomers). One year my gardener did prune one of my once bloomers hard in the late Winter, (I forget which one), and it barely managed to produce a few blooms in the following Spring. If you want maximum bloom, take those long laterals which flowered last year, "self peg" them by bending them around to form hoops or circles and tie them back to themselves. The plant should respond by pushing short flower stems from the hoops of last year's wood, providing you with nearly wreathes of blooms. Then, after it finishes, you can prune those laterals back to the length you desire. Yes, they will grow longer over the summer, but any shortening needing done after then should be done in fall so all of the remaining growth should be of sufficient maturity to provide you the flowers you want for the following year. "Pegging" is literally like training a climber, only not limited to only two dimensions and not solely against a wall, fence or trellis, though it can be.

Yes, that is how curtains work.  You buy as many panels as you need for each window.  The general rule of thumb is 2x the width of the window in panel inches. The place to start is finding grade on drive and both sides of drive from garage to street.  There appears to be a drainage swale between drive and large tree.  If need be, make it deeper.  A mixture of masonry cement and adhesion additive can be used to create a raised hump across door to prevent water running into garage and divert to swale.

A good assumption is the slab near the garage was originally installed sloping away. If it is now not doing so, and there is a lip at the garage entry, then you can raise the slab via mudjacking. Then, a review of the grades around the slab, making them lower than the slab so water does not run onto the concrete, will help. If you are resodding, the entire yard should have grade addressed to add swales and slopes where needed to direct water away from the house and driveway. If your grade has only an 8" or so drop to the street, a trench drain (or french, or catch basin, etc) would not work well as those would be lower than the discharge elevation to daylight to grade within your property (because you most surely cannot tie into the street sewer, and probably not the storm sewer if one exists). You can measure grade elevations with a laser, or a string and line level. Even a water level for those 8th grade science aficionados.

I see an easy and inexpensive fix in my book of knowledge.  If the slab isn't heaved up like 3onthetree suggested think about my doing the below. Using a concrete saw cut a 4" to 6" strip out of the driveway concrete right next to the garage floor apron.  Install a channel drain and grate across the drive that drains into a leach tank on the right side.  Install a sump pump and run a 1 1/2" poly hose out into the yard on the other side of the tree. A leach tank just has holes in and before installing put a healthy layer of gravel underneath.  Set the tank in and fill the sided with gravel.  in lighter rains the water will leach into the ground so the pump won't run a lot, but when it rains enough to fill the tank the sump pump will move the water into the yard. Some people will run the poly hose all the way to the street, your choice, but a lot easier and cheaper from what you want to do with the same results.  What I described is common practice for many applications, low drives, egress windows or just moving water from a low spot in the yard. So far, we are all telling you a version of the same thing: Skip the separate filtered water faucet and filter the cold water to the sink(s). If you have access to run the plumbing you can use a single filter. I like my solution because it's a standard cartridge holder and you are not locked into a proprietary filter - you can buy any one of several types and brands. It's really designed for high volume with a large filter and 3/4" plumbing connections. Mine is located in my basement and provides filtered water to the kitchen sink, refrigerator ice maker, and cold water faucets for the bathroom sinks. Just a note about any carbon cartridge filter: They require regular replacement - even before the carbon "wears out". The filter I linked to has a capacity to filter up to 95,000 gal of water, which would last for many years on a single faucet if you just looked at it that way.  But in every case the carbon removes chlorine - or chloramine if it's a catalytic carbon filter. These are disinfectants and one of the things that make the water taste and smell bad. Over time, these filters can become a breeding ground for bacteria because the disinfectant has been removed. Most carbon filter cartridges should be replaced annually. The specific one that I linked to has KDF 55 that prevents bacteria buildup and extends the carbon filter life. I replace it every 2 years. I would not go with the 2-4 year recommendation on any carbon filter cartridge as was suggested in a previous post.

First, why duplicate shower heads side-by-side? Second, every shower head should be a hand-held.  They're more versitile.  A plain in-the-wall shower head has no benefit over hand-helds ... except cost. Is there an easy way to clean these wet rooms that doesn’t require a hand held shower head? A couple off-the-wall thoughts: - If you do go with duplicate shower heads, be sure they're on separate controllers.  Yeah, seems like common sense, but that's not so common these days. - This board often suggests you place your shower controllers in such a way that you can reach in /turn them on without committing your body to the initial cold spray ... that doesn't seem possible here. - Consider where you'll hang your towels in a wet room. - Consider where you'll place grab bars ... if you are elderly in this space one day, you may not feel comfortable walking across the open space without something nearby. - Consider those windows.  When it's a matter of water + window, water always wins in the end.  A good option might be glass bricks.

Many of the "Teas" can be encouraged to have stronger stems by pruning out all but the strongest growth. The thinner and wispier the growth, the greater the potential for thinner, weaker peduncles which will then "nod" or hang their heads. Teas don't generally like to be pruned hard, but thinning out the weaker, thinner growth will result in stronger, thicker shoots which will, in turn, produce stronger stems which will hold the blooms more upright and "HT-like". You'll find those with naturally stronger peduncles are literally more HT in character. Tea X HP or the reverse, created HTs. The HP genes resulted in the stronger, thicker peduncles. When I allow my Teas to grow larger, more what they are genetically programmed to be, I get more of the weaker, thinner peduncles and more "nodding" blooms. By thinning out more of that wispier growth, thicker, stronger shoots are encouraged with correspondingly stronger stems and more upright blooms. Is the method perfect? Nope, but it works much of the time.

I'm very interested to read other responses to your question. Here are my thoughts & experiences: Almost always, what you are getting when buying a plant labeled Dracaena indivisa "Spike", is Cordyline australis.  For some reason, growers persist in mislabeling this species, I really don't know why.  I'm in zone 8b and there are a lot of fairly big Cordyline australis around, and because of their size & age, I assume a lot of them have withstood temperatures below 20F and down to 15F, which is what zone 8b is now.  Zone 6 (a&b) is from 0F to -10F.  So this species is not hardy to zone 6, but it probably can withstand brief forays near 15F if properly sited.  And yes, above ground containers = reduced hardiness to cold, but in this case it just wasn't all that cold.  That said, keep watching the plant.  When a cold event happens around here, Cordyline can be very, very slow to show their displeasure. Often times the bulk of the plant looks fine but if you investigate the growing point at the very top center you can see the damage, and that dead tip can often be pulled right out.  One more thought, here in zone 8, if cold kills Cordyline australis to the ground, it almost always grows back in spring and can look quite nice by the end of the growing season. Of course this is for plants planted in the ground, all bets are off for container plants.

I believe Klark - artinnature - is correct. The plant in question is not a dracaena but a cordyline. The dracaena is not even frost tolerant, let alone able to withstand a zone 6 winter but as noted, the cordyline can tolerate temps well down into the 20's or teens for short periods of time. And can grow to a significant size if not cold damaged. I had several mature 15-20 footers in my previous garden but I would not choose to plant another as they are incredibly messy, dropping dead fronds constantly when they get that tall and mature. And they don't exactly offer much of the genius loci to a PNW garden :-)) Soil in a container will most closely mimic ambient air temps so certainly a potential for them to freeze solid in zone 6. And that will severely limit what can be successfully grown all winter. However, it is easier to create microclimates with containers simply by moving them to more favorable or protected locations. And different plants will display different root cold tolerances quite separate from their above ground growth, often being significantly sloped to be more or less cold tolerant. That the cordyline survived I would attribute to just pure luck, as it certainly would not be hardy enough to tolerate that degree of cold under typical circumstances.

Contrast effect. It's likely the current color of the walls. In a perfect world, a neutral gray would frame the samples. A white border is less than ideal because viewing a color on a white background will make a color look darker than it is, feel bigger in mass and volume, and at the same time weaken its hue - white breaks hue so it looks duller. Additionally, it's only when the walls reflect off each other that a paint color's character fully develops in a 3 dimensional space. Especially true with colors of white. Painting bigger samples can help - like from the corner to the window and at least 5 ft vertically. Tenting on entire wall isn't a crazy idea.

(((Lyban))) I’m so sorry for your loss. My heart hurts for you. I also lost my DH after a long and brutal cancer (his second one) and BMT. Fruiting fig trees, Ficus carica, are a lot more cold hardy than many suspect. They are certainly frost hardy as frosts are not uncommon in zone 9 and these trees flourish here. In fact, the cultivar Chicago Hardy is good to zone 6 (-10F) but may die back to the roots in a hard winter however will resprout and produce fruit the following season. So hard pruning as indicated is definitely possible but never a requirement unless one wants to keep the tree small. And that is purely a personal objective as the trees never get huge (20-25' typically) and will produce fruit without receiving any pruning attention.

Below is a pic of our 2 fig trees (Brown Turkey & Celeste > both fruits seem identical to me) they're about 12 ft tall and I wouldn't want them any taller.  Last winter I pruned out the center limbs of both "bushes" since they seemed to have a very light crop the year before. This opened them up for more sunlight and this past year they went gang busters, best crops ever. To pick the figs up top I use a long squeeze grabber to pull over a limb which are very flexible and don't snap.  They have frozen down to the roots on 2 occasions a while back, temp dropped to 3F.

Hello Nicola Normally building works like building a home can't start until all necessary Permits have been obtained, so without me having a better understanding of your situation, it is actually not possible to advise if you should dissolve your contract or not. It sounds like you have had a contract with a builder since 2022 but they have not started? However the advise here from contributors seems to be based on the assumption that your build (of a Building) has started and is somewhat advanced. In areas that can be very bright and hot, such as parts of SoCal, it can actually be beneficial for even full sun listed plants to have some protection. Shade cloth is often listed in various percentages for the sun blocking amounts. 30-50% can be fine for many plants, such as sun grown vegetables, especially if there are a lot of sunny days in your area. If you are close to the coast and experience frequent and extended overcast conditions, the extra screening might be more shade than true full sun plants would prefer. It is difficult to tell from the photo the percentage of shade your screen would provide. The color of screening matters a bit, too. Maybe you can compare it with some various percentages of shade clothes that are sold at garden centers to get an idea of the shading amount your screen provides. There are ways to determine light levels of an area using camera metering, but that gets a bit technical to explain. You can search for sites that explain how, and are similar to the way it can be done for indoor plants:  Greenery Unlimited | How to Measure Light for Plants (lazily, just the first site I came across--there may be better ones) It might give you a sufficiently close idea between screened vs unscreened.

Thoughts on Layout 1: - The bed is nicely oriented towards the door, room, and bathroom ... the walking patterns flow well.  However, I think the bed should be centered in the room. - What size bed are you thinking?  My bedroom is 13' wide, and we have a king + 2 large nightstands ... with the dresser on the side, I think you'll need to go with a queen. - 30" is enough width for a shower, but with 12' at your disposal, 36" would be nicer, and 42" would be nicer still, but 42" might steal too much from the other areas. - Where will you hang your shower towels? - With duplicate sinks you don't have any space for drawers at the vanity, and you will miss them ... better to go with one well-done sink flanked by a set of drawers for each spouse. - I'd move the sink vanity to the opposite side near the toilet ... this keeps all your water in one wall, and it streamlines your walking path.  Also, a pocket door behind the vanity (with its plumbing) isn't going to work ... unless you make the wall extra thick. - I understand this places the vanity under a window ... go with transom windows above the vanity. - Reverse the swing of the door into the bedroom ... you want to open the door and walk into the room /not a wall. - You have nice windows in this space. Thoughts on Layout 2: - I prefer the bed centered in the room + the dresser and TV dead-ahead of the bed. - The bathroom is more streamlined /flows better.  Many of the same thoughts from Layout 1 are still concerns. - The closet space behind the door is kinda wasted.  Maybe go with a pocket door on the closet. - This gets you a little more space in the bathroom and the closet. instead of a linen tower Oh, I just recognized the linen tower ... in Layout 2, I'd move it to the other end so it'd provide a pony wall for the toilet. For storage, there is an cabinet filling the space above the toilet between those walls. Practicality is more important than fashionability.  My concern is, If you put a cabinet over the toilet, where will the towels hang? Do not have the closet door in the bathroom. It would allow moisture from the bathroom (mainly the shower and tub steam) to get into your clothes. I don't think this is a real problem.

No way to repair that.  The particle board laminate substrate soaks up water like a sponge, swells and falls apart.  So you can't clamp the sink down tight to the laminate and water will continue to seep under the sink rim and eventually ruin the cabinet.  Counter top replacement is the only solution. If you install another laminate counter top, seal the raw particle board edge when you make the sink cutout.  A couple of coats of oil base primer and make sure to use a sealant under the rim of the sink--plumber's putty or, preferably, a continuous bead of Lexel (caulking department at Lowe's). In the interim, I would roll up a microfiber towel and place along the back edge of the sink so help soak up water that gets splashed back there.

No, 4000k LED is not correct for a kitchen.  There is ONE Houzz commenter on this forum that says that 4000k is correct for a kitchen, and she says it over and over, on hundreds of posts, so that it seems like it is being recommended a lot if you don't notice that it's the same person saying it over and over.  LED lighting for a kitchen should be 2700k-3000k.  The 4000k level is for a hospital operating room or if there is a family member with visual impairment. Placement of the lighting is important.  Ceiling cans should be placed along the perimeter of the upper cabinets, about 12-18" from the edges of the upper cabinets.  Undercabinet lighting should be placed toward the front of the upper cabinets - though contractors like to place it toward the back because it is easier for them and will save them 15 minutes.  If you place undercabinet lighting toward the front of the upper cabinets it will shed light onto the center of the counters beneath them where it is most needed.

Yes, Patricia, you're confused.  The OP has a full-masonry fireplace that had a wood-burning insert which has been removed.  They simply want to install gas logs in a masonry fireplace.  I did that in my former home.  The clearances they are inquiring about for a mantle and surround which they depicted in white.  It's not clear what building code applies to the OP's installation, but the 2018 IRC, which forms the core of most statewide building codes, specifies them in section R1001.11  Here's the pertinent specification from that section of the code: (4) "Exposed combustible materials or trim is permitted to be placed directly on the masonry fireplace front surrounding the fireplace opening providing such combustible materials are not placed within 6 inches (152 mm) of a fireplace opening.  Combustible material within 12 inches of a fireplace opening shall not project more than 1/8 inch (3 mm) for each 1 inch (25 mm) distance from such an opening."

I second what Charles Ross said. I have been selling Gas Logs for over 35 years and I can tell you that the clearance specifications remain the same for the fireplace whether you burn wood or gas logs. Charles has provided the typical accepted clearances for a masonry fireplace, which is what you have. Prefabricated zero clearance fireplaces have their own clearances, which you would get from the owners manual. Unlike typical gas logs, a gas insert may have it's own clearances, which will be provided in the installation manual.

text: This is a little confusing. The optimum suitability for plants isn't about fluorescent or LED. It's more about the color of the light. "Daylight" (5000-6000K, bright white) is somewhat more appropriate for plants than "Soft white" (2700-3000K, muted white, sometimes called "warm white"). "Daylight" has more blue. You can get either color with both LEDs and fluorescents. As I said, either color should work OK, for bulbs with similar luminous output, assuming the seedlings get enough of the light. For general indoor lighting, many people dislike "Daylight", though, so it may be a little harder to find. But the difference between LEDs and fluorescents is wholly the electrical power per lumen and how much heat they put out. The color of grow-lights might be slightly more optimal for long-term plant growth, but considering how little they are used for seedlings, where plants are eventually planted outside, they can't make much of a difference, except in the thickness of your wallet. Not well appreciated but a cloudy sky has a higher color temperature - more like 8000-10000K. So it is bluer than daylight, but of course under a cloudy sky plants get a lot less light.  Of course, when the sky is clear, but your plants aren't getting hit by direct sunlight, the blue sky has a color temperature of 15,000K or so. The rising and setting sunlight has a much cooler temperature. So grow-lights try to reproduce the illumination that plants outside really don't get that much.

author_name: daninthedirt (USDA 9a, HZ9, CentTX, Sunset z30, Cfa)
text: True about incandescent and fluorescent bulb intensity dropping over time. The intensity of LEDs drop over their lifetime too, but their lifetime is ENORMOUS. As a result, don't bother to replace old LEDs. Actually, the spectral absorption of chlorophyl is a little complicated. It strongly absorbs blue AND red light (and obviously reflects a lot of the green). About 30% more strongly for blue. So you need BOTH blue and red light. Red light appears to promote fruiting growth, and blue light tends to promote foliage growth. So I would be inclined not to call 3000K "poor".  But again, if you're worried about how much light your plants are getting, at least outside, the main issue is clouds. Don't get much "daylight" with those. Of course, if you're concerned that your seedlings under lights aren't getting enough illumination, just keep the lights on a bit longer.

"But again, if you're worried about how much light your plants are getting, at least outside, the main issue is clouds." UV light penetrates cloud cover.  Of course, it's stronger without, but still...plants still get exposure to light on cloudy days.  Regardless, the topic is inside lighting, and I do agree that 3000K light is not "poor", plants need light from the red through the blue spectrum through the UV spectrum.  Hence why I think plants do well with a mix of "warm" and "cool" bulbs.   This whole thread has me tempted to switch out half my bulbs for "warm" LED tubes and see what happens.  Except they're kind of expensive, so maybe just on one shelf (2 tubes).  That still doesn't address the lack of heat output, though.

I've notice there may be some misconceptions about Florescent lights.  All kelvin temperature bulbs must emit blue, green and red light in certain ratios or otherwise we wouldn't get white or yellow light, and the only difference is the ratio or intensity of the different wavelengths. Technically 3000K or 5000K florescent bulbs alone will grow seedlings OK because both have a sufficient intensity level of blue and red, but 5K lights have more blue while 3K have more red.  Plant seedlings will benefit more from higher levels of blue light and grow stronger and healthier stems and seeds,  but only during the seedling stage which lasts from germination to a few weeks after, and this is why I said 3000K was a poor choice for seedling. After the seedling stage more red is required  and the ratio is actually 4 parts red and 1 part blue,  or 4:1.  This is the ratio mostly used in commercial greenhouses and somewhat emulates the ratio as an average of the sun throughout the entire day,  If after the seedling stage you want your plants go grow faster research and studies have proven adding far right red light in with a peak of 730 um will increase size from 30% to 70% depending on the amount, and believe Dan covered this.

This is all borderline: Your lab is showing slightly less than 1 grain per gallon hardness - which is the definition of soft water. Your plumber is showing 2 grains - not very different from lab and within the limits of accuracy of his test kit. Neither reading would prompt me to install a softener. I understand that you believe that once the neutralizer has been added, the hardness will go up - thus the softener. The lab is testing the PH at 6.5 - which is the bottom recommended by the EPA (under 6.5 calls for treatment). The plumber is measuring 6 - but again not very different and within the limits of his test kit. I think you could be fine not treating this water. Keep in mind that any treatment that you do adds in more maintenance and such and so using a minimal amount of treatment has a lot of advantages. Here's what I would do: I'd completely plumb this so that I had the option of adding a neutralizer and softener - so with the bypass loops, drains, power etc. - but I'd hold off on installing anything. If you add a neutralizer later, I'd check the hardness after that's in service and see where it is. If you need to change the PH of the water - it's not going to be by much. Ditto with the water softener.

Multiple random thoughts: - Okay, so you have to keep the clipped corner ... you need to move the dishwasher one notch to the left.  With an angled sink, this is going to make all the difference in the world.  Why?  Imagine you are standing at the sink and you open the dishwasher ... see the problem?  The dishwasher door is where you need to stand. If you scootch the dishwasher to the left /insert one small cabinet between the dishwasher and the sink, you'll have the space you need to stand.  This is MAJOR. - Overall, your kitchen is not laid out for efficient cooking.  You'll walk to the far end to get your food from the pantry /refrigerator, then walk to the other end to wash things in the sink, then backtrack to the mid-point to the stove.  Note that you have no cabinets next to the refrigerator for glassware.  Inefficient flow, inefficient storage. - In a perfect world, you'd bring in your groceries, and your storage would be right there ... you'd bring it out of storage, and you'd have only a step or two to the sink /prep area, then you'd continue on a few more steps to the cooking area, and finally on to the table.  And you wouldn't backtrack during cooking. - Bouncing off that thought, consider that the most numerous things in every dishwasher load are silverware and glasses.  Ideally you want those things to be stored within one step of the dishwasher, and you then want the glasses to be right next to the refrigerator. - Will you have a microwave?  If so, where? - Where's your trash going to go?  Where's the pathway for carrying trash outside?  Consider that you want this pathway to be as short as possible; just last night I had a leaky trash bag, and it dribbled on the floor as I went out ... we all know this just can't be avoided.  Where's your recycling bin? - Where's your pathway for bringing in groceries? - Can you reach the middle of a 5' wide island to clean?  I could not, but I'm very small. - A 6-burner stove and a 54" refrigerator?  No, downsize to standard items.  I'd lose the duplicate ovens too.  You're showing a French door refrigerator ... look at the plan and consider how that'd work out.  The door you'll open with your left hand will block access to the main work area.  This spot would work better with a single door hinged on the right ... that'd allow you to open the door /access the whole fridge. - 3'6" is an okay aisle space ... IF it's from countertop to countertop ... countertops tend to hang over the cabinet 2" ... so you might only have 3'2", and that's a difference.  Be SURE of what you're planning.  And go down to Lowes or Home Depot and walk through their sample kitchens.  They'll be 3'6" from countertop to countertop ... see for yourself if you find that convenient. - I agree with those who say, "Put the laundry near the bedrooms, where the dirty clothes are /where the clean clothes need to be put away."  Yeah, I know, you're saying you want to wash where you are ... but the choice you're making is to carry baskets between the bedrooms and the kitchen.  It's easier to walk yourself back and forth to the laundry room. - Regardless, you should definitely flip-flop the washer/dryer and the sink ... the goal being to put the dryer on the exterior wall.  Cheaper to build and more fire-safe. - Have you gone to Lowes or Home Depot and measured washer/dryers?  When I bought a new set (during the pandemic), I was amazed at how much BIGGER the new machines are.  Be sure you're allotting enough space. - I see you have a cabinet next to the washer/dyer.  I don't know what type of cabinet you're considering here, but I'd go with something like a skinny Ikea cabinet (not a built-in cabinet).  The idea being something you can easily remove if your next washer/dryer is larger than the one you go with initially.  Just a future-proof idea. - Ask yourself whether you want to spend the space on a laundry sink.  We had one growing up, and the only time we ever used it was to thaw turkeys.  As an adult, I've never had a laundry sink and have never wanted one.  Consider that you have a sink only a few feet away in the kitchen. - You're plannig a skylight in the laundry room ... remember that water works against skylights 24/7, and eventually water will win.  Every.  Single.  Time.  Could you go with a window on that wall instead? - Definitely change the door on the pantry ... as presented right now, it's covering almost 1/3 of your shelves.  Imagine what that means:  you walk in the pantry, and you're forced to close the door to access those shelves.  A pocket door here would be better. - I'd absolutely want a motion-sensored light in the pantry so it'd come on when you enter ... to allow you to come and go hands-free.  Is that a skylight?  No .... light is the enemy of food storage. - I love pegboard in a pantry.  I'd lose the shelves at the back of the pantry /add a floor to ceiling pegboard on that wall.  This will give you great hanging storage, and it will remove the difficult-to-access pantry corners. - Look at the inswing door on that nose-to-toes half-bath.  Imagine you enter the room ... you have to scootch up against the sink to close the door /reach the toilet.  This should be an outswing door.  This 3' wide half-bath is going to "live small".  Uncomfortably small, and I'm a small person. - I like that you have a broom closet!  That's so often left out.  But what's that little indent near the broom closet?  Could you skip that wall /incorporate the broom closet area into the laundry room?  Make the laundry room a little wider /have a little more utility space across from the brooom closet?  Alternately, if you do keep the sink, would widening the laundry room just a bit allow you to have the sink and the washer/dryer on the same wall?  This would mean fewer walls with plumbing lines ... less expensive to build, fewer opportunities for leaks.

Tjhe first thing I would plan for is shade for the house from trees.  For morning shade, plant to E/SE.  For shade from the hottest sun of the day, trees to the W/SW.  Large trees should be some distance from the house and smaller trees--ornamentals and understory trees between the large trees and the house.  Layered shade like this provides the most cooling and also nestles the house into its setting.  Of course, the same placements would apply to anything you want to shade, deck, patio, etc. You mention you want privacy from a neighbor's driveway, but don't want to lose the view.  So what you want is not trees, except possibly small trees, perhaps to 20-25 feet, but large shrubs.  Some shrubs, like Magnolia stellata for example--good to zone 4--can easily get to 20 feet as can some Viburnums. Start your planning with the slowest growers and largest plants first.  Figure out the placement--and get it right because you don't want to be moving trees around.  Then work down to smaller plants. You have a beautiful home.  If planning all this seems beyond your present skill, get a good landscaper to  provide you with a basic design and plan to do the work yourself.

A bit of historic background about this rose.  I was given cuttings by Bill and Lorna Mercer, in 1988, from their garden in Bermuda.  I brought it home in my carry-on luggage (under Federal import permit), and propagated it at Florida Southern College.  After the 2-year Federal Quarantine, to be sure it had no pests or diseases we wanted to keep out, it went into the college gardens.  As far as I know, all commercial sources of this rose in the U.S. are from that importation.  The thing that makes that interesting is that Bill told me the plant he took the cuttings from was one he'd been working on for years.  He wanted a plant that was completely, permanently white.  So he always selected cuttings from and all-white branch.  He had done that for multiple cutting generations.  But it never worked -- sooner or later, he always again got red stripes.  But I do think he made a change in the variety; US-grown plants seem far less frequent in their production of red stripes than their Bermudian counterparts.  I'd like to get fresh material of a more "stripey" version, but at this point, importing roses has become a real nightmare, and I don't plan to do it again.

Grout is not waterproof!   Your issue is with the way the shower was built and how it was (or wasn't) waterproofed.  A properly built shower doesn't need tile or grout to be waterproof, but wouldn't look very pretty. Here is some information to get you started on how it can be done. Do even more research so you know what to ask a contractor and how to check that the correct methods are being used during construction. https://www.finehomebuilding.com/project-guides/tiling/waterproofing-tile-showers There are some other/older methods that can work well, but tend to be region specific, like California, where you can still find companies that specialize in waterproofing with hot tar.  Run from any contractor that tells you he does it some other way and hasn't had a problem in his 30 years of work!

If the tree is not currently infested with beetles... you have little to worry about. They don't tend to attack dead wood after the fact. If the tree is still up and you can get it taken down before spring emergence- do it. Though they can overwinter in bark, they like to emerge for spring feeding on tender new bark. Taking the tree down while still dormant can help reduce that risk. And if you do have an infestation, you can spray the tree with insecticide- follow the instructions on the label. Fortunately, a ten foot tall sapling isn't likely to be mature enough to be very attratctive to the beetle unless you are in a very infested area.

I agree with @millworkman that vertical shades will solve each of the problems you listed.  It used to be that vertical shades looked lower-end - but that was 30 years ago.  Now they have beautiful options in many fabrics and different levels of transparency or opaqueness.  You can have them entirely closed at night for privacy. The stackback for vertical shades is much less bulky than the stackback for draperies.  You could have the vertical shades with a stackback just on one side. I had standard vertical blinds previously, and the chain at the bottom got frustrating to use;  with it, the vanes sometimes wouldn't 'stand' uniformly even;  without it, they'd get moved all sorts of ways. The vertical sheer shades fit the bill;  the sheer fabric between the vanes helps to keep the vanes hanging uniformly, while also providing some level of light filtering.  At night, we twist the wand to close the vanes.  Have attached some photos here as comparison; closed and open vanes vs. glass only.     You'll definitely want to get samples of the ones you want to purchase, to ensure that the vane material gives you the privacy level you're looking for.  There are different levels of sheerness, and depending on how sheer the blind is supposed to be, the vanes may be either opaque plastic (like these are; these are not the sheerest ones in their line), or doubled panels of sheer fabric (which would give filtering, but likely not the night privacy).

Smooth hydrangeas like Annabelle and Incrediball can propagate via suckers. They send new stems from the crown/base of stems once the soil is warm in spring but you may need to wait longer in cold areas. The stems tend to be winter hardy and look dead or dried by the end of winter. Not sure if you can do a scratch stem test with a tiny plant's stems. Just let the plant get the sap flowing again. A tiny new shrub may not behave exactly like an older smooth hydrangea yet. That being said, if you have wildly fluctuating temperatures and had a sustained warm spell that broke dormancy, a temperature crash overnight may have killed the stems. Another possibility, winter was dry and they did not get enough water, in which case the stem or the plant itself could be dead. That occurs often in dry, mild winters. Going forward, avoid letting the soil get bone dry and water if the soil is dry at a depth of 4 inches or so + the soil has thawed + it is above freezing. Live stems should leaf out in spring but sometimes as late as June. If you do not get leaf out nor stem growth by the end of June, the shrub did not make it. Note: I usually grow 4" container plantings for a year in a bigger container before planting them outside. Active new growth should become visible once soil soil temperatures overnight are much warmer, maybe when typically above 50F at night or thereabouts  Good luck!

Tea roses (which hybrid teas are hybrids of) are from a monsoon climate. They are adapted to drought dormancy, rather than cold dormancy. They have to basically be hit over the head, repeatedly, by cold, to even begin to think of going dormant. I think hobby growers would be well served to give up the focus on "growth" as the reward for caring for plants and as the yardstick by which care practices are judged. Instead, judge your prowess by the health and appearance of your plants. This frees the grower to remove growth that does not add to the health or especially the eye appeal of the plant. Adding more plants/ cuttings to the pot is a strategy often employed by growers who don't understand that the same end can be achieved by pruning to make a single plant fuller and more compact. WHEN you prune has much to do with how full the plant is capable of becoming because internode length (distance between the nodes or leaves) decreases as days become longer and light intensity increases and short internodes = a more compact plant. Pruning now ensures you'll have lots of lanky growth before the compact summer growth occurs. That means your desirable growth is at the end of undesirable (lanky) growth with no way to remove the lanky growth unless you cut back hard, which also removes the desirable growth. On the other hand, if you wait until just before the summer solstice (21 Jun in the Northern Hemisphere) to do an annual hard prune, you'll remove ALL lanky growth, and the growth that follows will remain compact through early Sep in most of the US. During this Jun-Sep interval, regular pinching of the branches/ stems after 2 leaves have grown will force new branching from the leaf axils. This rooted ficus cutting was pinched after it had grown 2 leaves. You can see it has 2 new BRANCHES now growing in the axils of each leaf.  When each of the 2 new branches have grown 2 leaves, they too will be pinched. So, 2 branches become 4, 4 branches become 8, then 16, 32, 64, ..... . For reference, prune hard in Jun to remove all last winter's lanky growth. Pinch all branches from Jun to Sep. Stop pinching in Sep and allow the plant to grow all winter. The following Jun, remove all long growth and repeat the process year after year. This is the pruning/ pinching regimen that will produce the most compact/ full plants, but your other cultural practices will determine things like vitality levels and growth rates, so it's very important to pay attention to and mitigate any stress factors you're able to identify. Most of the limitations will be associated with light levels, over/ under-watering, and issues relater to lack of effective nutritional supplementation (fertilizing). Back to the sizing question.... Using a rule of thumb for sizing HVAC equipment e.g., SF/ton,  can, and usually does, lead to erroneous results.   I caution against concluding the OP's system is oversized or undersized based on any rule of thumb.  Ditto for using a rule of thumb to justify disposal of the OP's engineer. The OP's system is a heat pump so sizing needs to consider both the heating and cooling loads.  Those loads are proportional to the indoor/outdoor temperature differential.  Consider data for Buffalo, NY (IECC zone 5) for an example.  Winter design temperature is 6F.  Summer design temperatures are 85F d.b. and 73F w.b.   So the indoor/outdoor temperature differential in winter is 72F-6F = 66F The indoor/outdoor temperature differential in summer is 85F-75F = 10F  That's a factor of 66F/10F = 6.6 I suggest the OP asks his/her engineer to review the calculations to see if the assumptions are logical or not.

Your first picture is that of a slight positive reveal which is the best for an undermounted sink. It makes for the tightest maintenance-free caulk joint between the sink flange and the bottom of the stone, the sink protects the bottom of the stone from chipping, and it's the easiest to clean. Plus it looks great. The second picture is that of a top mount sink. It's easier to do so it's cheaper, you'll never get chipped edges, but every time you wipe your countertop you'll run into the sink flange which makes cleaning more difficult. Flush reveals create an elongated silicone joint that frays and becomes contaminated and ugly. Negative reveals don't protect the bottom of the stone and create a ledge under which crud can hide, however, fabricators love them because they don't have to be as accurate with their sink centers at template. Do you believe there is a need to add mycorrhizal fungi to your soil in addition to the present native mycorrhizal already existing?  In a closed loop ecosystem mycorrhizae association is beneficial and these soils will contain 1000's of different mycrrhizal spore types to help the plants along.  But in an open loop environment where soil is disturbed, irrigated and fertilized the plants will less likely form a partnership with the fungi.  When plants are under nutritional stress they release organic acids to attract and stimulate mycorrhizal growth on the root hairs, but when everything is available there is no stress and no need for the fungi. You really have no need to apply commercial mycorrhizal fungi, native fungi spores already exist in your dirt regardless of how poor it is, and if your plant is stressed from lack of moisture or nutrients it will call out for help.  You'd be better off spending your money on a bag of humic acid.

"Heat pumps should be sized for the cooling load, and not the heating load."  Not as such.  Air conditioners need to be sized based only on the cooling load, because they only operate in that mode.  By contrast, heat pumps operate in both cooling and heating modes.  Accordingly, sizing a heat pump needs to consider both the heating and cooling loads as well as the particulars of the climate zone.  If you size a heat pump for an application in southern Ontario, CA based on cooling load, it will be undersized for heating which will be the operating mode for the majority of the year.

"  a LOT of ticks fall from trees so treating the yard would be fruitless. " They don't fall from trees, they're virtually never in trees.  And they don't jump - they just crawl towards a heat source to reach their next meal, and they require contact with that heat source (people or animals) to get there.  There would be no reason for a tick to climb up a tree; conceivably, there might be a just-fed, full and lazy tick that falls off a bird when it is in a tree, and if - by some weird miracle of coincidence - it were to fall on you, it would be just-fed and full, and so wouldn't bite you.  More likely it would just sit on a branch to digest, and then wait for the next bird to come by - it's not likely to sense your heat from the ground.

Assume that every point on a pan base (and some of the side area in the case of a wok) is an emitter of plume effluent.  Effluent here being mainly grease, oil, and/or water.  In the case of gas cooking, combustion products are also rising with the cooking plume, adding to the plume flow and somewhat to upward velocity. The effluent from this elemental emission point rises and diverges into a conical shape.  Think ice cream cone with ice cream filling.  The convolution of all these elemental cones yields a cone truncated at the pan base and extending to the hood.  The velocity of the effluent "rays' composing the overall plume will be highest at the center dropping off with angle. The actual cone in free air will cover more angular space than the hood would cover, but the more extreme rays will be low velocity and easily entrained into the overall flow of air to the hood, assuming that the overall flow is sufficient for containment, not covered in this message. The hood has to directly capture the stronger part of the cone, and the relevant cone angle w.r.t. the vertical can be the better part of 10 degrees.*  And this has to be performed for every likely pot or pan to be used on every burner. So, at a minimum, for a wall hood the hood capture boundary on three sides has to extend past the likely pan edges.  With enough flow we can treat light bars and thick side edges as part of the capture area so long as they are outside the plume-divergence-angle-from-vertical boundary of the potential pan array.  For a wall hood, the vertical wall surface acts acts as a reflector to the plume rays. So what does this mean, practically.  Assume that the particular range-top has a pan outline of 48 inches by 24 inches (relative to the wall).  If the hood capture plane at the base is at 36 inches above the pan bases, then the 6.5-degree angle (see footnote) implies 4.1 inches of plume growth on the three sides.  This would require a hood entry area of 56 inches wide by 28 inches front-to-back -- slightly less at 30 inches high. What saves us from having to go that deep, particularly with side skirts, curtains, or even cabinets, is that with a wall the hood intake air velocity profile is tilted toward the cook, and this makes it possible to entrain some of the plume rays that would escape over the cook's head into the hood flow. I don't think any of us can do computational fluid dynamics (CFD) ex mente, so we have to go from experience.  And that tells us that 24 inches front to back is likely to be sufficient, particularly if the most greasy odorous cooking is done on rear burners. Now for the bad news.  This monologue was directed at conventional hoods with reasonably defined capture boundaries at the base.  What happens with an insert, more or less flush with a flat surface as Wolf directs?  Well, all rays that diverge away from vertical toward the cook that hit the flat surface will in principle reflect outward due to momentum conservation.  The weaker ones will be dragged inward by the air flow, but note that at a boundary, the drop in air velocity tangential to the intake face falls rapidly, within mere inches. Let me take a moment to take a stab at "why 'quartz.'" Once upon a time DuPont developed Corian.  Corian is a plexiglass type resin loaded with aluminum oxide (sapphire) and some coloring.  It is durable, cleanable to sterile level, easily worked.  Careful application of heat can allow some permanent bending.  It can also develop burn marks.  Amateurs with carbide tools can work it like hardwood.*  I finished my 2.5 baths with Corian, and the Manchester, NH airport lobby was built with seemingly acres of Corian. Corian is, however, somewhat plain, and far from the look that can be achieved by polished granites quarried from various places around the world.  So in an attempt to fill the 'gap' between Corian and granite, 'quartz' was developed, using resin and larger stones.  One can argue it provides some advantages of both Corian and granite, and also argue that it provides some disadvantages. As a kitchen counter, granite is far more heat resistant than 'quartz,' but in some cases susceptible to staining if porosity is not fully blocked and is also susceptible to chipping.  Very hot pans can cause internal moisture to spall stone, so there is that slight risk.  Fabrication is a job for pros. Soapstone is inherently safe against heat, but softer and thus more susceptible to scratching and chipping.  Dark is the usual color, but inclusions can make it attractive.  DIY fabrication or modification is possible, but probably not generally desirable. So while 'quartz' can bring the granite look into a kitchen, there is a heat damage risk.  In my view, 'quartz' should not be used as a countertop anywhere an accidental or uninformed placement of a hot pan can occur, or on walls behind ranges or gas cooktops in island trim. ______________ *At some point after ca. 1990 DuPont went out of their way to block amateur acquisition of Corian sheet and bonding cements and adhesives.  I don't know its present availability status.

Looking at the picture you posted, that hood system is installed much too high to be effective -- unless it has a super strong suction that would likely also extinguish a gas flame. As Kaseki mentioned, FOGSS (Fumes, Odors, Grease, Smoke, Steam) spread as they rise and the farther (higher) the exhaust fan is from the cooking surface, the greater the spread.  In your example, It would need to be quite a bit wider than the cooking surface to be effective, yet it appears, at best, to be the no wider than 6" wider than the cooking surface -- which is too narrow for this particular setup.  If it was installed at what is probably the recommendation of no more than 30" or 36" above the cooking surface, it might work...except there is no "cup" to capture the FOGSS for exhausting. (The hood actually appears narrower -- look at the right side & where it ends.  It might be light reflection, though, that makes it look narrower.) I will say that I have a VAH (from 2008) and it's the most effective hood I've ever had.  On low or medium, I can easily carry on a conversation with others (on high, it's a bit more difficult).  As to cleaning, it's not that difficult -- remove two screws put it in the DW, put it back in, and you're done. I understand that not everyone likes VAH, but there are others out there as well that many like.  I don't remember if anyone has commented on Wolf.

Oh, and we have a 42"W x 24"D hood installed over a 36" cooktop.  It's installed per the spec - 30" above the cooking surface. We don't hit our heads on it and we're a tall family -- ranging in height from 5'10" (me) to my son at 6'7".  From my experience, you "sense" it and don't hit your head.  The only time I remember my husband hitting his head is when he stuck his head inside the hood to look at it and hit the back of his head when he was backing out of the hood!  It also does not "block" our view of the food on the cooktop. I got the one with the "emerald lip", though, just in case.  I didn't know at the time whether hitting our heads was going to be an issue. In your case, I recommend the hood be 6" wider and, if available, 27" deep.  If not available, then 24"D. Assuming @Buehl is referring to @clinresga's comment, please note that the image is described as an inspiration photo.  @clinresga has been here for a long time and has likely endured many repetitions of my commentary w.r.t. overlap. If the hood base is at 7 ft from the floor (typical commercial placement and what the inspiration image suggests), then indeed the overlaps should be more than 3 or so inches, not only because the placement is further up the expanding plume cone, but because drafts from HVAC and/or turbulence from movement of persons near the hood will cause more plume disturbance and potentially missed capture of some plume portions.  I'd consider 6-inches on each of the three sides to be effective.  Higher flow rate will slightly improve capture (commercial hoods depend mainly on hood overlap); flame disturbance 4 ft below will be slight due to the rapid drop in air velocity that far from the hood aperture. Due to the huge reservoir volume below the baffles typical of commercial hoods, they can operate with lower specific flow velocities at the capture boundary.  See Fig 4 from the Greenheck Guide below.  For residential style hoods and cooking I recommend 90 ft/min due to the lack of volume to spread and slow the plume rays before reaching the baffles.   If this were my cooking nook, I would make it deeper front-to-back, put the insert higher, and trap all the the rising plume into a large inverted pan that feeds the insert.  Due to momentum reflections, the insert still has to cover most of the overlap area.  (As a guideline, a ray hitting just outside the baffles that reflects down and out should hit a side surface that drives the ray back into the main flow.  So this is a geometry problem.) Note also that we don't know from the inspiration photo whether the wall at the back is properly constructed to be non-combustible.  With an island trim gas cooktop it needs to be even if the facing/backsplash is stone.  (Judging from the island in the photo, the backspash may be 'quartz' and not non-combustible.)

It is the nature of hot, greasy, moist cooking plumes to rise.  Searing and stir frying plumes can reach velocities up to 1.2 m/s.  Diverting plume momentum to the side or downward is possible with an enclosed fume hood, but not with the devices attempting side-draft and down-draft functionality for residential kitchens.  They work for low velocity steam emitted close to them, as well as similarly low velocity plumes from simmering. I recommend leaving the cooktop at the wall and revising the window plan.  Put a prep sink on the island and a real sink next to the dishwasher, wherever it is. Or anticipate having a "chimney" duct from the island through the ceiling to the roof with a proper island hood above the cooktop. Do not design a kitchen with serious cooking equipment requiring an appropriate CFM hood system without designing in parallel the make-up air system.

How is your Spinach doing and what hydroponic method are your using?  Your questions are complicated, and answers may be long but I'll try to keep it short and brief.  , It's nothing like growing outdoors in soil and requires additional knowledge to learn to be successful in hydroponics.  To be successful It's best to have some knowledge of plant and hydroponic science, and not just how to put a system together out of a box. For a perpetual growing system you desire it will require 3 separate hydroponic tables. After you seedlings sprout in plugs and set true leaves they are tranfered to  the first table for the first vegetate stage circulating a predetermined lower solution concentration.  Once established they are transferred to the table best for what you're growing.  One for  leafy crops an the other for tomatoes.  Changing the ratio of nitrogen in the last week before harvest would reduce chlorophyll production to reduce bitterness, so I don't know how you'd accomplish this without effecting other plants not ready for picking.   withholding any nutrient would not apply to tomato plants because you don't eat it's leaves and the plant will continue to grow to harvest the next cluster and so on. To address your other question, plant nutriment requirements will change over it's life span but depends solely on what you're growing.  Leafy crops like spinach or lettuce are never allowed to go into flowering or produce seed so these type plants will have the same nutrient ratios from start to finish on the 2nd table.  Crops producing flowers and fruit (seeds) will have a different ratio to support the nutrient demand when they flower and set fruit.  BTW, indeterminate tomatoes will grow for years and each single vine will produce a cluster of flowers every 21 days so I don't understand the need to replant every 4 to 6 weeks, and the process is completely different than spinach. There isn't a  premixed nutrient recipe which fits all. Lettuce and brassica like spinach need more nitrogen than phosphorous and potassium, while fruiting plants need a different recipe during it's different stages. Plants have an ability to compensate moderate high or low nutrients levels through the growth of their roots and transport process and somewhat forgiving, but are not able to compensate for the wrong ratios of all the nutrients so the recipe is critical.  Once a recipe is zeroed in the solution quantity can be refined using a EC meter to check the solution.  The electrical conductivity of the solution represents the total dissolved solids and using some mathematical formulas can translate the EC numbers to total parts per million, but does not indicate a lack of or excess of any specific nutrient and only the total.  So if the ratio of the recipe is right and the EC number is low or high then the quantity can be raised or lowered.  Since you studied this subject for years I'm sure your aware of water PH but suggest diving into the science behind the process to be successful.   Good luck

HI, Kara, An air conditioner removes moisture from the air when the dewpoint is greater than the temperature of the air leaving the coil.  The condensate produced is collected and directed to a drain..  You could have a problem with the pan or drain.  If that's the case, you should be able to see the source of the leak. The sooty mold in itself is not harmful......unless it covers all the foliage. That can affect photosynthesis. But if it is just scattered around, you do not need to do anything to it, although it can be rubbed off with water. To actually treat for sooty mold, you need to get rid of the source, which in this case is allegedly scale. There are a number of different kinds of scale and they are typically treated differently, although a systemic will work for most types. Get rid of the scale and the sooty mold will disappear.

Hi Bart! First, during rains, half strength isn't really necessary. If you're getting good amounts of water, regular strength will get diluted very quickly. If the plants are newly rooted cuttings or bare roots which have just broken into growth, half strength is safer as it shouldn't be AS likely to burn young roots. Weakly, weekly would mean cutting the "dose" in half and put it in the ten liters of water, then apply that solution every week. Your plants are well watered prior to the application, which should be standard practice. I use an old fast food drink cup of about 24 oz (710 ml) and apply however much the plant seems capable of utilizing. If it's a large budded plant, perhaps two or three of those cups poured over the foliage and canes (liquid fertilizers to absorb into the plant through the growth and any excess drains into the root zone). If you don't want to wet the foliage, then apply it to the drip zone, where rain would fall off the plant's canopy, where the concentration of feeder roots normally occur. You might actually add some inorganic nitrogen sources to the application of your organics. The bacteria require a readily available source of nitrogen to start digesting the organic material. If there isn't available nitrogen there, they literally rob it from the plants until they start releasing enough excess nitrogen for the plants to take it back. Applying pellitized fertlizers between rains is perfect. The plants are turgid, full of water and the inorganic stuff will be dissolved by the rains and flushed through the roots and quickly absorbed by the plants with all the rain water. I'd also apply that pellitized fertilizer in the drips zones where it would do the most good. Good luck!

You have repeatedly mentioned stone.  But these counters are Quartz, and you mentioned a "manufacturer".  Quartz should not be sealed.  That is one of the reasons people like Quartz.
