I have a rather unique (not completely unique) view on picking colors for our homes. I believe that the colors in our homes are linked to our happiness and our homes should make us happy. I like to start with the colors that make the decision maker's heart sing.   Not the person in charge of financial decisions, but the one in charge of buying bedspreads and area rugs and throw pillows and art. . .   There is usually one person who is the decorator/artist of the couple and one who accepts the aesthetics of the other. I think that everyone has a few colors that they are drawn to.   Some color psychologists say that they are colors that we relate to happy memories.   Then I hear that my 2 year old niece blurted out "Purr Pull" when her older sister picked what color cup she wanted and what color cup her little sister wanted and wonder if we aren't born loving certain colors.   Doesn't matter, what does matter is that there are those colors that make your heart sing.   The colors that call to you when you walk through a store and make you bring it home with you. To me that is the perfect place to start building a color palette.   I think that is why I love taupe.  It works with the colors that pull at my heart strings.   I love smoky purples, wine reds and blue greens.  Violet gray and the stronger purple/pink undertone taupe colors work with the things I have bought and love to look at.  It is the perfect backdrop for the colors I love. I have never found a neutral that always works.   If you love olive green and I love teal will the same neutral make your colors sing and my colors sing?    What if you love cornflower blue and I love cherry red, should we use the same neutral? Specifying a specific neutral as the perfect neutral or one is good and one is bad is like saying that a certain foundation, lipstick or blush is the perfect color for every woman.  It simply cannot be true.   The colors that work for you may not be the same colors that make your sister or best friend or boss look good.

OK here's my go round. I know you want to sit at the counter to eat but I honestly don't feel that's the best for the kitchen layout. I added a table that will partially be in your family room. What is your climate/location? Will you actually use this outdoor space? Are you designing for your actual lifestyle or the one you wish you had?  We all get swayed by the cool and pretty photos of amazing entertainment space ... I used to live in LA and we didn't spend that much time on our patio, specially as it faced west. We had a fireplace that we used twice in 10 years. We built a house in FL and luckily the lot we found allowed us to have our patio/pool face east. Didn't bother with a fireplace (too hot most of the year) and didn't include a TV (also too hot/humid most of the year to sit outside). I did add 2 water/fire bowls to the pool.  The water/fountain part is tied into the pool filtration system and runs at the same time as the filter.  The fire part is tied into our underground propane tank and are easily lit with gas lighter.  We only use these when we have people over as they are also visible from inside (when it is too hot to be outside). Most of the patios in FL (called lanai) are under roof to provide a large area with shade.  It is the only way to even attempt to use the outdoor spaces.  The covered patios are also useful for rainy days. You have no covered patio area in your design. Think carefully about what you will really use, as you will have to clean and maintain all those outdoor features.

My personal perspective is that nutrient testing of container soils - the equivalent to inground soil testing - is unnecessary. What is it supposed to evaluate? Container soils are not comprised of very nutrient dense materials for a variety of reasons and therefore it is incumbent on the grower to provide nutrients as and when needed in the form of regular fertilization. Plus, whatever nutrients may exist are constantly being leached out with the frequency of watering required for container plantings. Any soil test results would immediately become invalid. There are also very valid reasons why better soil labs do not routinely include nitrogen analysis as part of their tests. N is the most mobile of the essential plant nutrients and levels will vary widely by time of day, time of year, recent rainfall and a number of other factors. This makes any evaluation just a momentary snapshot in time and therefore not a reliable assessment. One can safely assume that N is almost always deficient in both inground soils (most) as well as container soils and supplementation in some form will typically be necessary.

A "tell" in the context used is an indicator or a revelation of something hidden. Poker players watch for "tells" from other players to help them make decisions. A fever is a "tell" that the patient is trying to cope with an illness/injury. A completely defoliated plant might be a "tell" there is a root infection or perhaps an abiotic pathogen at work. See below for more re using a "tell". "Potting Soil" covers a lot of territory. Some commercially prepared potting media are reasonably good and others virtually unusable. I've been growing trees in containers since the early 1980s and I've found that media which hold a lot of excess water (perched water) are generally not a good choice for trees because the excess water limits the oxygen roots need to function normally. It's particle size that primarily determines how much water a medium can hold. The finer the particles that make up the medium, the more water it can hold. If a medium is based on a large fraction of fine ingredients like peat, coir, compost, composted forest products, ....., it's almost certain it well hold enough excess water. Adding more peat to a medium already comprised of a huge fraction of fine materials is a step in the wrong direction because it increases the water-holding ability of a medium that might already be too water-retentive. I'm guessing you should be able to find a source for pine bark. If you have any interest and think you can find the bark, I can help you make a very good grow medium using the bark + a fraction of commercially prepared potting mix + perlite + lime. It will look like what you see in the middle of this image when dry:  The bark products at 3, 6, 9 o'clock, show an appropriate size bark from 3 different packagers. If you'd rather not make your own medium, there are some tricks that by using some simple science you can limit the amount of excess water your planting is capable of holding. Since these work passively (no effort on your part other than some easy adjustments at potting time) and very effectively, you get an immense amount of return (some in the form of personal satisfaction) for only a little effort. The 'tricks' I'm talking about can allow you to use a grow medium that without the tricks would be a poor choice. Raise your hand if you're interested. Using a 'tell' Over-watering saps vitality and is one of the most common plant assassins, so learning to avoid it is worth the small effort. Plants make and store their own energy source – photosynthate - (sugar/glucose). Functioning roots need energy to drive their metabolic processes, and in order to get it, they use oxygen to burn (oxidize) their food. From this, we can see that terrestrial plants need plenty of air (oxygen) in the soil to drive root function. Many off-the-shelf soils hold too much water and not enough air to support the kind of root health most growers would like to see; and, a healthy root system is a prerequisite to a healthy plant. Watering in small sips in order to avoid over-watering leads to a residual build-up of dissolved solids (salts) in the soil from tapwater and fertilizer solutions - which limits a plant's ability to absorb water – so watering in sips simply moves us to the other horn of a dilemma and creates another problem that requires resolution. Better, would be to simply adopt a soil that drains well enough to allow watering to beyond the saturation point, so we're flushing the soil of accumulating dissolved solids whenever we water; this, w/o the plant being forced to pay a tax in the form of reduced vitality, due to prolong periods of soil saturation. Sometimes, though, that's not a course we can immediately steer, which makes controlling how often we water a very important factor. In many cases, we can judge whether or not a planting needs watering by hefting the pot. This is especially true if the pot is made from light material, like plastic, but doesn't work (as) well when the pot is made from heavier material, like clay, or when the size/weight of the pot precludes grabbing it with one hand to judge its weight and gauge the need for water. Fingers stuck an inch or two into the soil work ok for shallow pots, but not for deep pots. Deep pots might have 3 or more inches of soil that feels totally dry, while the lower several inches of the soil is 100% saturated. Obviously, the lack of oxygen in the root zone situation can wreak havoc with root health  and cause the loss of a very notable measure of your plant's potential. Inexpensive watering meters don't even measure moisture levels, they measure electrical conductivity. Clean the tip and insert it into a cup of distilled water and witness the fact it reads 'DRY'. One of the most reliable methods of checking a planting's need for water is using a 'tell' (more reliable than a 'moisture meter'. You can use a bamboo skewer in a pinch, but a wooden dowel rod of about 5/16” (75-85mm) works better. They usually come 48” (120cm) long and can usually be cut in half or in several pieces, depending on how deep your pots are. Sharpen both ends of each tell in a pencil sharpener and slightly blunt the tip so it's about the diameter of the head on a straight pin. Push the wooden tell deep into the soil. Don't worry, it won't harm the root system. If the plant is quite root-bound, you might need to try several places until you find one where you can push it all the way to the pot's bottom. Leave it a few seconds, then withdraw it and inspect the tip for moisture. For most plantings, withhold water until the tell's tip comes out nearly dry. If you see signs of wilting, adjust the interval between waterings so drought stress isn't a recurring issue. Al

I am always a bit anxious about jumping in on these sorts of discussions cos growing in the mild and temperate UK is a world away from the freezy north US but...the last few years, I have become even more inclined to dismiss a lot of horticultural dogma in favour of simply trying stuff out. I have seen numerous examples now of people transplanting willy-nilly, whenever it is possible to use a spade. Jimi Blake of Huntingbrooke Gardens in Ireland has cheerfully transplanted mature plants at almost any time of year, including perennials in full summer growth and a range of woodies. Presumably, he has access to plentiful running water (which I don't) so my decisions are usually decided by the question of how desolate would I be to lose this plant'?  Which, as a hardened plant killer is usually 'not very much at all'. I think the tortured point I am attempting to make here is that while there are usually ideal times and ways to do anything, I have to make extra allowances for my personal circumstances and my somewhat optimistic (but slightly negligent) methods. Best of luck whatever you decide, Faith.

text: Yes they should be fed, but nothing applied upon their foliage...NOTHING, or serious burn results.  That goes for fungicides and insecticides sprayed upon their foliage, don't do it or burn, the foliage most certainly will. Granular fertilizer, organic or conventional, applied to the soil that targets acid loving plants is the way to go.  Of course , manure that's aged is always good.  Milorganite....worth a try.   If you liquid feed, use a fertilizer for acid loving plants and apply it only to the soil, even just a little splashed upon the foliage will burn. Hybrid Rugosas are pretty tough and rarely need any fungicide or insect problems addressed.  However, they are very acid loving like azaleas and rhododendrons.  Chlorotic foliage is frequently seen on HRs.  Fix it with acidic fertilizers. Moses

With indoor temperature of 70° and 38% Rh, the dew point temp would be around 43°. With outside air at -10°, then the edge temperature of the window glass should be around 35° or so, or 8° below the dew point temperature. However, since you have ice on the lower edges of the windows, they are below below freezing at the bottom edge. Because of the design of the window wall the bottom edge of both the lower windows (floor level) and upper windows (resting on the cross beam) are going to be colder than they would be in a different set-up. This combined with very cold outside air plus excess humidity (or so the windows think), results in significant water and ice on the (especially) lower edges of the windows. Given the conditions that you describe, you would need windows with a Condensation Resistance Factor of around 70 to avoid or seriously limit window condensation. This is possible with triple pane windows, but not any dual pane that I am aware of. If you have dual panes without a surface 4 coating, your windows are probably have a CRF of 50 or so, but if you have dual pane glass with a surface 4 coating then potentially looking at low 40's CRF. If you could lower your indoor Rh to around 20%, by removing moisture, not warming the air, then you would be approaching the Rh level you would need to be at to avoid condensation, but that's not very realistic. Your friend's "square one" may be a sink that has what are called "0-radius corners".  The radius refers to the angle of the corners. Sinks come in different radius corners, i.e. there are different degrees of roundness or squareness in kitchen sink corners. A sink with ”tight radius” or "small radius" corners means about 10-15° corners.  That is as opposed to 0° in a ”zero radius” corner.  There is also a very rounded corner, also called a "standard radius".  The more rounded "standard" sink corners are seen on builder-special style sinks which are lower priced and often lower quality. I have never heard of cleaning issues with a sink with tight radius corners. The tight radius corner is a nice compromise of still having a modern look without such an extreme corner, while not having the very rounded corners of older-style sinks.

Don't confuse terms. It may vary from place to place but an agent/salesperson's licensing requirements are less substantial than what's required to be a broker. A salesperson needs to work for a broker, a broker can work for themself. I knew that. And I believe that set-up is unique among those professions (or if I'm wrong, among MOST professions) that are required to be licensed. As I noted above, lawyers, accountants, architects, doctors, etc., once they get licensed they can immediately hang out their own private shingle like I did as an architect. Realtors HAVE to go work for somebody which of course, reduces their income. And the problem with the two licensing requirements, and the sales person needing to work for a broker, is in most markets that results in just a few large realty companies for Average Joe to choose from. Which from there it's naturally a very small step to "price fixing" where those few all charge the same high fees. Which is exactly what happened, the result being the lawsuit. And of course in that same geographical area, Average Joe, while having a limited choice when it comes to realty companies, has a choice of hundreds if not thousands of lawyers, accountants, architects, doctors and building contractors to choose from. That whole arrangement is very bad for the consumer and very good for the brokers and it's gotta go. And if that means upping the standard to get initially licensed as an agent then so be it. Licensing requirements exist to protect the consumer. Requiring an additional exam for licensed realtors to set up their own shop does nothing for the consumer. It only limits competition and lines the brokers pockets.

3 important tests would be calcium hardness, pH and Total Alkalinity. Make adjustments as needed. I would not worry about a stabilizer. Chems should be dissolved in a bucket of pool water individually and added to the pool a little at a time. Muriatic acid is best to control pH and Total Alkalinity. It must be diluted and not poured in straight as it can harm the finish. I generally hold off as long as possible before adding chorine and, I will only use liquid chlorine initially. Most likely your area does not have a high demand for chlorine as we are in the winter months. So, I would say you're ok. What type/form of chlorine was added? Brush at least twice a day for 2 weeks. Brushing even more frequently is perfectly fine. The dust you see is mostly the plaster dust when you brush. Keep an eye on your filter and clean it when pressure builds and the flow slows down. The brushing will cause the dust to be suspended and the filter will pick it which is its job. No auto vacs for 2 weeks. Manual vacuuming should be done with a vinyl vac head that has brushes to protect the finish. No salt for at least 30 days. Go longer if you can. The plaster will take 28 days to fully cure but the 48-72 hours after filling and start up are critical to balancing.

First, questions: - You're showing two different sizes of washer/dryers.  One is a rather large stacked set, the other is a smaller set -- like you might expect in a beach condo. If you're unsure, go to Lowes and touch the real washers/dryers. - You need to pull your dryer out from the wall every year (every 6 months if you have a large family and run your dryer constantly) to clean out the lint that gets inside the machine.  This is a fire safety thing.  With stacked machines, how will you do this? - Is one of these walls on the exterior of the house?  Dryers are best on the exterior so they can vent directly to the outside.  Again, fire safety thing.  Also cheaper and more efficient. Second, suggestions: - You're trying to get too much in a small space.  Those cabinets towards the back are going to be impossible to reach, and you really don't have space for a sink.  Cut back on the cabinetry -- significantly.  Neither of these designs allows enough space for you to comfortably reach those back storage cabinets. - Consider that washer/dryers do wear out, and you'll need to eventually need to change them.  Consider going with freestanding Ikea wardrobes, which can be removed in the future, if you choose different sized machines. What I'd do: - Side-by-side washer/dryer across the back, where you have them now.  Cabinets across the top of the machines.  Freestanding Ikea wardrobe on the right as you enter the room. - Add good lighting and bright colors.

Soffits in a kitchen above wall cabinets generally serve the purpose of filling the gap between the top of the cabinet and the ceiling, eliminating the greasy dust collection area on top of the cabinets.  They serve a purpose, much like a control joint, and mostly go unnoticed in the daily operation of a home.  Build without kitchen soffits, and you get greasy dust on top of the cabinets if they do not go to the ceiling.  Build without control joints, and you get random cracks in the stucco-like finish on the exterior walls. In a production home, less attention is given to detail than a custom home.  If this were a custom home, the control joints would have to still be there, but they may have had more attention given to them in the design of the house.

Mark Bischak, Architect, I don’t think the point being made is about the necessity or purpose of soffits or expansion joints.  It is about implementing that necessity into the overall design.  If you need a soffit above 30% of your cabinets, then put the soffit above 100% of your cabinets.  It is just going to be an eyesore otherwise.  Basically, just because something less desirable is required that doesn’t mean you should end that element where it is no longer required. Likewise, the expansion joint above would look better if it were carried into the area that doesn’t require it.  In its current state it calls attention to itself, but if the joint was considered both as a necessity and design element the results might be more pleasing.

There are basically three categories of legal duties (1) arms-length, (2) due care, and (3) fiduciary.  These duties largely just establish the care for the other party that your actions must adhere to.  Any time you contract to perform a service for someone you have at least a duty of due care. The elements of negligence are rather simple.  There was a duty, it was violated, it was foreseeable that the violation could cause damages, it did cause damages. Here, there was a duty of due care.  The builder knew, or should have known, that the house wouldn’t look like the drawing.  The OP wouldn’t have bought the house were he aware of what it would look like, so there are damages.  The only question is: were the damages foreseeable?  So, could the builder predict that someone wouldn’t want the house if it were properly rendered?  That is questionable and I am not sure the OP can establish that.  The little I can see doesn’t seem all that bad to me. So to again directly answer the OP’s question.  The builder has a legal duty to address foreseeable concerns.  This would likely include a reasonably accurate rendering or a notation that the rendering is not reasonably accurate.  However, you are asking “reasonably accurate” to do a lot of heavy lifting here.  I am struggling to believe that the joints pictured above would cause significant concern for a typical buyer.

Many of the currently available cultivars have been developed from southern provenances, and mature redbuds often have weak branch crotches that can result in storm damage. They are also susceptible to verticillium wilt and cankers. But in spite of these potential issues, they can sometimes be surprisingly long-lived. The term "deadbuds" was likely coined by maackia's fellow Wisconsinite Mike Yanny of Johnson's Nursery, who gives a detailed explanation of the challenge of growing young redbuds in the north in this article: Redbud in Wisconsin. To the OP, I’m not sure I would want to second-guess the engineering specifications and/or warranty instructions on any cooktop when it specifically says that it cannot be flushmounted. I do completely understand your frustration that they did not make it obvious which they clearly should have. But even if the cooktop you purchased was specified to be flushmounted, I would not do so and for some pretty straightforward reasons. In order for flush mounting to be done properly, you first have to find someone who knows how to do it. It’s not very common to see fully flush mounted appliances and so, no surprise that there are very few people who know how to do it properly. Don’t get me wrong, I really do see the interest and attraction to the idea, and I actually don’t think it’s “technically“ impossible to get this to work, but that is in theory, and not in the field, where you have appliance installers, who need to accomplish getting your appliance, installed, fully flushed within the counter, all while not damaging the appliance or the counter. Adding to this is that when and if your cooktop needs to be removed in order for repairs to be made, who then comes to remove it? Repair technicians, most of whom have no experience with this, may scoff at it, and refuse to work on the appliance altogether. And at this point, you now have a project that has ballooned  into something a lot more complex which is the last thing you want when it involves one of the most important appliances in your kitchen for food preparation. You might continue to search for a technician who will (eventually) take on the task and at the end of the day, your appliance has been repaired (hopefully 🙄). BUT THEN, you discover that the appliance has been scratched or damaged in some way or your very, expensive countertops are now marred or chipped. No matter how many kitchen designers promote this idea in HGTV or other Home fashion media,I would chalk up the flush mounting of appliances as one of those things that is often marketed mostly in concept to help sell product, but is actually rarely undertaken due to the realities and complexity of actually pulling it off with the installers and technicians that are currently available to most homeowners. Maybe this will change in the future if the concept can continue to grow and takeoff, but for now, these are the risks you will run, and this includes cooktops as well as the new trend in “flush mountable” wall ovens.  For those people who live in very large metropolitan areas and are willing to wait and pay for the very few specialists who can get this accomplished, I salute them. But the reality for most consumers in most geographical areas does not support making flush mounting actually happen without everything ending in tears and unnecessary $$$.

One thing the zone map has NEVER taken into account is winter snow cover. Plants can grow in gardens covered with snow that won't survive in "warmer" zones, just because of the insulating properties of the snow they get. Tonight, my garden will experience the coldest temps we've seen since the early 2000's. BUT, unusually, there is an 8" blanket over everything, so I'm not nearly as worried about my teas as I was Christmas of 2022 when we had a sudden drop from 50F to 4F in 36 hours, with NO snow and a brutal, continuous 30 mph wind. Also, as Diane B. so often reminds people that are technically in the same zone as her, her latitude makes a huge difference in her seasons, both in a shorter growing season, AND snow cover. I grow many of the same roses as Diane, usually with zero snow cover, and have to prune them drastically each Spring just to reach living wood. Surprisingly, against conventional wisdom, it's not *usually* the pure teas that suffer the most. So I do agree that we need a very localized map, tied to a plant data base of what WILL survive where. That would be ideal. A boy can dream. EDIT: As an aside, when I first started gardening, this area was considered a solid Z6. According to every reference that actually offered zone ratings, aucuba was NOT hardy here, but only to Z7. But as I saw the old-fashioned "spotted laurel" in gardens here, I tried them myself. Now I have one of the most complete collections of Aucuba species/varieties in the country. I've always been a zone pusher, lol.

I have a couple of possible sources for your toilet water drip but I would have thought your plumber would have been specifically looking for my proposed sources....it's just so common I think he would have been looking for it.  I assume the drip IS from the toilet since it stops when you turn off the toilet source water. The answer might be different, or troubleshot differently, depending on the type of ballcock your toilet has....the system it uses to fill and shut off when the tank is full.  If I had to guess, I would say the valve that shuts off the water when the tank is full has a small leak.  When the tank fills, typically, a float rises with the water level and eventually rises high enough to shut off the fill water.  If that valve leaks a bit, the drip will ultimately raise the water level enough to enter the overflow pipe and enter the toilet bowl.....one drip at a time so you won't notice water entering the toilet bowl at that rate.  The easiest way I know to check for this issue is to leave the cover off the tank on the back of the toilet and either watch for the drip....or look to see if the water level rises to the overflow line after some period.  If the drip is very slow, water might even be evaporating from the tank faster than the drip is filling it. One other possibility is very much related.  There is in many/most ballcocks a small flexible line that ends just inside the overflow pipe.  This line helps to refill the toilet bowl as the tank is refilling.  If the drip is coming from this line, the drip will be bypassing the tank and dripping down into the toilet bowl (via an inner route).  You can pull this flexible line out of the overflow pipe and watch it for drips.  If it drips, the solution is still replacing the ballcock.

What  power rating does your microwave oven claim to have? It is unlikely to have suddenly gained performance. Have you checked the timing? Milkweeds put on a lot of root growth, right after germination, so it's best to start them in a container that allows for root growth, and not the small cell trays. They are also dependant on macchorhizae, so I recommend either a potting soil that contains maccorhizae or adding it to the potting soil. I grew zizotes milkweed for a couple years in northern Illinois, and then it fizzled out, but Asclepias fascicularis and Asclepias subverticillata both are able to overwinter here, and their agressive rizhomatous nature might be the reason. They get kicked back in winter, keeping them in check. The Monarchs seem to prefer laying eggs on the A. subverticillata, because it still has fresh green leaves, when A. syriaca is getting shabby looking in late summer. Asclepias incarnata and Asclepias texana have shallow, fibrous roots also. It's a good idea you are letting your's get larger before planting out,

We went through something very similar not long ago, also with a volume builder, and had a lot of the same questions at the start. You could Google something like “construction contract lawyer Victoria” or “HIA contract review solicitor” and see who comes up locally. As for building inspections, yes, you can definitely arrange your own independent inspector. Builders don’t always promote the idea, but it is quite common now, especially for people building for the first time. It might be worth flagging it early so it is included in the contract wording. We used a private inspector from Building Inspection Mornington and had them do stage inspections at slab, frame, lock-up and final. You can also do pre-handover if needed. Ours was a registered builder with years of experience, which made the whole process much less stressful. They picked up a few framing and waterproofing issues early, and the builder was fine correcting them once flagged. Best of luck with the build. It can feel like a lot at first, but having a few professionals in your corner makes a huge difference.

Part of the problem is the term "veneer".  Veneer brick can be 3.5" +/- thick and require a foundation to support it and metal ties to attach it to a wood or masonry structural wall; or veneer brick can be 0.5" +/- thick and adhered to a structural wall like ceramic tile. I agree with Mark.   "veneer brick" is not a clear specification.  If it was in writing please post it. In today's residential specifications brick walls are  either "brick veneer cavity walls" (a full wythe of brick supported by a foundation or relieving angle tied back to a masonry or wood framed structural walls) or "applied thin brick" (thin brick applied in thinset mortar to a masonry or wood framed structural wall. Manufacturers and suppliers will sometimes misuse these terms leading to consumer confusion so it's best to let your designer/architect write the specifications. And a homeowenr should avoid directing a contractor in a conversation.  Always put it in writing and ask for a written confirmation.

Brick veneer, is almost universally used as a shortcut description to a brick veneer cavity wall construction detail, with a poured brick ledge, and brick ties binding the single brick stack to the rainscreened sheathed wall behind.  That is the detail that would work with your desired decorative accents. The cheaper and less capable choice of material requires a redesign, minus most of the decorative details. Carla, it was a very easy rose to root. I've had one bloom so far, and it was quite yellow. But the first blooms on the florist roses usually aren't real true. It takes a few bloomings to get them to look like they're supposed to.  I buy most of my florist stems from Safeway. I love that they have the names and the sell by date. It makes it easy to see how fresh they are. I rarely buy ones that have sell by dates less than 2 days away. If they aren't fresh, the leaves will fall off and they won't root easily. Altho I did recently buy a bunch of BARISTA stems that were expiring the next day. I just couldn't believe I had found it there, so I thought why not. Interestingly, I did get about 5 to root! Usually they are too far gone by then. But those were still supple and the leaves were tight. In the last couple of yrs I've rooted well over 100 different varieties of roses. Sometimes I get only one to root out of the 12 in the bunch. Sometimes it's 5-6. Sometimes all 12. It's a lot of fun. I'm having a blast rooting them.  Some tips for rooting them... make sure you tamp whatever soil medium you use very tightly, and when you get the stems put in the soil, make sure they are tamped down tightly again. Loose stems don't root. Leave at least 2 leaves on the stems, and I cut them at about 8" length. The longer cuttings seem to root better and make a nice sized plant faster. And keep them well misted! You should get roots in 3-8 wks depending on the temperature. Mine are in a greenhouse and I had to get a heater to put in there in this extremely cold weather. Right now they're taking 4-6 wks to root. Good luck!!

The distance betwwen the bottom of the hood and the cooktop needs to be between 30” and 36”.  That is the measurement you use, NOT how far it comes down from the ceiling. Any hood that says it should be mounted less than 30” above the cooktop does so because its cfms are so low and anemic that the hood needs to be lower than standard to suck up anything.  An island hood needs more cfms than a wall hood does because it does not have adjacent cabinets that would help corral the smoke. The hoods you linked are 36” wide.  How wide is your cooktop?  An island hood needs to be 6” wider than the cooktop.  If your cooktop is 30” wide, then a 36” hood is good.  If your cooktop is 36” wide, then you need to buy a 42” hood.

All sites have views, views in and views out.  Some views are wanted and some views are unwanted.  The house should respond to those views. Site vegetation should be considered. And vegetation of adjacent sites. Site circulation is important.  A first time visitor should be able to know where to park their car and easily find, and get to, the front door. There are things in the current design that I would change as long as do not conflict with the site. Provide coat storage at the main entry and at the service entry. Locate the dining room immediately adjacent the kitchen. Locate the family room so a view to the outdoors is not inhibited by a roofed space. Locate a master bedroom on an exterior corner as opposed to having the master bathroom there. Keep clothes washer and clothes dryer out of a 'study'. If a room has an exterior wall put a window in it. Do not have so much circulation space in a living room that it overly limits locations for furniture arrangements. Eliminate angled walls. Forego step-in closets for a reach-in closet or a walk-in closet. Do not turn corners with hanging clothes. Make reach-in closet doors no less than 12 inches narrower than the width of the closet. Have only one door into a bathroom. Rethink the kitchen with a kitchen designer. If masonry does not go all the way around the house get rid of it.  Continuity is key.

L C - a toner is applied in a consistent layer over a sealed wood surface.  When stain is applied, it soaks into the wood fibers - and may produce uneven results. What type of wood was used for your island?   Some woods are known for not taking stains well (= being blotchy).  Examples: pine/birch/maple/cherry/poplar (there are others).  Oak is a type of wood that is known to take stain evenly. There are wood conditioning products that can be used to try to help prevent uneven results - but it’s safer to use a toner. I have two showers with linear drains of similar design to yours. I believe your problem is the baskets.  I've never used them and never had a problem. Most everything just goes down the drain without the baskets in place to interfere.  I probably pull up the grate 1-2 times a year to wipe a little gunk from the inside of the tray, but that's about it. I think if you remove the baskets your problem will go away.

I do have my basket in place and we clean ours every two months maybe. I suspect you are doing something to create extra solids in the shower- maybe using bar soap or shaving? I’d be interested to see how many other people have skipped the basket, I use it because I assumed I was supposed to!

While you might have to "unclog" it more frequently, you should actually be grateful that the clogs are occuring at the top rather than making their way down the pipes where they might still cause a clog which would be more difficult to dislodge or extricate. I don't have a linear drain but a standard drain with a hair catcher below which I think is equivalent to what you are calling a basket. One day it just stopped flowing and fortuitiously my GC was coming around that day to follow up on some stuff. He did the dirty work of taking out the gook that had accumulated and sent me a photo - luckily he didn't bring it to where I was sitting but a photo more than sufficed. He was the one who told me that the clog could have gone further downstream. FWIW, the clog didn't really have what seemed be a lot of long hairs although I also have long hair. It just seemed to be a gooey mess of some kind. When I remodeled I deliberately opted for a drain cover that had no screws so that it could easily be lifted for cleaning.

I could have written the same response as Kudzu9! The baskets caused our linear drains to back up with anything that wasn't plain water. A few guidance points for you, as well as a link to experts Heritage House: What does the pointing process achieve? Walls need to breathe – and if the pointing doesn’t allow this, the wall will rapidly deteriorate.  Mortar joints are the lungs of a wall. Incorrect pointing causes irreparable damage to older buildings. It is essential to understand what the mortar joints actually do: Mortar in the wall is to act as a bedding between stones and varies from fine joints in ashlar stonework to larger joints in rubble masonry walls. Joints are effectively reduced in size by inserting small stones and ‘snecked’ pieces of stone. It must be flexible to allow movement/settlement of the structure due to thermal responses and settlement within the structure.  Many earlier large buildings are not designed with the modern expansion/contraction joints of today. Old Houses: If the house is built using lime mortar, it is most likely that the walls are solid – they won’t have a cavity.  These walls need to be treated very differently to ones with a cavity. Old walls need to breathe – the stone and brick from which they are built is usually harder, and less absorbent than the lime mortar. Heritage House: Heritage House are experts in their field on on all types of internal and external masonry work, they break down the entire process with images to illustrate the types of mortars to be used depending on the age of the home and if it has a cavity within the existing structure. If you look to the left after clicking on the link (see attached image): you will see the categories to select which are most relevant to you and for ease of use: https://www.heritage-house.org/stuff-about-old-buildings/raking-and-re-pointing/methods-for-repointing-brick-and-stone-walls.html Please keep us posted, these types of projects we adore Warm and best wishes, have a great day Team SPEAK

The current rating of an appliance is the highest value that can be achieved with normal operation, accounting for any hob "sharing" when one of a pair is on power boost.  An induction top/electric oven rated for 30A will have lower rated coils and/or hobs than one rated for 50A.  The circuit breaker should be sized to the conductors used to power the appliance, and those should be rated such that the appliance doesn't continuously draw more than 80% of the rating.  (Refinements on and exceptions to this generality may be found in NFPA  70.)

text: Well, once the water gets to the end of the channel, and hits the drain pipe, it can drop anywhere. But in order for the water to flow to the end of the channel, the channel itself needs to be slightly sloped. My question is that if the driveway isn't sloped in that direction, but the channel is, how to you keep the grate over the channel level with the driveway around it? Yes, I guess the channel doesn't really need to be sloped to get rid of a lot of water, but then you'll end up with a permanent puddle in there.

Any concrete flatwork should at least have a wash to it (even if unintended), so sloped towards some direction. A trench drain, or any pipe for that matter, can be perfectly level yet still drain water. Because at some point while seeking level the water will rise enough to overcome it's edge surface tension and pour out a lower outlet. And, AFAIK, any channel profile will have a lip below an end cap outlet hole anyway. It could be possible to shim the grate at a slope to match the concrete but not the channel, but with a driveway and vehicular traffic it probably isn't a good idea. Also, you would have to sawcut to install the channel into an existing driveway. I'm sure there is a scenario where you cut a bit beyond the channel footprint, and infill concrete which slopes towards the drain to alleviate what you are trying to accomplish.

text: You want to limit horizontal growth, right?  Train anything back as far as you want, then train new growth coming from the reduced canes in the direction you want as it extends and is the most flexible to cooperate.  Do the training right away as it is putting on size early on from spring on.  That way you have the growth growing in the direction that you want without having to force it as you would if you waited until it progressed to a hardening off stage later in the season.  At that time getting it to cooperate if you want to change its direction may be problematic. Moses

I have grown all the climbers you list and some of them are going to resist any attempts to keep them reined in. Even in what used to be my zone 5, my Mme. Alfred Carriere wanted to eat the south side of my house alive and bitterly resented any pruning by refusing to bloom on anything but old wood. Since she was marginally hardy in my zone, I only got blooms in one out of 5 year or so. In warmer zones she's happier and blooms longer, but also much huger. If you are training a climber vertically only without any horizontal growth, you run the risk of the plant blooming only on the ends of the canes. With my climbers, in order to get more lush bloom you need to train smaller canes growing vertically from horizontally trained canes. Yes, those laterals then become "real" canes when you train them sideways and more laterals grow from them. In that case, all the rose canes ("real" and lateral) all bloom at the end of the canes but since you have a lot of new canes from the horizontal it looks like you have a full round of blooms. If you're looking for a tall structure of a rose on your French Tree guards that has a small cluster of blooms at the top, then you can keep some of the other roses you mention more or less constrained on this structure. Dublin Bay and Quicksilver aren't huge climbers in my zone, and frankly both Iceberg climbing and Generous Gardener were weak growers and poor bloomers in my zone so they would barely climb here at all anyway. Florentina is very robust and a great bloomer when you train her horizontally, so I doubt it would last long on this structure, particularly straight upright. What you could do if you want more blooms is train the rose to gradually spiral around those tree guards. A happy Florentina will swamp those 42" supports quickly however (any mood of MAC would swamp it even faster). I train my Florentina on 8 foot arches and it needs a pretty strong structure. Think mature canes with a diameter of a half dollar or so that get stiffer with time. Just my two cents - you can always give it a try and add a more firm support over time. Just don't plant them somewhere that you'll be disappointed or skewered if they grow more than is feasible on that support after a few years. Most climbers take a good 4 years to grow anywhere near their mature height so don't just them to be tame by their performance in their first couple of years. Cynthia

You let it grow for a while as it is, until it gets a few roots that are an inch or more long, then either cut that node with the little plant attached, off of the original bloom spike, or you gently pry the baby off the old bloom spike (your choice), and plant the baby in a pot of its own.   Recommend you use orchid seedling mix, or grind the regular mix until it is a bit finer.  This will help it retain a bit more moisture until I grows up a bit.  The baby is an exact genetic copy of mama, unless there is a major genetic event which is very rare.  Have fun. Bill

Test wine, coffee, salad dressing - things that are likely to spill on a counter besides water. Is this stone polished or honed?  If a stone is more prone to water absorption I would only get it in a polished finish which seals the pores and makes it more stain resistant (honed finish does not). I’d want to know from the salesperson who talked about water stains whether those homeowners had sealed their granite or not, and whether the finish was honed or polished. Once sealed, most granites won’t stain.  Sealing takes 5 minutes and no skill at all; anyone can do it.  Having said that, there are a couple granites that will stain easily and behave more like marble, such as Kashmir White granite.  You need to test a sealed sample to be sure.

text: Worn out, old leaves (5-6 month or older), lose their resistance to diseases.  I think those leaves have a black spot variant, but the infection is of no importance, nothing to be concerned about. The old leaves, the lowest down on my bushes are pretty much  black spotted throughout my garden at this time, and have been so since fall, after all significant growth was finished for the season. I garden in a climate where black spot pressure is intense every growing season no matter how variable it may be some years.  It is always hot and humid which black spot revels in.  I now grow varieties that have proven black spot resistance or down right immunity so that I do not have to spray anymore.  This limits me from growing many choice roses, but there are still quite a few beauties that I can grow. Moses

Hi JMc, Our compliments to you on selecting such a beautiful colour choice and fabric finish for your new interior treasure. Try not to forget about your overall interior design style: is it modern, contemporary and is this the theme you want to convey in this space? There are three things will which enable you to tie together your new colour scheme: 1. Wall Art: Known as a focal point painting – normally above the central wall in your space 2. Accent Fabrics: Not just in terms of the colours, think about adding contrasting textures here to add more warmth to the beautiful rust shade. Choose a fabric in a colour or pattern that will complement your room, details such as small tablecloths for end tables or even lampshade covers using fabrics. Think about the frame included with your wall art (small details) does it tie in with your theme? For example: if your room has a country feel to it with soft blue, cream and yellow tones, you’d want to choose a painting with these colors, in a light oak, pine or white frame. 3. Decorative Rug: Decorative area rugs are another excellent way to pull a room’s decor together. Place one under the coffee table in the sitting area between the sofa and accent chairs or under the dining room table to tie the room’s colors together in that space. Blend the colors from the area rug with the room through the colors of the drapes, curtains or walls. A decorative area rug can bring a room together and give it a warm, cosy feeling. The beauty of rust is that many colours suit this shade: especially classic Navy, take a look at how this lounge has been arranged: it is not what you would call ‘matchy matchy’ but because all of the colours in the space are complimentary it works really well on the eye!

“Quartz” is a man-made engineered material.  Did you mean ”quartzite”? Quartzite is a natural stone mined out of the ground.  Dolomite is not quartzite.  Dolomite is a stone made from calcium carbonate like marble is.  Dolomite is harder than marble, but will etch like marble.  If the stoneyard is calling a stone ”dolomite quartzite”, it is dolomite and will etch, but is probably a beautiful stone.  Many people put up with etching if they feel the stone is beautiful enough to make up for that.  All the kitchens with marble counters go through that decision process. The kitchen is one of the worst possible places for seed storage... not only due to heat, but to the increased humidity caused by cooking. That combination of heat & humidity is deadly to seeds. Hopefully I'm wrong, since I hate to be the bearer of sad tidings - but some of that seed may already be severely damaged or dead. A cool location is best for seed storage. Cool basements are not a bad idea; but basements are also damp, so the humidity would need to be controlled too. Refrigerators which also contain food would have the same issue. In both cases, storing the seeds in sealed mason jars - with some desiccant enclosed for any moisture which might leak in - would provide the best conditions for seed storage. The refrigerator would be the best option. There are color-changing desiccants which are best for seed storage, since a color change tells you when the  desiccant needs to be changed. The native seeds are a separate issue. Some seeds (including many perennials & wild/native seeds) require specific conditions to break dormancy & germinate. Seed stratification is one of those methods; there are tutorials online that would be helpful. For the annuals, I would recommend either performing a germination test before planting time (if there is enough seed to spare 10) or starting them indoors as transplants. Doing so early gives you time to get fresh seed if needed, and to avoid disappointment. I do not recommend germination testing of perennials or natives, because of conditions mentioned above. Lovely list of roses Clara! I like the Austins too and you picked some good ones that will look great against the neutral palette of your house and yard. For starters, most of the Austins really like sun or they're not going to bloom nearly as much in our colder zone, though a majority of them will survive fine. For instance, I had Queen of Sweden in full sun on the south side of my house and part shade on the east side of my house, and they were night and day. The one on the east side rarely put out a few blooms a year vs. the one on the south that was in and out of bloom all season. They also like a LOT of water to bloom well, so if you're getting any of the drought conditions we're getting you should plan on some supplemental watering strategies. Some folks do underground sprinklers, but I'm low tech and prefer the sprinklers you haul around with a hose (also easier to control). Elena says she's had better luck and I agree that Olivia can take some shade. If those are the conditions you have (including at least 1/3 of my planting areas), you work with the spaces as needed. If you have pots, there is the potential for adjusting where they are after you see how the sun works in your yard. I've grown nearly all the roses you list except Oxford Girl, Like No Other, Silas Marner and Eustacia Vye. Of those, the only ones I've had do OK in part sun are The Lark Ascending, Lady of Shalott, Olivia Rose Austin and to some extent The Alnwick Rose. Scepter'd Isle I had in full sun but it's robust enough it might do OK. Olivia is a robust and sturdy self standing rose and she gets a lot of people's votes as a favorite Austin. I find she's among the bigger of the roses you list, even more than some that are listed as "climbers". Gertrude Jekyl never cleared 6' for me and bloomed rarely if ever in part sun, so she wants full sun to have a chance. James Galway and St. Swithun climbed OK (maybe 6-8') but didn't bloom much at all in part sun, so they like more heat and sun too. There is no separate rose that is Lady of Shalott climbing, just the note from DA that under some circumstances she can be induced to get tall and lanky. By "some conditions" that means places like California or England. In our climate, she is notably short, staying no more than 4' tall. That's an asset and she's a wonderful rose, but don't expect her to climb in our zone at all. Probably the same goes for Claire Austin, and there's no climbing form per se for that one either. She is listed with the wildly disparate heights of 5' to 11 feet. In our zone, probably no more than 5-6', California/England, most Austins will get "octopus arms" that can climb to 11'. Crown Princess Margareta did get very long thin canes that I wound several times around an obelisk in my yard, so she was genuinely a climber. What she wasn't (for me) was a bloomer. At all. In the 13 years I had her (grafted from DA roses), I got exactly one bloom cycle in one year (2013 if you care to note). Others have had much better luck for bloom including in my region - just stating my results. Zephirine D and Pretty in Pink Eden are both legitimately classes climbers and they can get to a good size in this zone. ZD has a reputation for not liking heat much and being a once or twice (spring and fall) bloomer in hot climates. YMMV, but you might not give her the most prominent spot. I couldn't overwinter PiPE, but others have and like her in my region. For your grandfather's grave, the rose planting is a lovely thought and there are cemeteries in other regions where heritage roses are grown. A couple of thoughts to consider, if you haven't already checked on this. First, ask the site if they support permanent plantings. The cemeteries where my in-laws are buried is very adamant that only artificial or temporary plantings like pots are allowed. I notice in your photo that only pots are visible and nothing else has a permanent planting. You might double check before you get your hopes set on a rose trellis that can only be done permanently. If they won't allow permanent plantings, you might be able to do a pot, but someone is going to have to maintain it regularly including watering. Most cemeteries make policy decisions based on what is easiest to do as a blanket control for neatness and that's why they may discourage or even rip out permanent plantings. Just check! The cemetery is definitely part sun at best so that's where (if you have permission) you might put something like The Lark Ascending or Lady of Shalott in a pot on each side of the grave. Their colors would complement each other with soft color in the shade. The good news is that in your house situation I don't think even those big trees would shade out your roses all day if they're in that central spot with the fountain. On the north side of a house is always less sunny, but that bed is far enough from the house to not be particularly shaded by the house itself. I've found that even my hottest sun bed on the south side of my house gets some shade in the afternoon from a big oak tree about 10' to the west of that bed, and they frankly enjoy a respite from the 8-10 hours earlier of sun. You could try all of your roses in pots for the first year and see how the light patterns change in your yard for the first year before planting. Koko Loko is the one that stands out as needing the most sun of the ones you mention, at least in my yard. Hope this helps! As always YMMV, just sharing other zone 5 thoughts. Have fun! Cynthia

Hi Sangam,   a new to you house, or was something wrong with the previous layout?    How best to proceed depends on several factors.   Firstly how do you use the room - lots of entertaining, just you, a family with littlies and teenagers or some other dynamic?    For the best results, unless you’re setting up to sell, choose function (practicality) first, then form (looks).   Set out your furniture so you have an easy path, for two, in and out of the room.   It’s not a huge room, so choose items than are slimmer (but still comfortable) rather than the oversized look.   Also you want items that are multifunctional e.g. drawers in your coffee table or a bench seat for guests that your cushions and blankets sit on.   Next search in Houzz for living room photos and decide what style appeals.  As your living room abuts your outdoor area and dining room, try to have a complimentary ‘feel’ for all areas which will extend to your kitchen etc.   There is a 65/20/10/5 guide for novice decorators that always helps me - 65% is the main colour or main shape/style, 20% is the main complimentary colour/shape/style, 10% a third colour/etc and always include a couple of outliers (a vintage piece in a modern setting, a touch of purple in a pale blue, off white and timber room, a Sputnik design lamp in a room with oval and circular furniture for instance).  And two last tips, take your time. Purchase, or reuse, your major item/s but everything else can wait.  Also, there is no substitute for seeing items in situ, so check return policies.  Houzz is a great resource, full of lovely friendly people, but more specific questions might help

The best homes are designed to suit the site and are a marriage of a well designed interior and exterior. The best houses come in at or under the design target square footage The best houses orient the public rooms towards the south for the best passive solar heating and cooling The best houses are L, U, T, H, or I shaped. The best houses are only one to two rooms deep. And covered lanai, porches, garages, etc count as rooms in this case. The best houses make sure kitchens have natural light, meaning windows so one doesn't have to have lighting 24/7 to use the kitchen. (I bolded this because you have a balcony outside the window and very little natural light will make it into the kitchen) The best houses make sure all public rooms and bedrooms have windows on at least two walls. The best houses do not if possible put mechanical rooms, pantries or closets on outside walls The best houses do not have diagonal interior walls making for odd spaces. The best houses keep public and private spaces separate. (It's not separate if the wall of the bedroom is also the wall of the living room) The best houses do not have you walk through the work zone of the kitchen to bring laundry to the laundry room. The best houses do not have the mudroom go through any of the work zones of the kitchen. The best houses do not use the kitchen as a hallway to any other rooms. The best houses do not put toilets or toilet rooms up against bedroom walls or public areas. The best houses do not have walk in closets too small to stand inside. (the closet near the garage) The best houses have separation, such as closets, between bedrooms and between bedrooms and public rooms. The best houses do not have roofs that are overly large, and dominate the exterior of the house. The best houses do not have stick on exterior materials only on the front façade. The best houses do not have multiple gables within gables. The best houses have an organizing “spine” so it’s easy to determine how to get from room to room in the house and what makes sense. Meaning they don’t have meandering circulation paths. The best houses design the inside, the outside and how the house sits on the site all at the same time. I agree with everyone else. It's time to work with a talented person such as a residential architect.

Both appliances were integrated. So apparently as of 2011, some people, including real estate agents had never seen panel-ready, integrated appliances. The Fridge was right outside the kitchen door, but it was a large cabinet with a big obvious door and two drawers and large handles, unlike anything else around it, and the DW had the only large handle in the entire kitchen which was mostly without hardware or minimal hardware. So there were some clues. I had to put Post-It notes on the DW and Fridge when the unit was being shown. I actually installed a rangetop in my kitchen made circa 1955-56. It has absolutely no electronics. The entire interior can be disassembled by hand for cleaning and the burners can be adjusted by a regular screw-driver. It comes with a manual with instructions how to service it yourself. I thought long and hard about using this, but there is literally nothing that can break. (I did not put the matching oven in the kitchen because it has a very small oven cavity, but it too has no electronics, the thermometer is a separate device that hangs inside the oven cavity, the timer is a wind-up mechanism, and it can be match lit. Let's look beyond the statement "Corner pantries are bad" and consider WHY this opinion is prevalent: - In general, corner pantries interrupt the work flow; that is, they throw a big honking obstacle in the middle of the room. - In general, the doors to corner pantries become obstacles themselves -- the door can literally block you from setting down the item on the counter /force you to walk around the door every time. - They aren't all that large, and a good bit of their space is wasted on that awkward corner. - The doors on corner pantries can be too small /uncomfortable. However, every rule has an exception, and I don't think your corner pantry's bad because - It's a reno, not a new build.  You have to work with what you have.  Sure, a larger, two-sided walk-in pantry would be better, but we don't always have every option.  This corner pantry is better than no pantry /better than sticking to cabinetry in that corner. - Your proposed corner pantry is at the end of your work space, so it isn't interrupting your counter top. - I would flip-flop the door /hinge the door the other direction so you can enter it /remove items "towards" the countertop and the main work area. - You can go with lazy susans in the corner to help with the awkward corner issue. - Finally, accept that this is a small pantry -- don't expect it to rival a huge walk-in.  Plan its contents carefully, and it'll work out fine. Other thoughts on this kitchen: - I'd eliminate the large massing with the duplicate ovens and tall cabinet.  That item is crowding the table and blocking light from the glass doors.  Visually, the door seems to be "in a hole".  Instead, I'd go with a practical range instead of the cooktop /add plain cabinetry near the door.  This would be an ideal place to store dishware -- right between the dishwasher and the table. - If you really need that tall pantry, I'd rather see it over by the refrigerator -- keep all that tall massing on the interior wall.  Could the door be scooted down a bit? - The island seems too small ... I'd like to see it grow by 50%. - The rectangular table doesn't seem to work in this space.  I'd rather see something oval /oriented the other direction.  Ovals are easier to walk around /no corners ... and that'll be nice near the door.

Out of curiousity... why are you having large temp fluxes in your finished basement? If a concern of your contractor is temp changes big enough to warp wood, that should be a concern to how your basement is finished. I got wood stored out in the barn that can see pretty serious temp changes, and the temps don't warp the wood. Humidity is another matter. Even with consistent temps, humidity can warp wood fairly easily. Well primed and painted cabinet doors can hold up well in a bathroom so long as there is good ventilation to help clear the humidity. So with a dry basement with good ventilation a good paint job should hold up on a standard cabinet door. However, since your doors are oversized for that kind of make, I would put in some extra bracing on the doors. I assume the doors will be taken back down again for the painting part of the project. Extra bracing can be done at that time while the doors are off. If you want some extra insurance, you could use a waterproofing or sealant like for outdoor use to paint with- if it can hold up to outdoor conditions, it likely will hold up to a basement.

Cold stratification of seeds takes place after the seed has been sown in media and watered in.  The process is a cool and moist period that some perennial seeds need to go through for at least a couple of months - 10 to 14 weeks of 35 to 45 degrees F would be ideal. Fluctuating the temperature helps perennial seeds that require stratification to germinate.  Most annuals do not need stratification but some germinate and grow better at cooler temps, under 70 degrees. Storing seeds that are dry in the fridge is only storing them, the stratification process needs moisture to be successful and only begins after the seed is sown, watered in and kept at cool temperatures.  The easiest way to stratify perennial seeds is to sow them in the autumn in a protected cold frame outdoors and they will germinate when they are ready in the springtime.

You are right, it does NOT sound like rust from any iron that might be in the stone.  And many granites have no iron at all, so  it is incorrect to jump to that conclusion without further photos and an indication of a rusty color rather than the stone just darkening. From the locations by the sink and dishwasher, it sounds like it‘s just water absorption by the stone.  You haven't posted any photos of the stains so I am guessing.  I would seal the granite which prevents absorption.  Sealing the counters takes 5 minutes, and requires no skill.  But first you must allow the water to dry out.  If you don’t, you’d be sealing in that water once you apply the sealant.  You’ll have to not use the sink and dishwasher for a couple days until the water stains dry out.  Or if you use the sink, be careful not to splash around it.  Once the existing water stains dry out, apply the sealant.  Follow the bottle’s instructions. After the seal has completely cured and bonded with the pores of the stone - which takes about 24 hours - .you can test the stone by dripping some water on it, wait 10 minutes.  If the water is still beaded on top, you are set.  If the water absorbs, apply another coat of sealer.

Raise  the bottom sash about 6”. compress the jamb with 1 hand  and and  pull the 1 top corner of the sash slightly  out of the track and do the same to other side. Tilt the window out about 90 degree’s Raise one  bottom side of the sash so that it  comes out the cam shoe and do the same to the other side, you may have to lift this side slightly. Lower the upper sash sash about 10” from the stool. Repeat procedure. This procedure will be done twice  since you have  get it by the raised portion of the track the lower sash rides on. Make sure to  get the pins  into  the shoe on the track or if it cams  it would go  above the track shoe. Get this wrong and you may break something . The sashes should be removed to properly  paint.    I would remove hardware  and weatherstripping. After painting  and or clear coating  remove any  paint  on the sides of the sashes where they contact the jambliner. Reinstall weatherstripping  and replace if needed. I like to rub parrafin wax on the check  rail where the the 2  sashes meet   to prevent the sashes from sticking   together together. This would be a good time to  clean the jambliners  and you could also rub parrafin wax  on the edges of the sashes  to ease operation. Be carefull with the jambliners as the  tend  to get brittle at this age.

On a side  note  , I have seen many  painters  screw up  windows . Many don't take the time to    properly break down the window, they paint  things they  should not  be painted  and   dont remove parts .  Painters are a dime a dozen , Good painters are rare  . text: Nitrogen is not well tested in a soil test. I typically ignore that number. The reason is that soil nitrates are very soluble, and leach rapidly. They also come out of compost to some extent. So at any one time, a soil test for nitrogen is not very trustworthy. That being said, note that many sources say that BER can be caused by over-nitrogenating the soil, though your nitrogen numbers are indeed very low. What's more, it is said that you should only use nitrate nitrogen as the fertilizer nitrogen source. Ammoniacal nitrogen may increase blossom-end rot as excess ammonium ions reduce calcium uptake.

Cryptomeria often develop bronzing or russeting in winter. There are practical reasons for a bullnose on hardwood stairs.  For one, a square edge is much more prone to splintering and damage and repair can be more involved (vs a rounded edge than can be sanded & eased to blend).  A rounded edge is more comfortable ascending vs a hard square edge cutting into your foot.   Also, it looks more bulky and, IMO, the build-up on these particular oak treads looks much too bulky. If you use a runner on the stairs, it is going to wear more quickly on a square edge than on a rounded one. That said, the red oak doesn't look bad with the stairs.  If you use them, then I would use red oak in the upstairs hallway. The vinyl treads look surprising good, at least in the photos.  If you use them, then use the matching vinyl in the upstairs hallway. I would be inclined to use the vinyl treads (even as much as I love hardwood) because the match looks so good.

I don't care for real wood next to imitation wood. As I said before, I'd replace what's there with solid wood treads. Regardless of the material you use, make sure that the person doing the install checks that there is consistent rise at the top and bottom. When we replaced the upstairs flooring and stairs in our previous home with hardwood, the wood floor raised the living room floor by 3/4". The rookie they sent to put in the stairs did not account for this, so the top step was higher than the others - not only a code violation, but a serious safety hazard (which is why the code exists, of course). The owner got to come back and do the stairs over - at his expense. Adding a layer - wood or LVP - to your existing stair treads could cause the same problem, though the higher step would be at the bottom. If that's the case, and the treads need to be changed anyway to solve the height discrepancy, you might as well put in solid treads.

I had just said this to someone yesterday. I lived in Mexico for a bit where it seems every person has a chef in their family and NO ONE uses ventilation hoods in their homes. I lived in Japan for about 2.5 years and again in 2018, and it was rare to find a venting hood in ANYBODY's kitchen... and their life expectancy is among the highest in the world... certainly more than ours. I just think there isn't much correlation between smelling food and manifesting life-concerning diseases. On the other hand, we do have research to suggest that if your food produces a lot of smoke (searing, frying, smoking), and you CONSUME that food, you're eating toxic products like NFCs, trans-fatty acids (TFAs), polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons (PAHs) and advanced glycation end-products (AGEs), and more. Fried, charred, and slightly burnt foods can contain carcinogenic substances. Is eating fried foods a guarantee you'll have health issues? No. But I would imagine it being a greater risk than just smelling it for a few minutes. 90% of the world doesn't have proper kitchen ventilation and they're doing just fine. But if your concern is health, then look at the food you consume before the food you smell. It all comes down to oils on high heat. Just my 2 cents.

When shopping online, LOOK at the photos and READ the description.  The sink you linked at Home Depot that is $649 in satin finish includes a disposal.  The same sink in your link at Home Depot that is $399 in stainless steel finish does not include a disposal. Furthermore, while I like Kraus sinks, I don’t like their farmhouse sinks.  That is because their apron fronts are curved and thick.  A big advantage of farmhouse sinks is that the apron front is supposed to bring your body more directly against the sink which is better ergonomically.  The thick curved apron of the Kraus farmhouse sinks removes that advantage.

"Does it still need to be 3" bigger than the sink?" Not if you use a standard sink base cabinet and a short apron sink that self-faces. You'll strap, not clip or block, the sink in place. The cabinets are 33", the sinks are usually 32 11/16" or so. Even a full apron will fit.

You won't need additional support. "Scooping" the cabinet sides doesn't weaken the cabinet when sinks are strapped, not clipped or blocked, in place. The strapped sink bears on the remaining cabinet side (or front and back) and does the support work the top of the cabinet used to do. You may ignore the sink manufacturer's cabinet size recommendations when sinks are strapped in place. I've done it hundreds of times over many years.

"...would this be something that I would need to address with them..." Yes. "... or is this something that I could possibly take care of myself?" No. Refinishing/repairing engineered stone is an art. Even experienced technicians who are great with natural stone struggle to get a finish match. The last guy to touch it owns it; don't let that be you please. The three reflections in your last picture indicates that no one has attempted a previous repair; the gloss and "snakeskin" are factory identical. If they try a mechanical fix, you'll want that replicated. The very straight sides of the mark were possibly created by something like a vacuum pod that would secure the slab to the CNC machine during fabrication. Measure the width of the mark and the width of their pods please. A simple poultice may remove it without changing the finish, but that's their gamble, not yours.

Simply have the fabricators imbed reinforcement to the underside of the stone. Insist upon stainless steel, carbon fiber, or fiberglass rodding, not cold steel, bedded with Integra Rodding Bonder please. No seams will be necessary unless dictated by your yield. If so, they could be made in the shop. They can transport the rodded top with a Sink Hole Saver to further lower risk, but a clamped 2x4 will work just fine. If they balk, get different fabricators. This is fabrication 101.

In this picture, note the hole in the ceiling -- this is where the hood's duct went into the space above the ceiling & below the floor of the second story (i.e., b/w the two stories):  In this picture, the hood is installed:  In this picture, you can see the installed hood on the left. How you run the duct will depend on the hood and the room on the other side of the wall. The one your husband purchased does require either a cabinet above it or some sort of chimney/enclosure built above it. The one you like can be installed as-is. Note, I strongly suggest you get a hood 6" wider than the cooking appliance (e.g., 30" range/cooktop with a 36" hood above) -and- 24" deep, not 30" x 18" or so like the one your husband purchased.  You want it to cover the entire cooking surface + 3" on each side. The extra width is b/c FOGSS (fumes, odors, grease, steam, smoke) expand as they rise and the expansion is beyond the width of the cooking surface. As to the depth, an 18" deep hood (or 19") will only cover the back burners, not the front.  If you never plan to cook on the front burners then I suppose the shallow one would work, but I doubt you want to be constrained to never cooking on the front burners! I think you'll find you won't need anything else flanking the hood (i.e., no open shelves, which are dust & gunk magnets!)

3 of the plants Evve shows are Portulacaria, which have the same growth habit as Crassula. Is there any negative in issuing very shallow planters as opposed to taller ones with room for way more volume of soil? "Negative" is subjective in that the pot typically looks better, but shallow pots are more difficult to grow in because they typically have a much higher % of saturated soil after a thorough watering. This makes it essential to either choose plants very forgiving of being over-watered, or ensuring you're using a grow medium that holds so little excess water it makes it difficult to over-water. As you learn more about bonsai, you'll find practiced growers are very particular about their choice of grow medium, and alter the structure and components to suit individual plants. Most grow media based on fine ingredients (peat, coir, compost, composted forest products) are not good choices for shallow pots because they hold excessive amounts of water. For example, if you use a medium that supports 3" of excess (perched) water at the pot's bottom, using that soil in a 3" deep pot would find you growing in a soil that is 100% saturated after a thorough watering. It would be challenging for even skilled growers to maintain a jade or mini-jade (portulacaria) healthy in a situation like that. Notice how pot depth affects the amount of well-aerated soil a pot can hold after a thorough watering:  The pots are completely filled with soil. The shaded area represents excess (perched) water. Note - if you shift your focus to using the upright form of portulacaria for your bonsai endeavors (or other trees with naturally small leaves), you'll be able to produce a much better likeness of a tree you might find in nature. This is due to portulacaria's leaf size which is more proportionate to the scale of a smaller plant. Al

Hi Dave. My condolences. The heart shaped one is Pothos. The dotted one is probably Calathea. They both like water. Pothos cannot be over watered. It will live in a cup of just water. It is an easy plant to read. When it is thirsty, its droops. If the leafs turn yellow then the plant is sacrificing leafs to stay alive so its time to fertalize and water. It does like fertalizer. Home Depot carries a brand called Dr. Earth that I like. Its tangible grannules that I can grab and toss in. You dont need much per plant. Around a tablespoon sprinkled over the surface of the dirt of one plant is usually plenty (depending on the size of the plant). It will breakdown and leach down over time when you water. If the leafs get brown edges, it can be cause by flouride or other chemicals in your water. To combat that, fill your pitcher of water and let it sit on the counter for a day so that those chemicals can evaporate. There are other plant things but those are the basics. This is a link I found for the two types of plants I think your spotted one might be. https://greenstreetgardens.com/calatheas-versus-marantas-whats-the-difference/#:~:text=Both%20prefer%20lower%20light%20conditions,harsh%20chemicals%20in%20unfiltered%20water.
