Gary, I have yet to meet an established (old and neglected) rose that did not recover from a very hard pruning. The roses you describe sound like modern repeat-blooming types, so I believe you’re safe to cut them back to 1 to 2 feet tall and they will regrow. There are always dormant eyes on the canes and at the base of the plant, ready to start new growth when needed. A hard pruning of an old plant is generally rejuvenative, so this is an opportunity to reclaim these roses and build them up with renewed vigor. If these are actually ”antique” types that bloom once in Spring (no repeat) then you can still cut them back, but you will sacrifice this year’s blooms. If these are once-bloomers, you can wait until they’ve finished blooming and then cut them back.

"can I taper the application of the self-leveling cement?" No. What you should use is a trowelable product, not a self-leveling product. You mention "feather-finish", which is exactly what you want. https://www.ardexamericas.com/product/ardex-feather-finish/ Self leveling products are mixed thin so they flow and seek their own level, and are made to level, not ramp. Also, they generally don't finish to a feathered edge. I'm unclear as to whether you're trying to ramp down 1/4" over a 3' span. If so, that's out of generally accepted standards of 1/8" variance in level over a 10' span. Going up 1/4" in 3' will likely yield a noticeable ramp and may cause issues with the material going over it. Grinding down the upper part so it starts sloping sooner could help, but you should probably figure on feathering the low area out at least 10'.

Sliding doors (aka "barn doors") are terrific problem solvers in certain circumstances. I have a slider between my small mudroom/laundry room and kitchen and it is what works there because of the small space and layout. But, I can't see a reason you need a slider to solve a particular problem, and you don't have room on that one wall in the kitchen proper anyway. Also remember that the back side of a slider isn't that attractive -- even when the door is finished nicely, the view from the room on the back side is kinda weird because the door sits atop the wall in the other room. In my case I don't care since the backside of my door is the laundry room, but in your case for one between the kitchen and the other room, even if there's enough space for a slider on the wall in the adjoining room, it's not going to look that great from the kitchen side. A pocket door isn't either, although the pocket would be better than the slider in this case. Why do you even need a door between the kitchen and the other room? Keep a regular door on the other two off the eating area, those aren't problem areas in need of a solution. If you don't like the looks of those particular doors, there is a seemingly endless choice of attractive interior doors.

Your best contact is not the Agent but your conveying solicitor. In Vic you can sell and buy properties with unapproved structures. I’ve done both although that property has a lot. The risk is that if the Council request (normally after a neighbour compliant) it the structures need to be demolished or retrospective approval sought. It can be extremely difficult to get retrospective approval because you can’t prove that things like footings were done correctly. So you need to make sure the purchase price reflects what the property would be worth without those unapproved structures. In a tight market you’ll be competing against people who are ready to take the risk or who aren’t aware of the risk beforehand. Good luck.

You will need to stay with Kohler trim as each manufacturer has their own design regarding mounting points, etc. for the different trim pieces used. What determines which trim pieces can be used is the underlying shower valve assembly itself. Kohler has an old version (now out of production) of the Rite-Temp shower valves (example: K-304) and a newer design Rite-Temp valve (example: K-8300). Hope this helps.

The open grain in oak as the OP pictured turns black when finished. I see that as giving that flat cut surface a two dimensional appearance without the multiple tones of cherry or walnut. You've seen this in Golden Oak kitchens used by builders in the 80s. in the US. Rift cut oak eliminates the open grain. Cerising fills the open grain with a light color paint to hide it. In Europe one domestic oak species without open grain is quercus robur,. They never went through the same phase. That species when flat cut shows off more character. Of course, your preference is a personal choice, which isn't debatable. Pale non-yellow wood is only possible with the development of water-based polys like Bona and Ciranova. The opl finishes 'warm' the wood appearance by yellowing it.

Hey, I’ve done a couple of new builds in NSW, so here’s my take: for internal walls, I usually go with fiberglass batts, they’re cheap, easy to fit, and decent for both thermal and sound insulation, though rockwool is better if you care more about soundproofing and fire resistance. Please do not sister 2x12 against the bottom truss chord. First, that's crazy expensive just to give you height for a platform only in the middle of the truss. Have you tried getting 24' long members, which weigh around 100lbs, and negotiating them into the rafter heel space? Do you realize the dead weight you are adding to the truss bottom chord? Also, please do not attach anything to the (angled) truss web chords. They certainly cannot have a load on them that will want to rotate them. Be realistic. Your bottom truss chord cannot take a lot of weight (typical 10psf, but you will have a ceiling + insulation). Your garage is very air leaky because of the overhead garage doors. So, do you think you will notice a comfort difference if a say, 4x8 area above your ceiling does not have R38? What if the entire ceiling is R38, but that small area is R15? And do you have a plan to cover the top of the bottom chord with insulation anyway, if you are just setting batts between the trusses? If you want to put a platform and have a little more insulation below it, run a 2x perpendicular on top of the truss bottom chords. Space 3 of them at 24"o.c. and use no thicker than 19/32" OSB (is rated to span 40") for the platform. The bit of deflection you feel when standing on it will ensure you do not store anything heavy up there.

Early blight spores need wet leaves or humidity above 90% to germinate in temperatures above 47 degrees so temperature really doesn't matter that much, but optimum temps are above 80 degrees.  Trying to time the application of Copper is not an easy thing to do and requires spraying the plants before conditions are right for the fungi spores to germinate.  Can't say I've ever been able to time the spraying before an outbreak, but I can usually stop the spread using copper (frac code M1) or chlorothalonil (frac code M5) and sometimes mix them together.  I may follow up if need be with mancozeb (frac code M3) but not often.  Chlorothalonil is better than copper which is just fair, but these three are about the only ones you'll find in a store under various brand names used on tomatoes. The names list above are the active ingredients and are found in most brand name fungicides.  Mancozeb is harder to find, but Chlorothalonil is common in many brands. There are many more fungicides but are for commercial applications and most require a license to buy and are from different Frac groups with strict precautions, so home owners shouldn't be spraying it around. there is another Fungicide available to home gardeners with the active ingredient teboconazole (frac group 3) which is approved for almost everything except tomatoes, peppers and potatoes but I don't use it.

You could have a leaking shower pan/drain or one of the shower water supply pipes could be leaking. In our previous house our new shower started leaking into the garage below a few months after the bathroom was finished.  My contractor came back and did several tests and determined it was the water supply pipe leading from the valve to the showerhead.  When they installed a hanging mirror on the wall behind the showerhead they made a small puncture in the pipe.  It was a slow leak that took a while to show up.  My contractor was able to fix it by removing the mirror, making a hole in the drywall and patching it all back up.  Worked perfectly after that.  They were extra careful when they put the mirror back up!   They also opened up the garage ceiling, made sure everything was dry and then closed it back up. Your contractor needs to do a thorough test of every component.  For example to test the shower pan, you use water from a bucket and not the showerhead ... you have to test each thing individually.

In answer to your questions: Stove Uppers:  Keep the upper cabinets, it helps balance the Kitchen.  It also provides storage for things you need near the stove/range.  Don't put in open shelves near the range b/c FOGSS (fumes, odors, grease, steam, smoke) that aren't caught by the rangehood will land on the shelves as well as the items on the shelves.  Regarding open shelves in general -- the fad, for the most part, is ending as people now realize that unless you use everything on the shelves every couple of days or you enjoy dusting & washing dishes over & over, they are more work than they're worth.  Ideally, the rangehood should be at least 6" wider than the cooking surface and 24"D to cover the front burners.  However. if you flank the hood with cabinets AND you don't do a lot of high-heat/high-smoke/high-grease cooking, a hood the same width will probably be OK; but it should still be 24"D to cover the front burners. If you forego the flanking cabinets, then the hood should definitely be wider than the cooking surface.  Oh, and do not get a flat hood, you want one that's concave so the FOGSS can be captured and held in the concave space until they're exhausted to the outside - your last picture shows a concave hood.  In addition, be sure you install it per the specs and no higher (usually no more than 30" or 36" above the cooking surface, depending on the specs & that's usually dependent on the size and fan strength). Ceiling-height cabinets:  I recommend taking them to the ceiling but leave about 6" or so for crown molding.  The crown molding will help disguise any issues with uneven ceiling heights and give the cabinets (and the Kitchen) a more finished look.  Store items that are rarely used in the top cabinets/shelves and, when needed, use a step stool to access the contents.  The aesthetic of stacked vs one tall cabinet is up to you. Pantry: Get two 18"W tall pullout pantry cabinets instead of cobbling together uppers & base cabinets.  The counter in front of the ones you show is practically useless, so don't waste storage space with them or pay for expensive counter material that's just going to be covered by the cabinets.  If the pantry cabinets are standard depth (24"), then don't get pantry cabinets wider than 18" as things get lost in wide/deep cabinets, regardless of shelving type, especially above about mid-chest height. Island:  Two sides for seats are better than one when there are more than 2 seats.  As you stated, seating on two sides is more "friendly" and more conducive to visiting and conversation.

I would paint the island the same white as the perimeter cabinets and the (future) pantry doors. Remove the ceiling light, and simplify your barstools...I would go with a style that has the back area max to your counter height. Our Shi-Tzu would sometimes get those ^*!&^$#  seeds in her tail and ears when we camped at the lake. A stitch in time saves nine so the best time to control it is when it first appears with a garden hoe.  Sounds like yours already has a good toehold so longest journey start with first step.  Being an annual the best approach is pre-emerge (once in Fall and again in Spring in Texas).   Corn Glutton as organic and herbicides that are mostly restricted to licensed applicators.  Hand control can be likened to Python control in the Everglades ,it requires lots of labor to track and kill a female but each kill prevents dozens offspring in following year, hundreds over her life.   Not very incouraging I know but maybe my little pep talk can make up for it.   Having grown up on a farm when weeds were controlled with hoes, 1k sq ft of garden bed looks like child's play compared to stareing at 30 arcres (only one of a dozen fields on our farm) of crop overgrown in Johnson,Crab and other grass.  Unless you own 3 or 4 already, keep your eyes open at garage sales for hoes where blade and sleeve for wood handle is a singe piece.  That's important ,one piece head.  If  it doen't  already have a handle put a Hickory handle in it.  This hoe will sharpen and hold an edge 5x or longer than what you can buy at big box.   For a quility one piece hoe check the farm Co-Op or feed & seed.  Ace can order them if they don't have them in store.   If  the hoe is so great,why would you need more than one?   (A) Because after realizing how well it works, you accidently run over it with the tractor and break the handle you won't cry as hard if there's another ready to go. (B)  I have 4 stashed at strategic spots so that I can reach it and spend 10-15 minutes or even dig out a single sprout of Johnson grass without trudging back the shed to retrieve a hoe.  I often carry a hoe for no particular purpose as I stroll checking on plants or just enjoying the garden.   As I see weeds I can take care of them without breaking a sweat. The lessened cintrifical force caused by 4" missing blade on each end took some uump out of it so I bolted an old 10" steel wheel with solid tire to belt pully to bolster force. If you still have Marathon growing in the shade, leave that alone and install UC Verde in the sunny areas.  Let the two mingle through the transition from shade to sun.  If you find the Marathon fading out on you, then you can use a zoysia in the shade. My problem with zoysia is that if something happens to it (drought, insects, disease), then it's gone for the rest of the growing season until April of the following year.  Here's a picture to show what I mean.   There is a low path running from the house to the street through the middle of the bed and to the curb.  We had had an excessively rainy few weeks, so the water never really stopped flowing through that dead area.  A fungal disease got started and knocked back the zoysia.  The picture was taken in July 2013, and the grass remained brown until the following April.  I had the same thing happen where I tried some zoysia.  It's been many years, so these folks have figured out a solution (no, I don't know what they did).  But had that been bermuda or St Augustine, they could have recovered in the same season and not had to endure the brown grass for so long. There are too many varieties of zoysia for me to keep up with.  If I were to pick on for my yard, I'd find an installation in my neighborhood and ask where they got their sod and use that.  As it happens, the house we bought in 2022 came with some very hardy zoysia, that my wife has been trying to eradicate.  We are having problems with our St Augustine in the front, so I'm about to propose patching in some of the happy zoysia and see what happens. As for buying UC Verde plugs, no longer is there only one source for the plugs, so the price is coming down.

This will probably turn out to be a multi step operation, so lets take them one at a time.  #1. The bloom spike with the single bloom.  From the bloom, come up the bloom spike until you come to the first branch growing off to the right.  Just below that new spike you will see a little white dot on the spike you followed to get up there.  That white spot is a scar where the first bloom once was.  about half way between the bloom scar and the new spike, cut the old bloom spike and discard it. Ok, on with the task at hand.  First off, terminology--The bloom spike you are calling terminal is not!  That spike is exiting from the main stalk of the plant and the axial of the third leaf---exactly where Phalaenopsis orchid bloom spikes should originate, so, no problem there.  Second,   WOW!!! You must be a world class corset maker!  How you managed to grow and bloom that plant with the roots bound up as tight as they are in that little pot and kept them as healthy as they look, is beyond me!  I say excellent culture, but Yes, your plant needs to be repotted, in my opinion, as soon as possible.  If you get a speck of root rot in that package of roots, you probably won't be able to stop it.  Now, If you want to, You can let the last bloom fade, but my suggestion would be for you to cut that old bloom spike off as soon as that flower fades, leaving about a 1 inch stub where it grew out of the main stalk.  The other bloom spike is young and healthy, so you can probably save it unless you accidentally physically damage it in the repotting process.  Be careful.  I don't know where you are located, or what your growing setup is, so I will leave some of these decisions to you.  You can use a clay or plastic pot.  Clay pots with slotted sides are my choice, since they are heavier and less likely to tip over, and the slots allow more air flow.  Plastic pots hold the moisture inside better, and that helps in dryer climates.  Phal's like to grow over the pot rim which mimics how they grow in nature, and keeps water from collecting in the top of the plant.  Plastic is lighter, and with Phal's usually are prone to tipping.  You will need a pot large enough for you to spread those roots out inside it, and cover them up with mix. You will need orchid potting mix.  My preference is a fir bark mix.  It should come dry in the container, and contain fir bark nuggets, some charcoal, chunks of peat, Perlite, and perhaps something like pumice stone.  The important thing is that the mix should be dry and chunky.  If it feels wet and mushy in the container, look someplace else.  Ask about pine bark.  If orchid mixes contain pine bark in any form, I don't use them.  Orchids don't like pine bark.  I live in SC, and have seen a large commercial orchid nursery experiment with it, and it proved to be a complete failure for us.  You will need sharp, clean, sterile cutting instruments, and an open work space.  When you have all this material assembled, and all the prep work done, post back here and we will go through the fun part.  Bill

Ok, sounds like you are ready to tackle a new project.  You have new roots starting to grow from the base of the plant, and a new bloom spike, so you want to be very careful of these throughout this entire process.  The growing tips of the new roots are almost like jelly, and the tip of the new bloomspike is not a lot more substantial.  The roots inside the "corset" are different.  Running down the center of all mature orchid roots is a tough woody core, that transports water and nutrients from the roots into the plant. The root material surrounding this central core is brittle, and acts much like a sponge.  In repotting an orchid, you are going to pop a few of those roots, at least I have never repotted one without breaking a few roots.  That is the reason you keep the plant on the dry side for about a week after repotting to allow these breaks to callus over. Now, you have a choice.  You can first, take the plant out of the pot, open up the "corset", remove it, and soak the roots in room temp. water, for a couple hours, or overnight,  or you can take the plant out of the pot, soak it for  a couple hours or overnight, and then take the roots out of the "corset".  The roots will soak up water, which makes them more flexible and easier to work with. While you are soaking the roots, take enough of the orchid mix out to fill your pot+ a bit, and place it in a pan and soak it until you are ready to use it. Once you get the roots out of the pot and unbound, gently open the root ball up a bit and try to get as much of the old bark mix as possible from around the roots.  You are not trying to straighten out the roots, just free them up a bit to make it easier to get into the new pot.  I usually build a small cone of mix in the bottom of the pot, and try to gently spread the roots over that, and then pour the remaining mix around the edge of the pot over the orchid roots.  While you are doing this, try to work as much bark around the roots as you can, so there won't be any empty spaces in the pot around the roots.  You want to cover as many roots as possible right up to the base of the plant.  Make sure you have the plant as stable as possible in the pot, and the vast majority of the roots well covered with bark.  When you are finished potting, put the pot in a sink, or outside and just flood it with water.  This is to settle the bark in the pot.  When you are finished this, put the pot in a warm shady location with moderate light, and let it stay there for at least a week to dry out.  This is the beginning of the healing process for any broken roots.  After the week of drying, you can begin to water the plant lightly when it gets d r y. After 2 weeks of light watering, you can put the plant back into its normal growing location, water and feed it normally, and every time you get close to it, smile and pat yourself on the back. Bill

YES, any dead black mushy roots you find should be removed.  Dead, Black, Mushy is the pure definition of root rot.  Cut them back to clean live healthy tissue, and sterilize those, or that blade before you use it on other plants.  When you have potted as many of those things as I have, it's just too easy to pass over a point like that when you are basically dictating each move to an inexperienced grower.  I probably should start off with a statement something like "take a large dump truck full of pure common sense and dump it in the middle of your work space before you start."  The commercial orchid nursery I worked for had a lady (aptly named Viney) who did almost all of their small pot potting (2.5 to 6 inch pots).  Viney had a "throne" built at the back end of one of the greenhouses, where she worked.  She had all her equipment and extra pots strategically placed around her seat, and places to put flats of potted plants.  They would bring plants needing to be repotted to Viney in trays, and drop them off in the designated space. Viney would take a pot in one hand and take the plant in the other, and pull.  The plant would pop out of the pot, and she would inspect it and remove dead leaves, pseudobulbs, and dead roots, she would gather the roots in one hand, take a pair of shears out of her disinfectant pot, and swish, off came the roots all but the 4 inches or so she had in her hand.  She would grab a pot, (all the plants in a group would be the same size) stick the plant in the pot, fill the pot with wet potting mix, mash it down with her thumbs, and put the plant in an empty tray.  Viney would do that all day, sometimes all week, and in the spring, maybe for a month at a time.  I would make sure if I was taking visitors on a tour of the business, to go by Viney's work space, hold Viney's hands in mine, and tell the visitors that those hands had potted more orchid plants than any other hands in the entire state of South Carolina, or maybe the Southeast USA.  I don't think I ever saw a single plant that Viney repotted die.  I'm sure they did, I just did not witness it.  We did have a remarkable record of repotting survivability.  Orchids are really tough plants, contrary to a lot of what you read on some places like this. Bill

"Any thoughts on what it could be?" Gas companies add trace amounts of chemicals to gas to enable humans to smell leaks.  Typically, sulfur-containing compounds called mercaptans are added.  Most people describe the smell as "rotten eggs" or "rotten cabbage."  The same smell can be produced by decaying matter.   If your home is on a crawl space and you have duct work in the crawl space, your system can pull odors from decaying matter in the crawl space into your home.  Grab a flashlight and inspect for mold/mildew or anything that might be decaying in the crawl and cause an objectionable odor.  And inspect inside the ductwork to the extent you can.  A dead mouse in a duct is a terrible thing.

Dave, absolutely not normal. The aforementioned delay in restarting after a run cycle is to allow time for the refrigerant pressures to equalize within the system, otherwise the compressor may be unable to immediately start anyway and kick-out on overload (maybe more than once depending how long until the pressures equalize).  The delay reduces wear/tear on the compressor and the overload protector.  Window A/C units that don't have electronics to enact a restart delay may have a label on the controls "Wait 2 minutes before restarting" (or 3 minutes or whatever time period the manufacturer deems as appropriate). I'm guessing your rapid cycling is caused by a system problem, not the thermostat actively turning it on/off. I suggest you set the thermostat to Emergency Heat mode which operates only the heat strips so the compressor doesn't keep short-cycling until you can get it checked by a servicer.

Something I wrote years ago about what determines appropriate pot size, and why: Choosing an Appropriate Size Container How large a container ‘can’ or ‘should’ be, depends on the relationship between the mass of the plant material you are working with and your choice of grow media. We often concern ourselves with "over-potting" (using a container that is too large), but "over-potting" is a term that arises from a lack of a basic understanding about the relationship we will look at, which logically determines appropriate container size. It's often repeated that you should only move up one container size when "potting-up". The reasoning is, that when potting up to a container more than one size larger, the medium will remain wet too long and potentially cause root rot issues, or at a minimum, limited root function. In reality, it is the size/mass of the plant material you are working with, and the physical properties of the medium you choose that determines both the upper & lower limits of appropriate container size - not a formulaic upward progression of container sizes. In many cases, after root pruning a plant, it may even be appropriate to step down a container size or two, but as you will see, that also depends on the physical properties of the medium you choose. It's not uncommon for me, after a repot/root-pruning to pot in containers as small as 1/5 the size as that which the plant had been growing in prior to the work. Plants grown in ‘slow’ (slow-draining/water-retentive) media need to be grown in containers with smaller volumes so the plant can use water quickly, allowing air to return to the medium before root issues more serious than impaired root function/metabolism become a limiting factor. We know that the anaerobic (airless) conditions that accompany soggy media quickly kill fine roots and impair root function/metabolism. We also know smaller medium volumes and the root constriction that accompany them cause plants to both extend branches and gain o/a mass much more slowly - a bane if rapid growth is the goal - a boon if growth restriction and a compact plant are what you have your sights set on. Conversely, rampant growth can be had by growing in very large containers and in very fast (draining) media where frequent watering and fertilizing is required - so it's not that plants rebel at being potted into very large containers per se, but rather, they rebel at being potted into very large containers in a medium too slow and water-retentive. This is a key point. We know there is an inverse relationship between media particle size and the height of the perched water table (PWT) in containers. A PWT is water that fills spaces between soil particles and defies gravity by refusing to leave the pot. As particle size increases, the height of the PWT decreases, until at about a particle size of just under 1/8 inch, media will no longer hold perched water. If there is no perched water, the medium is ALWAYS well aerated, even when it is at container capacity (fully saturated). So, if you aim for a medium (like the gritty mix) composed primarily of particles larger than 1/16", there is no upper limit to container size, other than what you can practically manage. The lower size limit will be determined by the medium volume's ability to allow room for roots to ’run’ and to furnish water enough to sustain the plant between irrigations. Bearing heavily on this ability is the ratio of fine roots to coarse roots. It takes a minimum amount of fine rootage to support the canopy under high water demand. If the container is full of large roots, there may not be room for a sufficient volume of the fine roots that do all the water/nutrient delivery work, and the coarse roots, too. You can grow a very large plant in a very small container if the roots have been well managed and the lion's share of the rootage is fine. You can also grow very small plants, even seedlings, in seemingly inordinately large containers if the medium is fast (free-draining and well-aerated) enough that it holds no, or very little perched water. I have just offered clear illustration why the oft repeated advice to ‘resist potting up more than one pot size at a time’, only applies when using heavy, water-retentive media. Well-aerated media are not bound by the same restrictions. Was the subfloor wet looking up from the bottom? So, you will see it all over this board - and any others - that grout is not water proofing. If it's leaking on the underside, it's not because of grout - it's because your floor pan/drain was poorly done. The standard test of a floor pan - before tile and grout - is the flood test. In that, they block the drain and fill the pan up with water and let it sit for 24 hours. If it leaks water it doesn't pass. Again the grout has NOTHING to do with it leaking. If it's leaking, you almost certainly will have to rip out and replace the shower. I'm sure it can wait until warmer weather, but it will eventually rot the floor. If it's not leaking, fix your grout, and then figure out how to fix your exposed plumbing for real. Don't count on things not freezing in TX anymore. Just insulating the drain line is not a great fix because it will slow down the freezing - but not much. BTW: So, that's not a great tile/grout job. On narrow grout lines you use un-sanded grout. On large grout lines you use sanded grout for strength. I suspect you have un-sanded grout on a big fat grout line. I stay away from the ready to use grout - but a better tile person than me can comment on them. My preference has always been Mapi that you mix with a latex additive.

I agree with needing an architect for such a large project with very specific needs (and restrictions). Bring to the architect your long list of needs and wants. Our family has a lake cabin in Minnesota, and I often fantasized about building something new. Here are some of the things I would plan for: - convenient access to the outdoors - flooring that is tolerant of water and sand - a bathroom (with shower) near an outside door - plenty of storage for beach towels - an away space for playing board games or jigsaw puzzles, for rainy days or just need to get out of the sun days - storage for said board games and puzzles - large enough bedrooms to allow for a comfy chair or love seat, so each family has an away space - more drawers and counters than sinks in the bathrooms - NO Jack and Jill bathrooms - Storage (either garage or shed) for water toys: canoe, kayak, PFDs, fishing rods, etc - windows and doors situated for good cross ventilation (I'm not a fan of running AC at a lake home unless absolutely necessary) - planned outdoor living space - grandparents' bedroom on the main floor - enough closet space for each family to be able to leave stuff at the lake between visits, but you don't need as much closet space as you would for full-time living We vacation with a group of friends at a resort every summer (last year we numbered 21). We are spread out among 5 cabins, but we eat our meals together, so a lot of cooking and most cleanup takes place in one cabin/kitchen. We generally use paper plates, so one DW (and lots of helpers) is sufficient. What IS necessary in that cabin is 2 refrigerators! When we all arrive the first day, they are both full. The other thing the kitchen in our cabin features is shelving on one wall, instead of cabinets. Because those are empty between guests, it's where we put a lot of our non-perishable food. Having it in the open wouldn't be my preference in my house, but at the lake with lots of people, it's nice to have everything out where folks can find easily find things. One more tip: an extra set of sheets for every bed. When a family gets ready to leave, they can strip the bed and put on clean sheets, so it's ready to go for the next time (I know when I arrive at the lake, I want to be outside right away!) Dirty sheets can be brought home to wash, or washed at your convenience while you're there.

Linnea, I have been rooting violets for many years, and my normal recommendation is for growers not to be afraid of them.  Patience is usually the most necessary attribute.  From here on, this is going to be an "I normally do this" discussion, but please refer back to sentence one of this post frequently.  When I get a violet that I want to propagate, I pop off a few leaves---I prefer to use the older, long stemmed leaves---Sometimes I trim the ends off with a sharp, clean, sterile blade, some times not.  Into the water they go.  My rooting container hangs in the kitchen window, right above the sink.  It is about 18inches under a light, and the window is west facing with a porch overhang outside, so the leaves only get an hour or so of late afternoon sunshine on clear days.  I just wait them out, and in my case a good 95+ percent of the leaves, over the years have rooted.   When I get a good set of roots, sometimes I pot the leaves, and at other times I let them stay in the water until I see the little green "Mickey Mouse" ears (leaves) appear.  sometimes--most of the time--I just pot the leaf with roots.  I put the tip of the leaf deep enough into well draining AV potting soil, and wait until I I get a large enough plant so I think it will survive on its own, then I remove the leaf by cutting it off at ground level--again, sharp, clean, sterile cut.  I have gotten as many as three plants with this method off a single leaf.  I do not think I have ever had an African Violet leaf die while it was rooting.  That usually occurs for me with the potted plant, and that is very rare. Plants, for me are an enjoyment, not something to get "up tight" over.  They seem to know that if they were growing out in the wild someplace life, wouldn't be nearly so comfortable and easy as it is growing on my plant shelves.  I encourage that. Have fun. Bill

Linnea,  Thanks for the "thanks', glad I could be of some help. The first photo is the overall setup in the kitchen window to show just how terribly complicated the whole thing is.  There are leaves from two violets rooting in the containers.  The top group is from a named plant, and the bottom group from an unnamed plant that I will use for give away plants. The third photo shows leaves from the other plant that has decided to just give me a nice set of roots.  When These get a bit larger I will plant the leaf stem, roots and all in potting soil, and expect them to soon afterwards produce little leaves.  I have cut the leaves (little plants) off these stems and returned the stems to the water, and gotten as many as three little plants off one leaf. I realize we are operating under different stress levels, because if I loose a rooting leaf, I can always go back to the original plant and get more leaves.  This time, you are trying to save a particular plant, and should you loose your rooting leaves, you have perhaps lost the entire plant. Brick is porous. It absorbs the water sitting in the soil which moves upward on the wall, and can lead to the algae growth like you have (probably not enough air movement/sun from behind some removed bushes). If you have improperly installed flashing/membrane/WRB behind the brick the water can get to the wood, and mortar sitting in water can deteriorate. Pests like moisture laden materials. I often see houses in Georgia with soil right against the brick. Really there should be a waterproof membrane (e.g. Henry Blueskin) up just past the grade height. It looks like you needed to raise soil to get a good slope away from house, but that causes the soil to be higher than before. You can pinpoint a height on the wall that grade doesn't go over, then remove the grade to get the slope away from house. It's also helpful to bury downspouts near the house to get them far away (min 10' away), keep the soil below the sidewalk to prevent wash onto it, and make sure there is a well at the crawlspace vents and the well bottom height accounts for puddling. Also, you may need to add a step up to porch.

text: That's entirely understandable. The tarps got cold, because they were touching, and exposed to the frigid outside air. That doesn't mean the air temperature under the tarps was below freezing, and it's that air temperature that plants are affected by. The tarps did provide insulation, so I'd have to assume that air temperature under them was well above that of the outside air. If the temperature under the tarps got below freezing, you'd be getting frost forming ON THE PLANTS themselves. Plastic should work fine. The function of the tarp is to prevent warm air coming off the ground from escaping. You want to seal in that warm air. Plastic will do that handily (as would steel and ceramic, if you could make a tarp out of those).

I live in zone 7a also,  in NC.   Winters are usually not severe here though some years it can get down to as low as 4 degrees.   I grow between 350 and 400 roses and don't do any winter protecting.   I  am wary of piling anything up on stems whether grafted or not.  Vernon Rickard,  the late owner of Almost Heaven Roses,  who also lived in NC,   used to make wire cages around some of his roses and would fill those with fallen leaves.  But I never do that. When I first got into roses  I thought own-root plants were much easier to grow ,  had prettier shapes as plants,  and  thrived better for me than  prior grafted plants I had bought.   But  it could have been due to me  being introduced to some rose varieties that I had never tried before.   Perhaps they were just  more vigorous plants.  Also  I may have bought poor quality grafted plants like " body bag"  plants from Walmart.  It's hit or miss with those.   I've had some good luck with them but  bad luck as well. If you're curious about whether own root ones would do better for you  why not try some?   There are plenty of opportunities on this site to observe what does well for other people.   The hmf site  has tabs at the top of each rose page where you can click on  additional pictures ,  comments from people in different locales,  and  ratings for hardiness,  vigor,  disease resistance, etc. We've had a severe cold snap here but I am not devoting any time at all to worrying about my roses in the ground.   Usually they do fine.  I think some roses do very well own root and some  seem to do better grafted.

While on this diet  there was no counting calories. I followed a food list, carbs were what was counted, eating less than 20 whole carbs per day. Your body uses up the glucose/sugar from the high carb foods for energy and stores what it doesn't use, by cutting the carbs there is very little sugar so your body uses its own fat as energy.   I had heard about this diet for a few years and though no way could I do it or how it worked but then I saw my brother lose 75 pounds he convinced me to try it.  I was a carb eater, loved candy, loved all the starchy vegetables and during Covid put on some weight especially in my stomach.  I knew I needed to lose at least 100 pounds. Pureed cauliflower with butter and sour cream and garlic for mock mashed potatoes. I was never pre diabetic or diabetic but eating this way can reverse Type 2 diabetes and get you off the medication sometimes in less than a few weeks.  I would rather eat bacon and eggs than take medication.  I have never been healthier. My A1C is normal, my heart is good, I have no blockages in my veins or arteries, my cholesterol is good.  I lost the fat stomach and my butt,  I can't wear any of my old clothes, had to buy new everything because I lost so many fat and inches off my body. I like neutrals and whites The key with white-on-white color schemes is Chroma. There needs to be a difference in Munsell Chroma of at least 0.20. It's that factor of contrast that ensure neither color will make the other look dirty or dingy. @bart bart without generous water, NOTHING you attempt is going to result in anything remotely resembling the photos you adore. Providing enough water to maintain them in the "alive" state will produce some flowers but to obtain that lush abundance of sumptuous flowers, they require LOTS of water. You could very likely not provide any more "fertilizer" and only the increased water and obtain the kind of flowering you desire. I've tried "conserving" the water and I got some bloom. The plants lived and were reasonably healthy but none of them performed until I just WATERED. I know you can't alter what Nature provides but the water IS the key. Without it, none of the other resources are going to provide you their money's worth, and some of them may even prove toxic due to excess salt build up. The water not only supports the soil flora and fauna which digest the resources and then provide them to the plant roots but it also flushes CO2 and salts from the root zones and draws in the O2 the roots require. That's one of the downsides of "drip" irrigation in arid, alkaline areas. Not enough physical water to flush the salts which build up from each drip application and flush the carbon dioxide and draw in oxygen.

I use a combo of natural and commercial fertilzer. commercial for faster immediate growth. water soluable tomatoe fertilizer in spring, should be a blue color when dissolved. then blooming fertilizer in mid june to help with seed production. the danger of all commercial is that you wil get salt build up in your pot mix over time, which will eventually stunt them. commercial nurseries can get away with it as they aim to pump and dump. sell them before this happens. the natural part for keeping them in a pot long term is to use composted manures. we keep chickens so i have the used wood shavings manure mix in a pile decomposing with high nitrogen, but also developing sub nutrients as it ferments, adding a little microryzome fungi spores and worm castings to the mix can only improve it. let it cook like a compost for awhile. then to build growth within the pot add the fertilizer compost to the bottom of the pot. add it in thirds. bottom hi nitrogen fertilizer compost, the middle gets straight mini pine bark nuggets for aeration and substrate for root stretch. then the top is your basic pro mix, which has your peat for water retention. then dig a whole in the middle of the pot and plant. the basic idea is the roots will grow and reach down to the lower part of the pot getting aeration along the way. renew the pot mix every three years. when you water them weekly, or more in hot climates, get a water wand with a medium fine spray, water below the leaves, you can even hold the head right down on the soil where it creates a bubble action at the top of the soil. this helps get  oxygen to the roots as slightly mixing nutrients in the pots. when there is not alot of heat stress, let the pots dry back a few days, this lets oxygen back into the pot as well as allowing air pockets in the bark, your next watering should then flush out the gases accumulated during dry back. this is my method, as i have learned thru trial and error.

Two important things: (1) what is the size of your cooktop or range underneath the over-the-range microwave? It is important to know the width of your cooktop/range that will be underneath the microwave.  Most cooktops/ranges in small kitchens are 30" wide.  There are some cooktop/ranges that are 24" wide, and you can find 24" wide OTR microwaves for them, but they will not have an air fryer or convection.  But if your cooktop/range is 30" wide, then your OTR microwave must also be 30" wide.  You cannot install a 24" wide microwave above a 30" wide cooktop/range.  That is against Building Code.  The reason is that it is a fire hazard to have a 24" wide microwave above a 30" cooktop/range. A small microwave could not also fit an air fryer and convection, because those features take up a lot of space.

3 of the plants Evve shows are Portulacaria, which have the same growth habit as Crassula. Is there any negative in issuing very shallow planters as opposed to taller ones with room for way more volume of soil? "Negative" is subjective in that the pot typically looks better, but shallow pots are more difficult to grow in because they typically have a much higher % of saturated soil after a thorough watering. This makes it essential to either choose plants very forgiving of being over-watered, or ensuring you're using a grow medium that holds so little excess water it makes it difficult to over-water. As you learn more about bonsai, you'll find practiced growers are very particular about their choice of grow medium, and alter the structure and components to suit individual plants.Most grow media based on fine ingredients (peat, coir, compost, composted forest products) are not good choices for shallow pots because they hold excessive amounts of water. For example, if you use a medium that supports 3" of excess (perched) water at the pot's bottom, using that soil in a 3" deep pot would find you growing in a soil that is 100% saturated after a thorough watering. It would be challenging for even skilled growers to maintain a jade or mini-jade (portulacaria) healthy in a situation like that. Notice how pot depth affects the amount of well-aerated soil a pot can hold after a thorough watering:   The pots are completely filled with soil. The shaded area represents excess (perched) water. Note - if you shift your focus to using the upright form of portulacaria for your bonsai endeavors (or other trees with naturally small leaves), you'll be able to produce a much better likeness of a tree you might find in nature. This is due to portulacaria's leaf size which is more proportionate to the scale of a smaller plant. Al

The division into individual pruning groups are just guidelines. At a previous garden I had way too many clems - around 60 or so - and there was no way I could keep track of who needed pruning when and how much. Other than the type 1's or no pruning required group - I treated them all the same - a late winter hard prune as if they were all type 3's. Other than delaying slightly the bloom period for the type 2's, when and how hard I pruned made NO impact on the flowering ability of the type 2's. IME, which includes decades of growing clematis in all its forms as well as working for a local major wholesale clematis grower, hard pruning of any clematis type will not affect bloomage....other than with respect to timing. Type 1's or old wood bloomers should be pruned back (if needed or desired) as soon after the initial bloom cycle as possible in order to allow sufficient regrowth and ripening of the wood for the next season's blooms. If hard pruning of a type 2 failed to produce any flowers, look to the timing issues or lack of sufficient sunlight. It is not the pruning that is the cause.

There are several plants or "crowns" growing in the pot you are asking about.  Sometimes they can be gently pulled apart, holding the plant and roots that it attached to at the same time and either teasing it apart or if you have to, cutting the plants apart with a knife.  Each crown has a central growth that all of its leaves radiate from. You can also leave it as it is if you are not comfortable dividing it.  Multiple growth african violets will bloom just as well as single crown plants.  With all of the plants in your pot, if it got enough light and was fertilized regularly it would produce more flowers than a single plant alone in a pot. Some people like single plants, other african violet growers will intentionally grow multiple crowned plants.  All trailing african violets are multiple crowned plants. If you decide to divide it and a plant breaks off from its roots, it can be set into a new pot of soil, remove a few of the lower leaves and it will produce new roots and grow into a separate plant. Good luck with your plant!  It is up to you whether you want to divide it or leave it alone, either way is fine.

Dolomite Dolomite is a relatively soft stone, so it can be badly damaged if exposed to excessive force. It can also be scratched and stained quite easily. I think you have misunderstood what you have.    You likely have a timber frame under the window with plasterboard on the inside and felt and horizontal planks on the outside.     The way it was constructed likely left an air gap in the centre of the frame and this was considered insulation at the time of construction….. since then someone many have filled that gap with insulation but it’s unlikely.   So I’m proposing that you make the gap bigger in order to create a space for thick insulation.    I didn’t think you would be doing this yourself so if you need a step by step build you need to consult YouTube for a video.   However if you are just looking to understand the process then you need to remove the horizontal exterior to check for rot and see if any timber needs replacing.    You need the interior plasterboard removing and the frame bolstered in order to create a thicker cavity for insulation.    You will likely use a board insulation as it’s better than fibreglass, use expanding foam and add tape to insure no drafts then replace the weatherproofing on the outside.   New UPVC cladding can also add to the insulation.   On the interior you can replace the plasterboard with an insulating one although most builders will tell you the incremental improvement in insulation is minor and the best result will be creating a bigger cavity under the window and insulating that.

When asked by any law enforcement agency in Minnesota they must also provide a disclose form to sign informing you of your rights about giving them your SSN.  Below are parts of the form summarizing a person's rights under federal law in Minnesota,  but even if your state doesn't have disclose forms all states must follow federal law. "The federal Privacy Act of 1974 (5 U.S.C. § 552 a) requires local, state, and federal agencies to inform individuals whether sharing that individual’s Social Security number is mandatory or voluntary, the basis of authority for requesting the information, and the uses which will be made of it." "You do not have to supply your Social Security number and may legally refuse to give it. The Social Security number will be used to identify you in the NCIC system. Consequently, failure to provide the Social Security number may reduce law enforcement’s ability to verify your identity or to investigate the crime." If you don't want to give your SSN to law enforcement you aren't legally required to do so and the OP was within her rights to refuse.

@oursteelers 8B PNW Austin dropped Cymbaline primarily as a marketing decision. Hortico  imported the early Austin roses into Canada, without Austin's permission, then exported them into the US before Austin had any legal representation in place in the Canadian/US markets. Once the rose is publicly identified, the clock begins ticking on your twelve months in which to patent it. That is the reason for the "AUS" names Vintage and so many others had to sell the early roses under. Because Hortico introduced his products into these markets, he was legally prevented from patenting them, therefore demanding payment for them, so he trademarked the fancy names (Tamora, Cymbaline, Heritage, etc.) which forced anyone wishing to sell the roses under those trademarked names to purchase a license from Austin Nurseries to pay him for the privilege of using those names. Everyone else was legally able to sell those roses, just not under their known names. Austin then set about making those roses undesirable and  unsalable by adding provisions in his contracts that anyone wishing to sell the new, therefore more desirable roses, could NOT sell the "AUS" trademarked varieties. Then, he set about to replace them with similar appearing but "superior" varieties and declaring them "obsolete". In most cases, to many of us, the new "superior" varieties were simply new and offered little improvement over the originals, which were, in many cases, marvelous roses for most of the SoCal climates. That is, other than the terminal RUST many of them suffer.

Place a straightedge over the crack please in several places. It should not rock nor should there be a dip below it. If the top is on plane, there is no flatness installation error. If it is not, the top was torqued and it failed at the easiest place to relieve the torque, the corner. Is there a cantilevered overhang? If so, how much? Does that overhang have additional supports? A sagging cantilever will torque a top. Estone cracks are very difficult to repair inconspicuously; virtually impossible. Mechanical fasteners into the top to secure the sink are not permitted under the Cambria warranty; all estone manufacturers prohibit their use. If the crack is from a mechanical fastener, Cambria is off the hook. This is highly unlikely. Estone has plenty of internal stress; sometimes it blows up on the saw table during fabrication. Sometimes it takes a while to manifest.

I just read "The Flowering Thorn" by Margery Sharp, which was written in 1934.  In spite of the title, it didn't have much to do about roses, but Marechal Niel is mentioned a few times and the end of the book has this passage: "Tell me what you're thinking about." "Rose-bushes," answered Lesley truthfully. Subtly his face changed. "In that frock, of course," he said; and there was a difference in his voice too, a sudden infusion of boredom.--'Like picking up a book and finding you've read it,' thought Lesley vaguely.  Then realising for the first time the implications of his remark, she woke up and defended herself. "But I mean real rose-trees," she explained, "not--not the conversational sort.  Three Barbara Richards, one Etoile de Hollande, three Madam Butterfly, three Mrs. Barraclough, and a Rev. Page Roberts.  Is that eleven or twelve?" "Eleven," said the man. "Then I can have one more.  Do you know anything about Julien Potin?" "He's a sort of hybrid-tea.  But why have another one?  Wouldn't it be more original to have eleven?" "At the place where I'm going," explained Lesley, "they have them at so much a dozen--assorted, you know.  I believe they practically throw one in. Not a pro, but I'm starting with this statement:  "Messy, dirty, needs repairs, many items need to be replaced or fixed."  I'd suggest that before you think much about prettying it up with decor elements you focus on making the space neat and functional. Prioritize spending money on furniture and storage solutions. Then, as budget allows, you can make a wish list and gradually dress it up with fun things like a new bedspread, curtains, rug, art, maybe painting a feature wall or adding wall-mounted sconces, etc. Start with furniture. What furniture do you have in the room that you want to keep? Or are you thinking of replacing everything? Do you have enough storage, or (as I suspect, from the comment about it being "messy") do you need more? If you want advice on furniture options, a diagram of the room with dimensions and showing the location of the door, closet, any windows, and the sloped wall would help. Some options to consider for storage: -A wardrobe. Ikea has some of the most affordable options (check out Pax), but placement might be challenging given your slope -One or more dressers -A storage bed with drawers underneath -bedside tables that contain storage or alternatively small (even wall-mounted?) bedside tables that take up as little space as possible A room like this with unique dimensions can be a great candidate for custom built-in wardrobes (we also have a weird-shaped bedroom of about these dimensions that was totally saved by a custom wardrobe) but those are usually a few thousand dollars and I recognize this may not be in the budget.

Moss is not necessarily bad for the soil although it is an indicator of soil quality. Heavy, consistently wet soils will tend to develop moss and a heavy enough coating over the top of the soil surface will block needed oxygen exchange. It will provide next to nothing in terms of plant nutrients but it can be incorporated into the soil if you can't easily scrape it off. The concern with moss growing on the soil of a container of any description is telling you the climate is too wet OR your container soil retains too much moisture. I grow my entire garden in containers and they will often develop moss across the soil surface in winter. I scrape it off every spring as I am tidying up or refreshing the soil.

Whether you cook in the oven or hob it creates steam and grease in the air.   To reduce how this impacts furniture in the same room and how much cleaning you do it’s important to have an extractor.   A £40 option to satisfy building regs will extract up to 250m3/hr. A good ceiling mounted extractor will extract up to 4 times that.    You can get one designed to sit on the ceiling https://pando.es/en/hoods/e-231/. They are designed to sit between the joists of the floor above and so look flush to the ceiling.    Given the cost can be upto £1000 I understand people wanting a £40 option but personally I think it’s an economy you will regret.

Actually, thinking back, I have never lived in a house where the windows were exactly centered in most rooms in the house because that would have put the windows in odd locations on the outside of the house because not every room was the same size. This includes two houses built in the 1830s in which symmetry was extremely important. But I have never lived in a house built after about 50 years ago. All of the houses had simple ordered facades with a regular window arrangement. The house I live in now has a fully symmetrical facade front and back. The house is almost like a cartoon. That said, because rooms have closets, and there's a fireplace, and it's a row house...that puts all the windows off center inside. My sister lived in a house where every single room had a window centered in each room or "space" because it was sort of open plan on the first floor. But this did some odd things to the windows on the outside. Her house was built in the 2000s. If you look at the plans of  bigger houses designed in this century every single room may have a window or windows centered on the room and that can put them all over the place on the outside, and this is compensated for by doing a bunch of bumpouts or different materials or gables or bits and pieces on the outside to conceal this. But look at the backs of some of these houses, if they don't continue those details on that facade. Window acne. The windows should make some sort of sense on both the inside and the outside, if possible, but that does not always mean centered. I know someone whose bedrooms all have centered windows, and in the secondary bedrooms, there isn't a decent wall to put a bed on in some of the rooms because the bed is going to overlap one of the centered windows on one of the exterior walls somewhere. So as has been mentioned I think you need to discuss with the architect why these windows are not centered inside, and there may be a really good reason.

The house wants to be a garrison colonial, but historic garrisons were set at ground level (no long entry stairs), had no portico, never had bay or double windows, always had a window over the front door, and rarely had shutters.  The closer yours can come to these characteristics, the more authentic it will look--but changes have to be reasonable and affordable.  So . . . What about building an iconic New England dry stone wall a little in front of the house and walk, to ground the house and visually cut the height of those stairs when viewed from the road?  Next, is there any chance of adding a small window above the door?  (I don't know what's inside that wall.)  That would make a huge difference in how "right" the house feels.  To me, the door also needs to be centered/symmetrical and the stairs would blend in more if they were darker (gray instead of white). Then there's the shutter question.  I'm not a purist when it comes to shutters.  No one closes them anymore (except in hurricane country).  They're simply decorative now, so I judge them as I would any other decorative element:  purely visually.  Does the house look better with them or without them? Here are several views with the stone wall and the added window, with various shutter options.  (I do think darker and wider would be better if they stay, so I've shown that.) Seems like an art form to me.  Is that not what bonsai is? Most art is 2D or 3D. It could be said that bonsai is a 4D art form, the 4th dimension being life. Science plays an important role in advancing and enhancing a growers' ability to keep plant's healthy and attractive in spite of the regular repotting, pruning, and major manipulations most plants go through on their journey to becoming a bonsai specimen. The answers depend on the degree of moodiness you desire:  Moody accent, moody lite or full-on moody.  Your new medium wood floors will reflect light up, and the openings to the bright white hallway will read as a "fifth" white wall in the rooms.  This will make all of your choices less moody from the get go. Also, what times of day will you be using these rooms and what direction do they face? Moody Accent - If you paint wainscoting white, the dark walls and ceilings are going to provide a moody accent color but will not make for a whole moody vibe at all. Moody-lite - Paint the whole wall dark color including wainscoting, and ceilings white. Full-on moody - Paint ceilings and entire walls a dark color and you'll have an actual mood in the room.  It isn't going to be nearly as intense as some examples you see online because of the white hallway next door, but will be much more enveloping than with white ceilings. Same ceiling treatment in different rooms - Using same dark color in both rooms --> treat the ceilings the same.  Using two different colors in the rooms --> can treat ceilings differently or the same. Your choice of window treatments, furniture, and other decor will also help lean the room more moody lite or full on moody. Moody-lite Examples All trim painted same dark color, white ceiling, white contiguous rooms, bright uplifting upholstery, frames, chandelier = moody lite.   Note difference between flat green paint above and this super glossy blue paint and how the blue reflects the light.   Moody-lite = White hallway, ceiling,trim, chairs, and bright curtains combined with some darker furniture too.  Full-on Moody Examples This dark green with white ceiling still reads as full-on moody because of the dark wood trim, dark moody decor, dark rug covering much of the room, and dark views into other rooms.  You will never achieve this dark of a mood with a white ceiling because the bright hallway next door. For you to get this moody, you'll need a dark ceiling too.    This blue-black opens on to white hallway, but looks full on moody because of dark ceiling and all trim painted dark.  This is a good example for you if you want full on moody.  More full-on moody with colored ceiling.   Painted Wainscot This is a good case for you painting your wainscoting and upper walls the same color.  With a white ceiling the room is moody-light. Your description doesn't sound so meticulous.  ;)  I would not feed a gravity toilet discharge into another toilet's plumbing. Re "how do you know."  I would know, as would most old house afficionados.   Can tell by the era house was built whether old growth wood was likely to have been used and by the quality and "beefiness" of the trim profile, perhaps some places like inside a closet you can find some unpainted.   Old growth wood in particular is prized and quite valuable (if youve ever checked out architectural salvage).   Can also get an idea of what kiind of paint job and how hard it might be to remove.  If multiple thick layers from previous decades (including lead based paint which is a beast to remove) Id be less inclined to want to attempt. That said, 1944 is getting pretty late in the game, woodwork starting to become skinny /skimpy and the probability of farmed lower quality wood increases.... so maybe less worth effort and expense to remove paint.  Still a knowledgeable renovator COULDVE done some really nice things with it such as apply toners or stains in current colors . I really feel for OP as unpainted vintage wood is becoming less and less of an option.  BTW anyone selling your house, don't listen to your realtor telling you you need to paint your woodwork white in order to sell - in most markets one can sell one's house many times over and people generally like to paint and make a place their own anyway .  If you do then apply a nice thick layer of clear shellac first which makes it more possible in future to get off paint which someone might want to do to either refinish OR repaint   ... while at the same time serving as a good primer for the paint.

You need to abandon any plans to move the drive to the front until you have checked if dropping the kerb is possible.   Driving over a pavement is technically illegal unless there is a dropped kerb.   It could get expensive for you if you damage the pavement or the utilities under the pavement, or hit a pedestrian.   You need the local Highway Authority to drop the kerb (usually the county council), so you need to apply to them.    Someone I know had a 20 month wait for it to actually happen.   You might also need planning permission from your Borough council too.    Furthermore there are regulations about dropping a kerb.  Proximity to junctions, obstructions, trees, road signs, parking bays, bus stops or utility covers can complicate matters, so a good planning consultant may be necessary.

"Our helpful contractor has offered to pour curbing 3' from the fence around the yard, but it will probably be straight. I'm trying to decide if that's best." As a professional landscape designer, I think this is a very poor design decision. First, a 3 foot width is barely wide enough to support most perennials, let alone any shrubs that would give the garden some structure and year round presence.. Second, concrete curbing is a far too permanent or hard to remove solution to keeping the lawn out of the planting beds. It takes very little effort to manually edge the beds a couple times a season or you could opt for an easy but less permanent solution and use flexible edging (available at most home improvement stores) or stone or concrete cobbles intended for this purpose. And finally,  straight, matching parallel borders are best in a more formal setting, whereas graceful and generously sweeping curves lend themselves to a more natural, casual style.

Because water is draining towards the house porch and pooling, it looks like you need a surface drain on both sides of the sidewalk. I would not cut the porch to install a trench drain, as you will still have water pouring over the front edge of porch to get to this new trench drain (and the porch looks sloped away so all the water will not reach the drain anyway). Also, cutting exposed aggregate finish will not be a clean look. So, you can eliminate cutting the porch as an option. Realize a french drain needs to be deeper within ground to function to it's potential (which might be lower than the existing driveway trench drain outlet so you couldn't connect if so). And has to wait for the ground to be saturated above the french drain "system" prior to functioning wholely. But water can still run on the surface without the ground being saturated, like in a rain deluge. So a french drain is secondary to grading properly, but when you can't regrade and have pooling like you do, you have to introduce surface drains. - You can install a trench drain right next to the porch all the way across (piped under the sidewalk to connect each side). Whether this connects to the existing driveway trench drain or bypasses depends on where the drywell is/outlet depth or a daylight opportunity (wasn't clearly understood on existing for that). - Or instead of a split trench drain you can install two catch basins a tiny bit further out from the edge of porch, and regrade the soil so it is all sloping towards the catch basin grates. Note the outlet depth of catch basins would be lower than a trench drain if that matters in how you discharge them. - If you have the depth to gravity drain a french drain pipe (to the drywell or daylight) then I would also install that all the way across. With the house being lower the water coming towards it will have some effect on something over time, whether a crawl space, basement, settling, sogginess of yard, etc.

Something more to learn about roses: when a cane emerges from another cane, there are lots of new buds close to the point of emergence.  Often they are so small, you won't notice them. As the cane matures, some of them will just be overgrown by bark.  One or two might grow. When you see this happening, you will see the buds not just on the upwards facing side, but all around that base. Farther out on the cane, the buds are different in their distribution.  A single bud has two much smaller backup.s Loose the big one, and a second will grow (unless a spreading canker took the first) Loose the first two, and there is a third. Sometimes two will grow.  BUT when RRD takes control of the growth, each of those three may have three more and so on.  The worst I ever saw was in the Royal Botanical Garden in Burlington Ontario where a short vigorously growing Floribunda had up two twenty (yes, I counted them) buds breaking from a single site, not just once but all up and down several canes. On kinky canes, it's more wavy and that's because one side of the cane is growing faster than the other.  When first infected the virus moves  down rather than around or up. Also, watch your prickles.  Right now they look good in your photos. Right now, relax, but keep vigilant. Ann

If you would look at the drop downs, it would give you a comparison to see if your cutter teeth are coming out right. It doesn't matter what kind of sharpener you're using; if the angle of the tooth isn't right, or if you aren't making the edge of the tooth razor sharp and/or your depth gauge (rakers) are not the correct height in relation to the cutter, you can't expect it to cut properly. It's a good idea to carry the proper file(s) with you because even with the best equipment, a light 'touch up' with a file every once in a while, makes the cutting a lot less work. Don't wait until the chain dulls completely before sharpening it. You'll also want a depth gauge checker (shown in the drop downs) so you can file down the depth gauges to the proper height in relation to the cutter tooth. Too tall and it won't cut very fast, too short and the saw can get dangerous and stick or jump out of the cut. You want nice big chips coming off the saw. If the chips are like saw dust, then somethings not right. Using a chain saw is a skill that takes time to develop. It's always best to work with someone that knows the language before attempting this yourself. It's not something you want to learn the hard way. What is efflorescence? Efflorescence is the process by which salt migrates to the surface of a porous material where it forms a coating. The appearance of efflorescence is often described as a white, fluffy or powdery substance, but it can range in color from white to gray, brown, or even yellowish hues, depending on the type of salts present. Found on walls and other brick, stone or concrete surfaces, it occurs when evaporating water leaves behind salt deposits on the masonry. There are many installation problems which may lead to efflorescence: IMO you need to address this problem before you even consider painting.  This might be caused because acrylic paint as opposed to masonry paint or limewash was used on your brick.  Your brick should be able to expel moisture and the acrylic paint is preventing that by sealing the moisture in.  You may find more significant damage in the future in the brick.

If there's meat in it, bake then freeze.  With potential travel misadventures, you don't want otherwise forgettable pathogens to assert themselves.   Highly recommend several Polar-Tech Re-Freez-R-Brix, which are foam, and superior.  3 for $15 at Amazon (informational—they may be easy to get locally).  Supplement with dry ice, rather than cubes, if you can.  Make sure to fill your cooler.  If you have extra space you can freeze disposable containers full of water.  Don't include travel snacks/drinks in the same cooler so you won't be opening it often. If you can make it there without problems, that's best, especially if you can buy the fresh ingrdients there.  For literally a couple of days—less than three—don't freeze the ingredients, including the meat.  Make the container ice supplements, wrap the ingredients well so they don't get damaged, and pre chill the perishables.  Make sure the milk and meat are right next to the cold packs.  Keep the fresh produce away from the cold packs.  Cheese doesn't care.  Don't pre-prep anything that needs chilling, though.  the quality will deteriorate and there's more chance of contamination, You can probably get away with making the bechamel ahead, but it could break. In the car, wrap the cooler in blankets or heavy towels. We've travelled for weeks with commercially flash frozen meat as well as pre-cooked, home frozen meals, packed with dry ice, with no problems.  The big thing is keep the cooler out of the sun, and don't open it unnecessarily, My feeling is there's more air in pastitsio than lasagna.   It should travel fine frozen, but give it every chance you can to keep it frozen solid (for quality as well as those pesky pathogens).  Let steam out well while cooling after baking.  Refrigerate over night, or equivalent time.  Freeze it with plenty of air room around it, if you can, and also, if you can, put it right where the freezer coils are, or directly in the path of the fan (but not blocking it), so it'll freeze as fast as possible, with less water migration.  Thaw and reheat at the same temperature and duration as it baked for (adjusting as needed for different oven, and elevation. Good luck!

If you use dry ice, be sure to keep the cooler closed and a window cracked.  I have friends who nearly killed themselves traveling with a load of dry ice in their car.  Their neighborhood had been hit with a power outage following a particularly bad storm.  Being sweet people, they offered to drive to the nearest place selling dry ice and pick up a bunch for anyone who wanted some.  On the way back, they realized they were getting very very sleepy.  They put 2 and 2 together, rolled down the window, got some fresh air and were able to continue on their way with the windows open.  Hate to be an alarmist, but I’m not sure I would have thought of the consequences.

Sanseveria does not mind small pots. It actally helps them stand. Ive had one for 25 years (and split and propogated many times) and the plant sits one figers with away from the edge. They just dont care about all the extra space. You could get a smaller plastic growers pot to go inside this pot? It will have drainage holes and you can set it on top of two or three small plates or a handful of rocks and the overflow will be caught by the blue pot. It wont go all over your carpet and you wont have to use a catch plate. This pot essentially becomes your catch plate. As for water, the water needs of a plant depends on how much sun they get, how much they transporate (let out of the leaves), how big they are, etc etc. Some plants can be soaked, some plants need less. My suggestion is to put it in a sink and water it until water comes out the bottom and dont water again until you can stick you finger all the way into the soil and pull it out dry. That length of time is dependent on your climate. I live in Albuquerque where its is 0-10% humidity most of the time and I haven't watered this plant in two months but its probably time. text: My advice is to wait to prune until the large flowered daffodils are underway in your area.  Prune all climber growth basal canes as well as laterals, until white/cream colored pith is encountered, AND the stem thickness is minimally as thick as a wooden writing pencil. At this point what's left can be further pruned to accommodate the support structure restrictions if necessary.  What guidelines I have given are subject to your interpretation. Once blooming climbers are pruned differently.  I will defer to those folks knowledgeable on their pruning to chime in. Very old looking basal canes on climbers are left in place as long as green, vigorous growth emerges somewhere   ithem,, even well beyond the crown.  My Lady Ashe, which recently succumbed to Rose Rosette Virus, had a 4" diameter trunk on her, from which about 4 laterals emerged which were a good 6 years old, quite old looking, and pumped out beautiful, thick additional laterals from themselves. Let's put this into perspective, since all we see as recipients is what happens with our package at it's final destination.  My DH was a FedEx delivery driver for over 20 years (stopped in 2022) and I helped him during peak times (hello holidays!) so I know what I'm talking about. On average, his day would be comprised of 125-150 stops with 300-400 packages. Multiply that by 300-400 packages at 125-150 stops.  It's time and effort, which is already at a premium for people who do this job. You know what I do when I'm expecting a delivery?  I watch for my package to be out for delivery and then listen for the truck.  I have a moderately long driveway and, because steps are important, I meet them at the truck for my package. Amy, I can tell you having a dolly out would make your delivery person very happy.
