text: If the cane is black or has black sections interspersed with green sections, prune back to where green begins without any interruptions with  black.  Then, look at the pith, continue pruning back by no more than 1" increments, nipping away until white/cream pith is encountered, then stop the nipping away until a bud below the last nip is reached.  That bud, as dormant as it may be, even if it is no more than a node, will break dormancy and become a new lateral. What climber(s), are you working on? What growing zone do you garden in? One last thing...don't be tricked by seeing robust looking shoots emerging from green sections of canes with black areas below the robust looking shoots. .  Those shoots are doomed to either soon wither and shrivel up as the black sections extend into one another, obliterating all the green sections as the entire portion turns black, or the shoots grow a bit further, but weaken and become extremely unthrifty.  Then, you eventually prune out the unthrifty growth to good green stem with white/cream pith. Moses

I have mostly done Mirage engineered flooring, on which they have increased the length of boards over the years, so I can't comment on lengths in their solid products. I'm not sure where you heard it's "too soft". but that's preposterous. White Oak is White Oak, regardless of whether it ends up in a mill to be prefinished or sold unfinished. I have seen valid complaints detailing how Mirage products with smooth surfaces and semi-gloss finish show indentations, but the wire brushing and matte finish should mitigate that issue. One thing to be aware of when purchasing character grade Oak is that it can often have short boards, because the better part of a board may have been cut off to sell in a higher grade, for a higher price. See if you can find a mill selling the wood you want in 2' to 10 lengths. You can likely find longer boards by going unfinished/site finished, which will not have bevels for a more seamless look, and you get to choose the perfect color/finish for you. The counterpoint to that would be the prefinished floor, which would take less time, make less mess, and have a more durable factory finish. My choice would be to buy the longer length unfinished wood and do a minimal sanding that would include wire-brushing. I really like the Bona NaturalSeal color on White Oak.

I recommend, having someone qualified and certified as a structural engineer to do all the calculations and the drawings, for the builder then to follow. There are standards and safety standards that structural engineers take into account, and in my experience builders often say that they over-engineer it, but structural engineers are actually liable to make sure that it will indeed be safe and consider every contingency. Their primary objective is to make the building safe. While a builder might decide that cost and ease of work are more important and would just do what they are used to doing. Builders are not structural engineers! Architects normally hire structural engineers to do all the static calculations as they are complex and time-consuming. So I would check with the team that has done the plans, and confirm that all that has been done correctly. Builders are people who follow the building plans that are prepared by the architects, who have checked and calculated static forces, either by themselves or have that work sourced out, and then specify exact materials and construction for the builder to follow.

Per Jake The Wonderdog's comment above, it sounds like your water has more a problem with iron than with hardness.  Certainly you may have both but orange staining is related to high levels of iron in your water.  The iron may either be in your water supply or it may be leaching from any iron pipe you may have in your home's plumbing.  Sometime folks use galvanized iron pipe nipples in parts of the plumbing, often the tub faucet for example.  So you may want to do a little more research before selecting water filters, softeners, appliances because your selection may be different for hard water vs. for iron in your water.  By definition, hardness is primarily calcium and magnesium and they leave crusty deposits after the water has evaporated.  Metals like iron and manganese leave black or orange stains, probably anywhere you have a drip or where water runs down the surface of your fixtures...sinks, tubs, toilet.  Iron and manganese sometimes makes water taste earthy but people sometimes prefer the flavor of water that has just a little hardness.  Too much hardness and you may feel like you are drinking water from a puddle on a limestone ledge! If you just had hardness, one option is just to dry your sink/tub/faucets after use.  Most of the lime will go with the water you soak into the towel.  Iron may bond to the appliance so drying may not work so well for it.

Start with a water test.  Seriously - it will cost you less than $100 and could save you a lot of headaches.  Sounds like you have iron, but how much is the question?  If you have less than 10 ppm or so, you could probably use an oversized softener with high capacity media and the salt in the green bags. If it's more than 10ppm it will be a lot more difficult to treat.  You also need to know how much hardness you have, as well as manganese.  The pH and various other factors will be important too.  So step 1 is get a water test.

@diggity_dude is absolutely right - start with a water test by a lab, not a treatment company. Be sure you get your sample before any water treatment such as neutralizer or softener. You can treat low levels of iron with a softener using resin made for iron and oversized. But you need an iron filter if it's higher - as he stated. I'd be much more concerned about getting the water fixed than fixing the tile in the shower. Fixing the water goes to the source of the problem and, again, solves it throughout the house.

You are right to be concerned.  I believe the Illinois residential code is based on the 2018 International Residential Code which forms the core of most statewide building codes.  The 2018 IRC requires a make-up air system be installed if the exhaust capability of a range hood exceeds 400 cubic feet per minute (cfm.)  It's intended to prevent depressurization of homes and attendant back-drafting of vented appliances like gas hot water heaters, fireplaces, etc.  Failure to install the required make-up air system will be an inspection "show stopper" for your final inspection and likely prevent your move in.  Tell your builder to open the code book and have a look.

To reiterate many threads here: No air leaves the kitchen via its hood system that isn't replaced (made up) one way or another.  The make-up air can be supplied by a deliberate MUA system (heated in Chicago), or via leakage paths in walls, ceilings, basements, and reverse flow in combustion appliances -- see Charles Ross Homes comment above.  So even if there were no combustion appliances or fireplaces to back-draft and thus no safety hazard, there would still be a gag on the hood system causing the actual flow rate to be very low, even as moisture is pulled into walls and wall dust into the living area. I suggest you search this forum and the HVAC forum for threads and comments related to MUA. As a short-cut, here are back-drafting levels provided by another forum member. Mechanical-Draft Appliances Heating systems with fan-powered exhaust systems can withstand higher negative pressures than natural-draft appliances. Some types of fan-powered systems are much better than others, however. In order of effectiveness, the choices are: * Sealed-combustion. Also called “direct vent,” these appliances draw all combustion and dilution air from outside. These can typically tolerate negative pressures in the range from 25 to 50 Pa. * Power-vented. These draw their makeup air from indoors and are also called fan-assisted, forced-draft, or mechanical-draft. These can typically tolerate up to 15 to 20 Pa of negative pressure. * Induced-draft. These have a small fan added for energy performance, not to overcome house depressurization. These can typically tolerate 5 to 15 Pa of negative pressure. By comparison, an atmospherically vented furnace can back-draft with as little as 5 Pa of negative pressure, and a gas water heater will have spillage at 2 or 3 Pa. Fireplaces can start having problems at about 3 Pa. Canadian codes limit negative pressures in homes with atmospherically vented equipment to 5 Pa. U.S. codes do not currently address the issue (in a plainly spelled out "prescriptive" number). 1 pascal = 0.00402 inches, water column 1 atmosphere = 407 inches, w.c.

To follow up now that we have had a few triple digit days... Bottom Line: The solution to ad an inch of foam board behind the medicine cabinets worked great. --- After pulling the medicine cabinets - we (builder's rep and myself) installed 2 layers of 1/2" foam boards (didn't find the 1" locally). I also caulked around the edges of the foam boards thinking that might eliminate hot air drifting in. The builder's original cabinet maker perfectly matched the trim and stain with a second layer to fir the cabinet out 3/4" or so. Everything fit back like a glove. Cosmetically it looks great. Yes the trim appears to be twice as thick but really it's not noticeable. It's partially covered by towel rings, I know it's there and I don't even notice it. So the average observer may never notice either. I found my IR thermometer and took some readings once we hit some 100s. With the indoor TStat at 78F the highest reading I was able to on the inside of the panel in early afternoon just after the exterior wall looses direct sun was 83F to 84F. That was the worst case scenario. After midday when the wall is in shade even with outside temps well above 100F, the surface temp on the back panel drops - eventually down to ambient 78 or 79F. The second cabinet had an exterior wall T in behind - so one half of the cabinet was exposed to exterior (no sun) and the other half to interior wall. It read 78 on the interior wall and 79F on the exterior wall. Interestingly, I had leave the cabinets shut all day and take these reading w/ my IR TStat immediately after opening at mid-day. Otherwise within just a few minutes of opening, the surface temps on the back panels quickly adjust to ambient air temps. For comparison other surface mounted cabinets mounted to various exterior walls in other parts of the house: They usually showed about 79F on their back panels, occasionally 80F. Simply touching the back panel of the medicine cabinet I cannot detect or 'feel' any warmth or heat coming thru whatsoever. Perhaps most important - none of the creams or heavier lotion items became in the least bit 'liquidy'. So bottom line is the solution to ad an inch of foam board behind the medicine cabinets worked great.

One thing needs to be kept in mind; the recommended air velocity into the hood entry air aperture (90 ft/min from me typically on this forum) may not be needed if the hood is commercial with significant reservoir volume on the cooking side of the baffles.  As long as the effluent can get to the baffles without reflecting down and out, and the entrainment air velocity at the baffles exceeds the up-rising plume velocities (e.g., 1 m/s), then containment should be achieved. So, for example, I have a Wolf Pro Island hood that has an entry aperture of about 12 sq. ft.  Using a 1500 CFM rated Wolf (Broan/TnTone) blower I get good capture and containment results with an upward flow rate of (approximately) 100 ft/min.  (Careful multi-position measurement and averaging over the entry aperture has not been performed; this is from a sparse sampling of the flow velocity at various locations under the hood.) With the OP's 17.5 sq. ft. aperture, 90 CFM/sq. ft. requires an actual 1600 CFM that would only be obtained using a blower rated perhaps as much as 2400 CFM, depending on pressure losses.  My point is that even 1200 CFM actual might be sufficient with a commercial hood depending on cooking style and assuming the total plumes' CFM did not approach the system CFM, thereby saturating the reservoir averaging process.

The ARS offers this: " Deciduous azaleas are very tricky to propagate from cuttings.  Take cuttings of deciduous azaleas when the new growth is soft and pliant.  This is often coincident with time of bloom in early June. The ability to root decreases rapidly as new growth matures.  Trim cuttings below a node (overall length of cuttings 3 to 5 inches) and dip in a rooting hormone containing fungicide.  Insert in a medium of 60% milled sphagnum peat moss and 40% horticultural perlite.  Usually bottom warmth of 75°F is used to encourage root growth.  In late August, transplant cuttings that are rooted and grown on in the greenhouse with supplementary light (14-hours a day) to prevent dormancy and induce new growth.  In the following fall, transfer to a cool, frost-free (35°F to 41°F) environment to induce dormancy.  As new growth develops in the spring, transfer plants to a shaded environment. Layering: This is the easiest form of propagation for the home gardener.  A lower branch is held down on soil (not mulch) with a stone.  A slit is cut in an area in contact with the soil and the cut is treated with a rooting hormone.  Then the cut area will sprout roots.  When the roots are developed enough to support the end of the branch, usually in 2 years, the rooted-branch is cut from the parent plant and transplanted.

The first apartment my husband and I lived in was part of a home that was split into 3 apartments with the landlord living in the top story and renting the two lower stories.   We had the first floor apartment with access to the yard for my dog.   We lived there for almost 2 years and had no issues with our landlord.   His goal was to gain wealth through real estate, buy homes, make them into apartments and rent them out so that they would pay for themselves and when paid off would provide him enough income to retire early. One of my closes friends rents a bedroom and bath from an elderly man.   He got married in his 80s and he and his wife each kept their own home and they split their time between the houses.   He wanted someone there to take care of his dog and to watch the home when he was not there.   She needed affordable housing (living on SS).   This has worked out wonderfully for her and her landlord. Another friend split her home into 4 apartments and rents out 3 of the apartments.  She got financially devastated during the 2008 crash and had to figure out a way to make the staggering mortgage payments on a home that was upside down.   It has worked out.  Her and her husband have managed to keep their home.   She genuinely liked most of the people who rented from her over the years and keeps in touch with several of the people who moved on. Would cook and leave their dishes, drop stuff at the front door and leave it sit, leave empty potato chip bags in the living room . . .    Her husband had passed away and she needed to rent out part of the home to make the mortgage payment until she reached 55 and could sell with a reduced tax penalty. There is risk that you will choose your renter poorly and have a huge headache trying to get them out, but it can also be a financial savior.

At this point, the most important thing is feasibility for your situation. 1. Look into/consider logistics, legal, insurance, and financial costs and how/what will be needed in addition to renovation (separate entrance, sound insulation, larger hot water tank, security, etc. 2. Think about effects and pro’s/con’s: maintenance, sharing driveway/yard, potential bad tenants (including not paying rent/utilities),  against the added income and how it would benefit your life and savings. 3. Value and rental feasibility: Will your home increase in value or it be detrimental if in a family neighbourhood (would a senior accommodation design address that), access to transportation, how much are rentals going for for what you have in mind (look on line), etc. If you decide to move forward, speak to someone who has been renting for some time -  what to avoid, interviewing, getting references, proof of income, setting expectations (that's a big one, as we learned). Given the above, there is no simple answer. The tenant/landlord experience can be so varied; just be sure you choose well and are willing to deal with the unexpected.

Are you using a grow medium you made yourself or a commercially prepared medium? If you made your own medium, did you include a source of calcium (Ca), i.e, dolomitic lime? An adequate supply of Ca must be in the nutrient stream at all times if tissues are to form normally. Even if there is an normally adequate supply of Ca in the grow medium, soggy soil can cause a cultural deficiency of Ca by limiting its uptake. Symptoms of the deficiency often include hooked or distorted leaf tips and localized areas of tissues formed by cells with walls compromised by a lack of Ca. The compromised areas can appear translucent, or, as cell walls fail and leak cell contents into intercellular spaces, a corky tissue similar to that associated with oedema forms and becomes conspicuous. This can occur from an actual deficiency of Ca or from a cultural deficiency (too much water in the medium/ too much phosphorous, zinc, or especially magnesium). Actually, identifying leafy houseplants isn't really as important as most think, except perhaps as a point of curiosity. The reasons are four. First, most leafy houseplants want nearly exactly the same things; i.e., bright light; then, a well aerated medium that doesn't hold a lot of excess (perched water); appropriate levels and ratios of supplemental nutrition, and a grower who uses appropriate watering practices. The four points mentioned will cover at least 95% of leafy houseplants. Of course, there might be an outlier here and there who wants direct sun or filtered light, or something other than a 3:1:2 ratio fertilizer like Foliage-Pro 9-3-6; but for the most part, getting the four most critical points right will normally allow growers to maintain their houseplants at a high level of vitality until root congestion starts to take a toll. Dealing with root congestion should also be recognized as an essential part of every grower's care regimen if their goal is to provide plants the best opportunity to maximize realization of their genetic potential in terms of growth rate, vitality (health), the ability to resist insect/disease pathogens, and eye appeal. @kitkay I'll watch for your info.

But will just say that 90% of the glass railings we do end up with a cap even if it was not originally intended to have one due to the lami polished edges and the way they turn out. For the most part we only buy IGU's from Viracon. Although we have a 10,000 sq ft point supported canopy that is getting 13/16" tempered low iron lami from Viraco and from what I can recall will be the first time buying lami from them outside of IGU's. We also use Agnora out of Canada for large light IGU's. They advertise as "Big Ass Glass" now, lol. They make beautiful IGU's and very large lights.

Agnora does make some big-ass glass, it's their thing! lol They are a quality organization from all I have heard. Also, Viracon is a good laminator, which is no surprise since they are good at pretty much everything that they do. What's really interesting is that you have to use caps over railing tops, even when they weren't part of the original plan, because the edges look like crap. That was the gist of the whole "can we polish after finished laminating" argument. If the glass is annealed then polishing after laminating is a given (or should be), but if it's heat strengthened or tempered, then....big controversy. Because it can be difficult to get perfectly aligned polished edges without interlayer squeeze out when laminating lites with exposed polished edges together, you get finished railings that need a capped top. A couple of the big-dogs of the commercial world were pushing for a code change to prohibit all polishing of tempered-laminated glass after lamination, but I don't know if that ever passed or not. I hope it didn't because it was a bad idea in my opinion. I remember one company's "solution" was to change the industry quality standard to allow for a greater degree of offset of the two glass lites. Might looks bad but at least "it's in spec". If the glass is for an inside application, then there is no reason whatsoever to use tempered glass in the lami, annealed is actually a much better choice. But outside tempered-laminated does improve structural and wind-load performance and that is the primary advantage over annealed. 10,000 ft² supported canopy is very cool! Would love to see it.

SDLM did well for me growing under the eaves of our last house (in St Johns, Portland).  It had the deep eaves typical of Portland homes, so it could protect the blooms from the rain. It did not blackspot too much. Some BS appeared after the spring flush, but it wasn't a problem, because the weather always dries up that time of year, so it didn't have a chance to spread.  It produced two reliable flushes a year, and there was something so magical about the late summer bloom - the big, cupped blooms with their deep scent was like a postcard from May or June when the whole garden was fresh. I am a fabricator.  In 20 some years I have done thousands of quotes.  My quoting process is set up so I can easily quote multiple stone colors. The material also can have a significant impact on shop hours as some popular stones like quartzite take a lot more time in the fab shop because the material is so hard.  All that said a competent fabricator should be able to provide a quote for different colors within a day or two of the customers selection.

author_name: Moses, Pitt PA, cold W & hot-humid S, z6
text: Late frosts are the nemesis of early pruners.  I had growth up about 4" one spring, forsythia were done blooming, then ZAP!, a killer late spring frost that killed all the growth.  The auxiliary buds (usually one on each side of the main shoot), kicked in.  As they got to be about 1/2", I went through the bed snapping off the weaker of the two.  The first flush was about a month later that spring.  This does not occur frequently, thank God. Moses

Moses, I have had roses in my 6 zone do fine in a month later snowy frost, after pruning, fertlizer , new soil, , lots of growth, and violets/bulbs were all blooming April 20th.  They all recovered in 2 days after melted-very good.  Maybe my NY roses are more hardy?

text: Snow can be no colder than 32°F.  If the air temperature was not too far below freezing, wind speed was low, <5 mi./hr., and the duration was brief, I can see why the growth rebounded nicely. My perspective is that if the roses are starting to leaf out, they're going to leaf out whether I prune or not. There's some stimulation based on pruning, sure, but the budding that they're doing is going to lead to leafing before long once the ground temperatures warm up. They might indeed get a late freeze that does damage or kills them, but my perspective is that for the most part they're going to get damaged or die by those late frosts regardless of what I do. Of course in zone 5 (apparently now zone 6), most of my pruning is cutting off dead canes and you can do that any time because the rose doesn't know dead canes are gone anyway. I don't do shaping pruning like what Diane is talking about till much later in the season, if at all, so that doesn't apply to my pruning decisions. That's why these pruning decisions are highly variable by region and types of roses. I prune as soon as I can see if a cane is alive or not, starting with the earliest or most robust bushes. Windows are rated for, among other things, U-factor and Solar Heat Gain Coefficient (SHGC). In cooling dominated climates SHGC is the more important of the two, that's why a low solar heat gain LowE coating is recommended (often mandated) for that climate, because the coating blocks direct solar gain helping to keep the inside cooler. Coatings also improve U-factor over clear glass as well. While argon gas between the lites does nothing to affect solar heat gain, it does improve U-factor about 8% over an air-filled space. Can i use the 5-1-1 mix but add some of the components of the gritty mix  to make the soil last longer? Unquestionably, you can do whatever you like, but I can offer some input insofar as what to expect. Either medium will last at least as long as the point in time when the roots become so congested a full repot would be required to ensure your plant has the best opportunity to realize as much of its genetic potential as possible. If we assume you're able to maintain the plant at a high level of vitality, roots will likely congested to the point where they would benefit from a repot in spring at the beginning of the 3rd growth cycle, and definitely by spring of the 4th growth cycle (probably stretching it but not endangering the plant's viability). As the 5:1:1 mix breaks down much more slowly than finer materials. By the time it has broken down to the point where you should be concerned about the soil's structure, the plant's roots are becoming a part of the soil's structure, so the real issue is the volume of soil (carbon) will be diminished by the soil gassing off (as CO2). The diminishing volume of soil will be unable to hold an adequate supply of resources, that, couple with the fact heavy (thick) roots with very few branching fine roots will have filled the pot at the expense of those fine roots that do all the plant's heavy lifting. The primary reason for repotting is to remove heavy roots to free up space for fine roots to grow.  Because the gritty mix is structurally more porous, it offers roots an extremely welcoming environment for growth, which typically shortens the interval between appropriate (timing of) repots. Will the gritty components just separate  out and not add any benefits? Are there reasons not to combine these two  mixes such as pH or nutrient conflicts? The gritty mix will not likely stratify in the pot unless you aggressively flood the soil before the roots have colonized the entire soil column. It's primary benefit lies in the fact that it is a healthier environment for roots until root congestion fills the greater air space it offers; then, it becomes just another medium until you repot. Al

Just because you mixed the 5:1:1 and gritty mix together doesn't mean you did anything 'wrong' or shot yourself in the foot. What it all boils down to is this: If you want to mix the gritty mix together with 5:1:1 you will introduce a perched water table, which the gritty mix is designed to eliminate entirely or almost entirely. You will have a medium roughly equivalent to the 5:1:1 mix in terms of usability and productivity, perhaps slightly but not conspicuously better than the 5:1:1, but not as good as the gritty mix in terms of drainage and air porosity. Still, you'll have a much better medium than you'd be likely find in bags or bales of media based on a high % of fine materials (peat, coir, compost, composted forest products, .....) . Other than make a couple of very general comments, I'm going to stay out of this discussion.  In my 50+ years of growing orchids, I never developed a great love for Brassia's for several reasons.  I would suggest you go to a well stocked library and see if they have a copy, or can import a copy for you, of Alex D. Hawkes ENCYCLOPEDIA OF CULTIVATED ORCHIDS.   This book is one of the standards for culture of a great number of orchid species.  The section on Brassia's has a few pointers that may be helpful for you in growing one of the less commonly seen species of orchids.  Brassia's include about 30 species, that are closely allied to Oncidium, and are found mostly in the tropical Americas.  They grow generally under Cattleya conditions, are best grown in pots tightly filled with osmunda or shredded treefern, or firmly mounted on slabs.  The plants do not care for the common bark mixes. I grew the vast majority of my orchids in pots with Fir bark mixes, and in my small portable greenhouse, could not provide the high light requirements for these plants.  With the exception of Brassavola nodosa, which did well for me in the climate I could provide in my little greenhouse that got moved around the country every few years. If you are new to this orchid culture adventure, my suggestion is to educate yourself, and learn to be the most inquisitive grower on the block.  Fear of doing something "wrong" is your greatest enemy, and an abundance of curiosity is your greatest asset.  Have fun!

You can very easily prune your plant so it has a single trunk with virtually no concern that the pruning will cause the plant life threatening harm. The trick to pruning jades and portulacaria is to leave a very short stub. You don't want to cut into the node on the trunkline that gave rise to the branches you're viewing as subordinate, or competing trunks. When you leave a short stub, sealing the wound is unnecessary because the wound will dry back to the first node proximal (closer to the roots or trunk) to the cut. Once the pruning is done, in 6 months to a year you'll be able to simply rub off the desiccated tissue with your thumb, making it difficult to tell it was even pruned. Cutting flush to the lower order branch  (the branch the you're pruning is attached) or trunk will cause tissue to dry out in the immediate vicinity of the wound, such that the wound will be larger, deeper, more unsightly, and it will take longer for callus tissue to cover the wound. I would advise that you carefully cover the existing wounds with waterproof wood clue, which will prevent the wounds from growing larger due to desiccation. Use a flat toothpick or similar item to carefully paint the wound only. Try not to overlap the wound and get glue on the periderm (bark); this, because it will make a lump when the callus rolls over the glue. Al

I would apply one coat of sealer and two coats of finish, then determine if another coat is warranted. It's a fairly common misconception that more finish is better. I mainly do residential work and in a well-kept home, clients have their floors recoated when they start to look shabby. Most are not worried about wearing through the finish, because their floors will be recoated when they look scuffed, soiled and  scratched, which is far before they wear out. Contrast this with commercial venues, where floors are going to get beat up and maybe not look perfect, but the establishment needs to have enough finish on the floor to ensure it doesn't wear   through and damage the wood. A similar situation might occur in a home where there's a resident with a disability, like someone using a walker or wheelchair. They might value having more coats of finish initially to protect the floor from wearing through, and they're prepared to accept that it's going to look shabby for a longer period. White Oak is less grainy than Red Oak. More coats can quickly fill in the softer grain, making the surface smoother and less interesting. I prefer satin finishes over matte, but some are so close that it's hard to tell them apart. I like the liveliness added by a little extra sheen from the floor.

Any downward light has the potential to cast shadows -- pendant light or wall-mounted sconces.  In the bathroom, your brows and nose can create shadows on the lower part of .your face. Keys to getting it right -- let's divide the lighting into tasks, and we don't really need to see a floorplan: General lighting for the bathroom -- This is for walking to the toilet, coming in to get some lotion, putting away clean towels.  The recessed lighting of which you spoke will be centered in the room, right?  This is your general lighting.  Since it'll be behind your head, it will throw big shadows on your face when you stand at the sink, but you don't really care -- you're just walking to the toilet or coming in to get your lotion or putting away clean towels.  Specific thoughts: - This should be your easiest-reach switch, as it's your most-used lighting. - I assume a 1940s house has small bathrooms, so one central light should be enough.  It is a one-room bath, right? - Since you like pretty fixtures (good for you!), this can be something nicer than a recessed pot light. - A budget-minded builder would tell you to skip this light, though it won't cost much while you already have the electrician on hand.  You could just use the vanity pendants for general lighting, but having a ceiling light is nicer. Task lighting at the sink -- I'm not sure if you're shaving or applying make-up at the sink, but the pendant lights of which you spoke will give you good, strong light in the right places.  Flank your sink with TWO pendant lights right at eye level /head level.  A single light could still throw shadows to one side, but two lights will eliminate this problem.  You can test this right now with a small lamp: hold it directly above your head, hold it just above your head and to the side, then hold it to the side of your face ... you'll see where the shadows fall.  NO to a single pendant above your head ... shadows galore.  Put them on dimmers, as their light will be "doubled" in the mirror.  And put them on a separate switch because you don't always want /need that strong light at the sink (like in the middle of the night). Specific lighting in the bathroom: - In addition to the above most-important lights, you also want a recessed light above /in the shower /tub area.  If you're really fighting against shadows, consider two small recessed lights on opposite ends of the shower ... as above, light from two directions will eliminate shadows.  This light will probably be combined with a fan ... don't skimp on your fan, and choose a model that'll turn itself off after X minutes. - Maybe a recessed light above the toilet.  As they aged, my grandparents (and now my parents) have all had some ... um, special medical needs at the toilet.  Extra light in this area might be useful.  Maybe not, but it won't cost you much to put it in, and then you're "future-proof".  At the worst, it'll make cleaning easier. - Consider a soft night light, so you can avoid turning on all these lights in the middle of the night.  You could place an outlet near the floor and run a rope light under the edge of the vanity.  Or you could place an outlet near the ceiling and hang a string of lights around the ceiling. - Yes, the type of bulb /amount of light matters, but PLACEMENT of these light fixtures matters most when we're talking about eliminating shadows.  Light of any type can only move in straight lines. - If you have a linen closet in the bathroom, add a recessed light to the front of its ceiling so you'll have good light IN that closet.

Bare plaster is usually prepped with a watered down coat of white paint. I'm not sure of the exact ratio but it's usually very watery and transparent.  In your case I might just try going straight to paint application as it was so long ago. Leave the door/s open for a while to get it as dry as possible prior to painting. Just do a small test piece first in any left over colour you have lying around. If it adheres well and doesn't flake its fine to paint. If not you will need to prep first as described above.

I agree that a mist coat is needed.  It doesn’t have to be white paint but it does have to be at least half water.   Bare plaster can absorb all the moisture from paint very quickly and just leave a surface layer of pigment that doesn’t adhere well, cracks and flakes off.   That’s why you seal the plaster with a watered down layer.  Use emulsion paint and after the mist coat is dry you will need at least two coats of unwatered paint.

There are soffits which create some sort of ventilation, but I think that just makes the attic really hot in the summer and really cold in the winter, The purpose of the soffits is to allow air to enter and is part of the attic ventilation system. Air needs a path to exit. This is done by either vents in the gables, or along the ridge line of the roof. The air flow helps the hot air escape in the summer, and the moisture to escape in the winter. You do not need to insulate the roof deck. The insulation on the attic floor insulates the conditioned second floor. The HVAC equipment and the supply ducts in the attic unfortunately are subject to very hot and cold temperatures. It is not an ideal situation but it can be made to work. One option is to build an insulated utility room around the equipment. The duct work should be rated at least R6 and preferably R8 insulation values. HVAC equipment in New Jersey attics is not typically done. Was the house built with the second floor HVAC in the attic, or was it added at a later time?

Yeah, I'm sorry about not catching it during inspection. A decent inspector should have caught it. The tank is a big "Heads-up" and the galvanized service line gives it away completely. A water utility has the responsibility to deliver water at suitable pressure - so the "top of the hill" excuse doesn't fly. The responsibility for the service line varies by utility. You should check with the utility. For some, the meter pit is outside and they are responsible for anything before the meter. For our utility, they are responsible for anything in the right-of-way (which is often several feet into a yard). Horizontal boring can be a thing - especially where there's a hill. They would have to come in under the electrical panel to avoid a 90 degree turn - or they would dig just that part of it to make the turn. Know that they will almost certainly come back with PEX or poly pipe (probably PEX) - meaning that it will not be usable as an electrical ground. You will need to install a ground rod (not difficult, but you need to do it) and bond your electrical stuff to it - including your copper plumbing. Electrical code calls for two grounding electrodes - although old houses often had just one. If you are installing a ground rod anyway, now's the time to make sure there are two grounding electrodes - and your water service will no longer be one of them. Again - if anyone so much as mentions lead pipe - check with the utility regarding federal funds for lead service line replacement. There was $15 billion to fund replacing all of it.

What rooting medium did you use?   Did you do anything to increase humidity?   Is your parent plant strong and growing well? I root The Prince  and don't find it especially hard despite the fact it doesn't have a lot of vigor.    For me  it doesn't work to  make a miniature greenhouse with something like a plastic Pepsi bottle.   In the past I've either rooted them in open air or used a misting system in which tiny emitters  are hooked up to a timer and they come on at regular intervals.   For most of the past 25 years I've rooted them with no additional humidity.   Your climate might be more arid though. Do you use a rooting hormone?   For years I used  something like Rootone but in more recent years I use Hormodin 2 or 3.   I take cuttings all spring and summer and even in fall and winter.   I  used  hard wood prunings just yesterday.    Do you score or scrape  the cuttings lightly at the base for about 1/2" before dipping in rooting hormone?    Do you remove all but the top two or three leaves?   Are the cuttings free of blackspot?   I think cuttings that are about pencil diameter do a little better,  and about 5 or 6"  long.   I bury the cuttings for about 1/2 or  2/3 their length in sand.   Keep  moist,  not too soggy. Where you locate your cuttings matters....too much sun and they'll fry,  too little and they'll rot.    They need at least bright shade,  or dappled light,  or occassional sun.   Not full sun I think unless you have a good misting system.  Malcolm Manners in FL  roots many of them  in lots of sun but has a misting system set up and he likes to keep more leaves than I do. Don't give up!    I have  some varieties  that have been consistently hard to root and all of a sudden one year a lot of them will root.   I think it has to do with how the parent plant is doing and if it is well hydrated at the time the cuttings are taken.    Once you have success your plant will know you  mean business and it'll fall in line.

I switched to compostable garbage bags. I use them in my compost bucket and in my trash can in the kitchen. I don't use any bags in wastebaskets in bedrooms or bathrooms. I can attest that they ARE compostable! Sometimes I put the compost bag inside the garbage bag to carry out to the trash. My cans are near my stand alone garage a ways from the house, so I usually combine trips to the garbage with when I am going to the car to leave home for something. Because I don't want to fish out the bag of compost from the bigger bag of garbage when I'm on my way out, I just put the whole thing in my garbage bin with the intent of separating them some other time. Sometimes it's a few days and the garbage/compostable bin is due to be picked up and I have to fish out the compost bag before I take all to the curb. MANY time, that smaller bag has already begun to disintegrate from the heat and moisture from the compost. I have been buying Target brand and am really happy with them. They are kind of expensive so I only buy them on sale or when Target has a coupon/gift card special.  I think they take a while to decompose in the landfill, but are not permanent plastic waste like plastic bags. Paper bags are not without environmental costs, too. We just always use reusable bags so get no extras at the store.

It's very common for their to be an ample supply of iron (Fe) in the soil and still have a plant with an iron deficiency, and any one or more of several reasons can be at cause. E.g., and as you mentioned, a pH level not too far above 6.5 can limit the availability of Fe. An excess of any one or more of several nutrients - calcium, copper, zinc, and especially phosphorous and manganese - will also limit uptake. So, if you are or have been using a bloom-booster fertilizer you should stop. Bloom booster fertilizers all provide far more phosphorous than your plant could ever use (relative to nitrogen usage). Waterlogged grow media, soil compaction, and root congestion can also limit Fe uptake. That said, it's not a good idea to start reaching for Fe chelates to supplement the iron supply, or any other concoction aimed at supplying only one or two nutrients. Almost always it will prove to be more limiting than remedial. If you check the roots and find them badly congested, you'll need to divide the plant and repot, perhaps into a larger pot. While checking, look for signs of root rot. If you report back with what you find and describe what you've been doing about fertilizing (how often? when last? what product? NPK %s? What you report will allow more informed suggestions aimed at resolution. It might be (if you've kept up on fertilizing) that all you need do is lower the pH of your irrigation water, or, perhaps a change of fertilizer might do the trick. Let's hear what you have to say before we start writing prescriptions. Al

Hmm - that is food for thought, chisue. Here's 1 answer: "Whats The Deal With Organic Honey? As of 2021, honey cannot be certified organic by the USDA. Any honey Certified Organic honey sold in the United States is imported from other countries and certified organic by that country. The imported organic honey is not certified Organic by the United States. The USDA recognizes other countries’ organic certification, so if it’s good enough for the other countries’ government, it’s good enough for the US. Hopefully, you can see the potential problem with this. Especially because most of the organic honey comes from Brazil. And Brazil has had a lot of issues with bribery and fraud in their government. A US beekeeper or company can have non-certified organic, pure honey that is raised organically. But it is nearly impossible to produce organic honey that can qualify for an organic label from the USDA. This applies to all Also, US beekeepers are currently unable to make any organic claims for their own honey. Beekeepers are not allowed to make any organic claims unless the USDA says they can. Is the government going to drop the hammer on the guy at the farmers market saying they have organic raw honey? Probably not, but those are the rules.... How Is Organic Honey Made? Honeybees forage from flowers naturally, and they will go to any flower producing the best nectar. This can be a flower 3 miles from their colony or 30 yards. They want to make the most of their time and energy. Both organic and inorganic flowers are visited by the bees. So it is not possible to get bees to skip inorganic flowers. The only option that beekeepers have to force their bees to visit organic flowers is to place the colony in a location that has 100% organic flowers in the area. Only then is the honey produced from those flowers organic. Organic Honey From A Wild Area A beekeeper can either build their apiary (group of beehives) in a location that does not use any type of synthetic herbicides or pesticides to care for their plants. The beekeepers need to be sure the surrounding 5 miles on all sides of the colonies are free of these synthetic chemicals. This is a large area and difficult to do in the United States, but it can be done in other rural areas of the world. The surrounding 5 miles will need to be free of these chemicals because honey bees will travel up to 5 miles in search of nectar, pollen, and water. A beekeeper cannot control where their bees go once they leave the colony, so it’s important for the beekeeper to know the surrounding area if they are wanting to sell certified organic honey. Migratory Organic Honey The other option for the beekeeper is to move the colony to an area that has an organically certified farm or a farm that does not use any synthetic pesticides or herbicides. Honeybee colonies can be physically moved around and transported on a truck from farm to farm across the country. This is how most of the world’s pollination of fruits and vegetables occurs. The trouble with moving a colony to an organic farm or similar site is the farm may not produce enough nectar or pollen for the bees to eat and survive on year around. When this happens, the colony would need to be transported to another place where they can survive. The beekeeper will need to feed the bees an organically acceptable corn syrup or sugar water feed for the colony to live on. Honey bees bounce from flower to flower, pulling nectar and collecting pollen from each flower. Day in and day out, they forage for these ingredients, To move the colony to the farm, the beekeeper would need to prepare the equipment for the bees to store the honey in. These are called supers or honey boxes by beekeepers. Once the colony is moved to the organic farm, the beekeeper would place these empty boxes on the colony for the bees to store their honey. As soon as the bees cannot store additional honey in the boxes because the nectar has stopped, the beekeeper would then remove the full honey boxes and harvest them. By doing it this way, the beekeeper would know the honey in those boxes came from that farm, and they cannot be contaminated by another source of nectar that may not be organic. This is actually how varietals of honey is made. If a beekeeper wants to make Tupelo Honey or Fireweed Honey, the beekeeper will move the colonies to where those plants are about to bloom. Then once the source of nectar they are targeting for honey stops blooming, the boxes are harvested...." https://blog.foxhoundbeecompany.com/the-truth-about-organic-honey/

Absolutely not RRD. It seems folks new to roses really worry about RRD but they shouldn't. This is exactly what new growth is supposed to look like and you'll get used to it after you've been doing it awhile. New growth is often very red, thorns are initially crowded but stretch out along the cane as it grows. The spots you see also look normal to me. I think it will green up more as the season progresses. And some roses are very thorny anyway and it's still not RRD. (If I remember correctly, RRD thorns are often soft/flexible as well.) RRD is very weird when you see it. It's not just red new growth, it's jam packed. The new growth doesn't usually elongate like regular new growth does. The thorns are jam packed and stay that way. Leaf shape doesn't often develop and they stay thin/narrow. They grow with a thick mass of stems all packed together. There are so many things to RRD but I don't see any of it here--just healthy new growth. Enjoy Don Juan--a terrific rose!

Can I lay wood laminate floors over old tiles? Hi Ann, thanks for your question and yes you can. Because no "transfer" happens (where the tile pattern shows through the new floor) with laminate floors, it can be ideal to go over tiles. Things to consider though is 1) the tiles need to be level and no more than +/-3mm up and down over 3 metres, plus free from any bumps or lumps (as in physical textured highlights that stand "up" too much in the tiles) then 2) the added thickness. Generally decent laminate will start at 8mm and will usually go on a 2mm underlay, with the popular ranges now being 12mm that also sit on a 2mm underlay, meaning your new floor height will jump up between 10mm and 14mm. This could impact how the new floor intersects with existing carpet, existing doors, front and back entries and of course fridge cavities, dishwasher spaces etc. Do I need to screed over exiting an existing slabs before laying glued down vinyl planks? Hi blgreader, thanks for that and the answer is technically no, it is not required as a standard that must be done every time. However, vinyl planks, just like any floor, will perform better when the subfloor is level. In the case of LVT, there is also the consideration of needing to glue them down, which requires the floor to not just be level (see above for that definition), but also clean and dry and able to receive the adhesive. Because of this, it is common for vinyl installers to want to apply a skim coat which can assist in both cases, and in more severe cases, a levelling compound which will also renew the subfloor and allow the successful installation and longevity of the new LVT installation. Make sure your LVT is being hardset and not being glued with pressure sensitive adhesive. Moisture in your concrete slab is important to measure and manage, as it can break down the adhesive holding your LVT product in. Make sure you discuss moisture content of your subfloor with your chosen installer and mitigate that risk by assessing the MC. If you download the installation instructions of your chosen product from the manufacturers website, you can see what their guidelines are and then discuss this with your chosen installer to ensure a compliant and long lasting installation.

Greek Villa and Pure White are an ideal white-on-white pairing. Because: 1. They're similar in hue family, they sit near each other in color space in the 102 to 107 range. They are literally related to each other in terms of hue. Color harmony is about threads of relationship between/among colors. Hue is the easiest dimension of color to thread. E.g. Greek Villa and Pure White. 2. In addition to the hue family thread of relationship, they're also similar in Value - another color harmony thread. 3. Most significant is there's a generous difference in Chroma. That means contrast so you can tell they are two different colors and neither will make the other look dirty of dingy. There is no logical, reasonable or technical reason not to use the two together. If you like it, think they look pretty together, then do it.

Your plan may not be correct.  The number of Jack studs may need to be increased to 2 on each side of the header.  And a 10" header is more than you need. More information is required to determine what is required.  The building span must be known and the ground snow load requirements for your area.  I would also like to know if you're just using one 2x10 or two 2x10's in your header. You could easily use just two  2x4 headers with one jack stud up to a 36 foot building width if your snow load was 30 PSf or less for the length you're spanning. Or just one 2x6 header with 2 jack studs up to a 36 foot width and snow load of 30.  This method of using just one header member allows 2" of insulation in the header space and a method I prefer. Use this header sizing chart to determine what you actually need.  But bottom line your present selection for a header is way oversized and the number of jack studs may need to be increased, and both depend on building width and snow.

text: I'll tell you exactly what they're like. Two years in a row we had brief temps below 10F in the winter. HIGHLY unusual, but as I noted in a recent post, USDA zones are for general guidance only. Can't depend on them absolutely for any given year. That's why you always buy perennials (trees, shrubs, at least) that can endure a few zones below what you're in. But almost every year we get temps down to 25F. As you should know, USDA zone 9 is rated for 20-25F winter temperatures. That's a hard freeze. In all cases (and I've been growing alliums for almost a decade) they come out of it happy with no protection. Well at 10K they sort of flop, but then pick back up when the weather gets warmer. These hard freezes typically happen in January, and we put in the alliums in November. I think what can hurt alliums is extended periods of hard freeze. Dixondale says explicitly that onion seedlings should be fine down to 20F. There are some varietal differences. Garlic is a rock. Almost impossible to kill garlic with low temps.

Tim, I've built my own trusses before, and as I remember all roof trusses were stick built by hand and those homes are still standing that people live in today.  I wouldn't do it today because it's a lot of work, savings are minimal if your time has value, and I can get a 20' common truss from Menard's for only $75 each with spec drawings that will meet code and satisfy the building inspector. If you must build your own trusses don't degrade yourself assuming only a carpenter can do it because most of today's carpenters wouldn't have a clue how to do it either, and all they do now is build from drawings and leave the engineering up to others.  I'm not one either but what I did was copy existing trusses using my tape measure to get the number and locations of the webs between the top and bottom cords. First learn the components of a truss (easy easy) and find a truss already built and copy it.  for nail plates use 5 or 7 layer plywood (not the 3 ply!)and a  FULL 1/2" thick or better and a lots of nails.  The plywood needs to cover much more surface area than those little metal nail plates (about 4 times as much) and you should use  4 or 5 penny galvanized ring shank nails, one or more for every  1 sq. in. If you can't find a truss to copy  go to Menard's web site and find the truss department to use their design software.  Give your zip code, which will build to your code, and then pick "common in stock trusses".  Click "continue to pre-built section" and select your desired length and pitch and  click "print spec sheet".  You will get a detailed drawing  showing where the webs are located and all measurements.  you can easily copy from these prints.  You can also click "built-to-order" and pick from any of the truss families and then fill in the data for what you want and even look at a 3D visualization, but you won't get a spec sheet drawing until you get a quote and by the item.  Using this option you will get a picture without measurements, using a flat ruler or a triangular scale ruler you can measure a known length to calculate a scale and using a little math you can figure out the measurements for web placements. Back to me, my trusses were always safe because I copied trusses engineered to be safe but even beefed them up and was overkill.  (just the way I am.)   Even today I'll order trusses beefed up to exceed code because I want minimal deflection and not just the minimum code.  My present garage is 30' x 40' and free span with  trusses built by the original owner.  I can, and have hung 8 cylinder truck engines from just one truss in the center, and using a laser from wall to wall I measured deflection.  It was 1/2" and 3 times less then maximum deflection allowed by code for live load using Length divided by 240 (L/240).  The guy built some stout trusses, and the reason I did this it make sure I wasn't overloading the truss or would of needed to spread out the load to multiple trusses. Most people here have never built a truss, couldn't tell what a draftsmen table or slide ruler is if it was sitting in front of them, and brainwashed to be afraid and helpless so don't let them bother you.  I wouldn't recommend you build you own but it's your choice I will not attempt to change.  .

Baby’s Breath + Chantilly Lace both belong to the Green-Yellow Hue Family. Only where lighting is imbalanced and peaks in the blue/violet area of the spectrum, are you likely to see either render with a note of blueishness. Neither are blue, nor do they have blue ‘undertones’. Where they appear that way its a phenomenon of lighting + context. Next to the lighter Chantilly Lace, Baby’s Breath is likely to appear a very light grey, in relative well balanced light. The combination doesn’t meet a minimum difference in Munsell chroma, (degree of colour) between two whites of at least 0.2. So Baby’s Breath has the capacity to appear a little dirty alongside Chantilly Lace. If you are determined to go ahead, I would view them carefully against each wall. For a more clean, crisp difference between the two? Choose a companion white with more chroma. e.g. PPG Delicate White + BM Snowfall White.  Both of these will meet that minimum difference of 0.2 chroma alongside BM Baby’s Breath. Alternatively, Baby Baby’s Breath in different sheens for wall and trim will offer a more gentle contrast.

Whites and you have a lot of choices. My favorite blue/purple annuals are "Mystic Spires" salvia, "Blue Planet" or "Blue Horizon" tall ageratum, and heliotrope. There's also "Black and Blue" salvia and similar cultivars, which are shrubbier forms of salvia. The only ones of these I start from seed is the ageratum.  I take cuttings of salvia and heliotrope for mother plants the following season.  You can get "Big Blue" salvia from seed which is similar to "Mystic Spires" and pretty easy to grow. It's a low-grower and covers itself in small purple flowers -- makes a nice low filler or ground cover.  you can get those seeds from Hazzard's (go to their home gardener site for small packets). 2.5 feet is not too much. It gives a landing space before entering the house. It could be even wider. I suggest that if possible make that step as low as possible. I had our path slanted slightly so that the step up is 4inches. This  makes it easier for the less nimble and also for rolators or other assistive devices.

Steps should be designed based upon a comfortable human stride as the steps are ascended or descended.  The size of the tread and riser should allow someone to travel the steps without a stutter in their stride or have to take half steps or stretch their step to negotiate stairs. There is a formula that can be used to determine the treat/riser ratio, but I have not used it in years.  There is also a graph in the seventh edition of the Architectural Graphic Standards where the proper size tread and riser can be determined.

It looks like this step would lead up to a covered porch, which then leads to your front door.   Given the amount of walkway room you have,  if possible,  I would not do a step at all.  Instead,  make it a gradual ramp up to the floor elevation of your covered porch.  This reduces the risk of someone tripping. What is the front elevation?  I'm not sure why you're considering putting windows in the side of the garage and removing brick.  You shouldn't add windows without reference to the existing windows.  New windows should be similar in size and proportion to existing or else the house will have a split personality.  You also need to think about how the windows are going to affect the interior of the rooms where they're added.  If the rooms are small it can be a good idea to have shorter windows so you don't lose valuable wall space for placing furniture. Builders just do whatever you tell them to do.  In general they won't consider much how something will look or function.  They are always thinking about how much something will cost.  I suggest you consult an architect for perspective drawings so you know what you'll end up with, and so you will have something to submit for a permit.  It's smart to spend your money on a solution that will be attractive and functional. What is driving your decision?  Is this a house in a lovely neighborhood where you want to stay and be more comfortable for years to come?

I make deviled crab that would be good with artichokes added to it.  Here's the deviled crab recipe I created: Deviled Crab Have all the ingredients ready-mince the onion and celery and set aside together; mince the herbs and peppers separately and set aside. If you are using crab in its shell, remove all the meat first and then put it in a small bowl. Add the optional crab or lobster soup base, if desired. If you can get lobster base, this will improve the flavor the most, but crab or clam base is fine. Adjust the quantity depending on the saltiness of the base. In a medium or large saucepan, melt 3 tbsp butter and add 2 tbsp olive oil. Add the onion and celery and saute for about 3 minutes, or until the onion is all broken up and separated. Add the Serrano peppers and cook another 2-3 minutes. Then add the flour and continue to cook to make a light roux, stirring constantly. Add the herbs and stir to combine. Add the water with soup base (or clam juice), and stir to make a paste and remove from heat. Add the mustard, lemon juice, cayenne, and pepper, and allow to cool slightly. Pour a small amount of the paste into the beaten egg and combine before adding the egg to the paste. Add the crabmeat and stir to combine. Lightly grease a 9"x6"x2" baking dish (or individual ramekins or muffin pan) with olive oil, and add the mixture, leaving about 1/2" space from the top of the pan. Press the breadcrumbs into the top and dot with butter (or drizzle the butter melted) evenly over the top. Broil for 5-7 minutes not too close to the heat or bake at 425° for 6-8 minutes, or until the breadcrumbs are crispy. Serves four as a main course or six as an appetizer. This is not a fritter recipe, but you could probably add chopped artichoke hearts to it and then fry it as you would hush puppies, but you would need to add the bread crumbs to the mixture instead of using them for a topping and increase the quantity.  The butter would not be needed, since you would be frying it. Alternatively, you could just add the chopped artichoke to the recipe and broil it instead of frying it.

Silvics manual says: Balsam fir has been reported as growing on soils of a wide range of acidity. In the northern Lake States it is most common on cool, wet-mesic sites with pH values between 5.1 to 6.0 (19). Optimum growth occurs on soils where the pH of the upper organic layers is between 6.5 and 7.0 (1). On gravelly sands and in peat swamps, growth is comparatively slow (41).

Yes, some Balsam fir do tolerate some wet soils.  But it may largely depend on what under stock the tree is grafted on.  Also it greatly depends on if phytophtora root rot is or will be present in the wet soil that it will be planted in. Generally I would advise against planting any valuable true fir cultivar in “wet soil”.  If you wanted to try it maybe go with a few cheaper straight species Balsam fir and see how they do.  I would just hate to see an expensive purchase end up getting root rot especially if you are unsure of what it’s grafted on.  Canaan fir, which is a subspecies of Balsam that grows in damp conditions in the Canaan Valley in West Virginia, may be the best choice as an understock for those conditions.

There are contradictory things said online about whether chickweed fixes nitrogen in the soil.   Some say it fixes other things in the soil too.   Some say it makes a good mulch...helps conserve moisture.   I  am not sure whether to believe it does that or  removes moisture.   It does certainly add shade to the soil.    I  find that taking a weedeater to it usually eliminates it  .   It  sprouts and grows when it's cooler here.  Once  gone,  it tends not to come back till cooler weather. Ann of TN  uses it to protect emerging basals  during cold snaps in spring.    It is not a bad looking weed..it's soft looking and green but I find I usually  don't want a lot of it in my rose beds. Could be due to the ORG- overflow relief gully being installed to high and allowing the stormwater to drain into the sewer system and the 100mm house service not coping with the influx of water. Other things to look at are - blockages in the sewer system affecting discharge flow. - back flow from the mains sewer service pushing up into your property and discharging out the next lowest point- usually the shower if the ORG has been installed incorrectly or is capped To fix check overflow heights- The ORG should be installed so it sits at least 150 mm lower than the lowest fixture in the house. For example, your shower or toilet. It also needs to be least 75 mm above the ground to prevent stormwater flowing into your ORG. Also camera the sewer and stormy service. Consider installing a reflux valve in the sewer service. Camera cost to get checked usually $250, any decent local plumber will be able to locate fault fairly quickly.

There are species that are on endangered list of some states, and those plants should not be sold across state lines. In practice there is no enforcement of this for cultivated plants. Some states (Arizona) are more strict.  Some states make growing their endangered plants by a (mere) hobbyist almost impossible. Check with your state authority. That's the exact reason for putting them in the vault. Smoke rises and it doesn't ring the alarm until it's a certain density, so it won't ring one mounted lower if the smoke and heat are all up in the vault. As the vaulted area fills,  it eventually fills enough to get down to a lower level alarm.  It probably won't ring the alarm on the way up to the vault because it won't be dense enough. As it gathers in the vault, the density of the smoke increases enough to ring the alarm. If you wait for it to fill and reach the lower alarm, it might be too late.

Will you have plug mold as well, or just wall outlets? The bottom edge of our sideways wall outlets is about 1/2" above the countertop. It's great--the countertop appliances completely cover the outlets. But we also have plugmold over the cabinets, for an easy place to plug in the once-in-awhile items. A good height for horizontal receptacles in the backsplash is 4" on center from the counter.  That is low enough to be hidden by coffee maker, toaster, paper towel holder, etc. but still high enough so that a thick plug (like for a toaster or blender) will have enough clearance from the counter to be able to plug in. Edited to add: some local Building Codes will have a stipulation for the minimum height of the outlet from the counter.  But most are silent on this measurement.  The local Codes that do have a stipulation almost always require minimum 4" on center from the counter for the reason I mentioned.  Building Codes do not want a chance for a plug not to be plugged in all the way or plugged in a bit crooked if the receptacle does not have enough clearance to the counter.

I'm in zone 8b Oregon.  The first Lepidote (they're earlier) 'Bob's Blue' started March 16 and I imagine the Elpidotes will continue until mid May or so. They're in sun from about 11am until sundown. I like Bobs Blue a lot.  The flower color isn't nearly as saturated as Blue Baron, but it blooms heavily.  All of these Lepidotes have non-green foliage in winter, and I noticed this winter that Bob's Blue has the most attractive winter foliage color of all of them, a hard to describe dark, glistening purplish-bronze. Blocking higher frequency sounds is relatively easy, blocking low frequency sounds, not so much. Unfortunately, as you already suggested in your post, road noise is low frequency noise. I would be very curious to know what the acoustical engineer told you about your walls, ceiling, attic, foundation, etc. before he offered you the 51db acoustical window inserts. I would also be even more curious to know exactly how the inserts were constructed to achieve a 51db performance rating. Considering just your windows for the moment and ignoring other possible contributing factors, a fixed window in general is going to offer significantly better acoustic performance than a window that can open and close simply because the fixed window is going to be air tight and almost all operators are not. One possible exception would be a European style tilt/turn window, but also possible to get very high quality casement or awning that close tight. Any window that sides. vertical or horizontal is very unlikely to meet your sound blocking requirements. To get an STC into the 40's you will probably be looking at (as mentioned) a high level of air tightness, thicker glass/offset glass, wide airspace between lites (1" minimum), possibly triple pane (assuming a total airspace combined over 1" minimum), and/or laminated glass. More reasons why I am curious about the 51db insert that you were offered. Simply for comparison here are a few examples of glass make ups that achieve an ATC value greater than 40db:  actual measured values, not simulated or calculated.                                                                   numbers in yellow indicate laminated glass.                                                                                     widths in salmon indicate the most realistic IG thicknesses Depending where you are can make a difference in what's available, so that would be helpful to start. Ultimately this is a comparison of a few possible glass packages with the one's in salmon are probably the best options on my list, but not only possibilities when looking for a window company to meet your requirements. Best bet to start would be to work with a company that offers a wider glazing channel for triple pane and/or hurricane impact products. Again could be location dependent. Once again keep in mind that this only addresses your windows and not other possible contributors to your noise problem, but at least a place to start.

Leaning towards a brown look, To pull that off you have to know what hue family the black windows and black garage doors belong to. Because the paint colors have to be spot on in terms of harmony with the black(s). All colors of black belong to a hue family. Those are top flange joist hangers (very old). When building, they would tack in the joists into the beam. Then later add the joist hangers. The "tacking" in apparently is enough to hold, and has lasted this long. The gap at bottom is both from notching the top so the floor fit flush, and from wood shrinkage. There is no problem here and no structural engineer is needed. If you'd like, you can add some wood shims in the seat to get touching. FWIW your floor joists frame flush into a built-up beam. A girder is a big beam that smaller beams frame into.

3onthetree thanks. However the floor above this is sagging noticeably. So can we jack this up? Also, the first of the four beams of this built up beam is now lower by 1/4” than the other 3 beams adjacent. The floor joists attached to this first beam are also sagging below the beam. Finally, how would Sheetrock work here with each of these straps 1/2” below the ceiling? Would prefer not to fur down entire ceiling. Can these be easily replaced with modern ticos?

The joist hangers have nothing to do with the sagging. The floor joists and beam may be overspanned. There is also a set amount of deflection (sag) that the members will have over a given span. There could be notches or cuts that previous plumbing caused failing members. You can jack up to fix it, but there needs to be a plan to keep it jacked up, like a column, wall, or sistering the joists or beam. For this you may want an engineer's input. For the 1 ply being 1/4" lower than the other 3 in the built-up beam, that could just be construction tolerance. Long nominal lumber has a crown to it, and it could have been upside down. If the plies are fastened together correctly, 1 ply wouldn't sag more than the others. For the drywall ceiling, you can notch out the backside of drywall for protrusions if it is thin enough. Or shim/strap the entire ceiling. Or if focusing on sound mitigation, 2 layers of drywall. Or change the hangers out to face mount (which all hangers will use hanger nails or "ticos").

The hangers only attach the joists to the beam for a solid connection. If that beam is sagged, it doesn't matter about the hangers, the joists will follow that sag. And if the joists are also sagged, the hangers cannot fix that. If you can't remove 2 rows of plank flooring above the beam to access the top flange of the hangers, you can surely try to beat up the bottoms with a sledgehammer. I don't expect it to do much. The time I spent doing family history research was precious because I got to spend hours and hours with my mom and her two sisters learning hearing stories of their childhood that I may have never otherwise heard, but I also remember the day my mom said "This is nuts - why are we spending time with the dead when we should be living." When I returned to California after my dad passed away I had a business license that was over due for renewal.   I drove to Carlsbad to renew the license and the lady who did renewals was out to lunch.   It was 30 minutes to my house, so I decided to go to the library next door while I waited for her return.   I went into the library and sat on a sofa in the entry and picked up a book on the coffee table.   The book was on the founding families of Colorado and there was an entire section about my dad's family.   By that night I had made several calls and got a return call from my dad's uncle.   I found out that my dad's dad hadn't abandoned his son, my grandmother had left, changed my dad's name and he had spent his entire life looking for my dad.  Even in his will he left instructions to try to find his son and he left much of his estate to my dad. Garden Mist, I'm going to jump in here again, with a few general pointers that may help.  Your plant looks healthy and growing well, so lets talk about some other things that will make it a more attractive house guest for you.  Hopefully you have taken James suggestion and not cut the bloom spike off yet.  let's talk about that a bit.  Bloom spikes when left alone after blooming usually turn brown and die back from the tip, farthest from the plant.  Unsightly!  Look at the flower spikes on your plant, The tip, out where the blooms were may already be turning brown, but close inspection will show that there is a scar on the stem where each bloom was attached.  The section where the blooms were will never do anything but die, so it can be cut off at any time.  Look at the bloom spike and notice, as you come down the spike toward the plant, the bloom scars will stop where the first flower was, and the bloom spike will begin to have joints.  At each joint there will be a little bump covered by a flap of plant tissue. That little bump is a growth node, and there are usually 1 to perhaps 4 of these.  If you cut the stem below (closest to the plant) the last bloom scar, and about an inch above the first growth node, you will may encourage one of the nodes on the spike to come to life, and produce a branch to the flower spike that will #1 bloom, or #2 produce a Keiki, or baby plant that is an exact genetic copy of mama, or #3 just go ahead and die.  Those choices are strictly up to the plant, it's genetic, you won't have much to say about the choice.  Remember, always cut with razor sharp tools that are clean and sterile.  Cut bloom spikes at an angle, do not crush--no scissors, or shears.  Now, your plant looks a bit nicer, no ragged dying tip on the bloom spike, and perhaps a new growth to brag about.  Have fun.
